content: Okay does anybody have any questions? Yeah. What makes something expensive?

Expensive expensive. Uh one is the energy content. Okay, expensive is also a relative thing. I mean, you know, for some people a five hundred watch is expensive. I mean you can buy a watch for ten dollars right. Um, you can buy a watch you know, and I wear Seiko for, I get for one fifty at Costco okay. Um, you can buy one for five hundred at Costco and they might consider that an expensive watch. You can start putting diamonds on it and okay, and then you can start having a name which has no functional value, uh it's all pride, and that could cost fifty thousand dollars.

So at the lower end of the material scale, when we're talking about steel and aluminum and copper, it's the energy content. We talked about that. I mean, I said you know it used to be labor and then materials, but today it's materials and energy. A little, the labor cost has sort of gone out of these things okay, in the last fifty years. I mean this is, you're seeing a revolution right now that's equal to the industrial revolution of 150 years ago, okay, in manufacturing productivity okay. I'm going to put up a slide today that 1990 steel was one hour per ton, uh one person hour per ton. Well today it's 0.3, you know. So in twenty-five years it's, you know, it's improved by a factor of three.

But then, we've talked about, so energy cost is one thing. Once you get there, now if you want to go to the really high value added materials, fancy composites and stuff, it's all processing. I mean I kind of said well, you know, for a pipeline thirty percent of the cost of a pipeline is the metal that goes into it, and the rest of us digging the hole in the ground, the inspection, and you know right-of-ways and things like that. For an automobile it's ninety percent is the processing, cause it's a more complex product. If you go to an aircraft or a spacecraft or something, you're getting to the point where ninety-eight, ninety-nine percent of the cost is all the processing and manufacturing, machining and joining and inspection and everything else.

So you really have to talk about the market you're in. Are you down here in the twenty, the ships and automobiles, where we're talking about less than two dollars a pound fabricated okay. Are we talking about the twenty thousand dollar a pound spacecraft okay. That's kind of where it's going with the watches. I mean you can have fifty thousand dollar watches, you can have ten dollar watches. So what makes something expensive in different industries really depends on which industry. The lower end industries is mostly energy today. The higher end it's all engineering design, you know marketing.

I mean what makes beer expensive? It's all the ads on TV and other places. I mean when I worked in, my first big consulting job was in a brewery in upstate New York, and at that time it cost them as I remember thirteen cents a gallon to make beer. But they were never selling it even in 1975 for thirteen cents a gallon. There's a big markup okay. I don't know, today beer might cost fifty or sixty cents a gallon to make but they get a big markup because there's an awful lot of advertising in that.

I'll give you, oops did I, maybe I didn't, maybe I put them back somewhere else, I had my scissors here. I showed down here there. So here are my surgical scissors okay. What makes these expensive? Well, they're just stainless steel scissors and you could buy stainless steel scissors for twenty bucks. Twenty-five years ago these cost three hundred, they probably seven or eight hundred now. Why? Because you're buying about five hundred worth of health, and not health insurance, medical malpractice insurance along with them. The big cost is medical math, the application it goes into.

So again, the answer is, it depends on the industry. Other questions? That answer your question? There is no simple answer okay. Any other questions? Okay. 
 §2 — Chaparral Steel and the productivity revolution

We were talking, well let's just talk about, so last time the theme was productivity is nearly everything if you want to live well in a nation. Um, in the steel industry, the productivity since the time of Henry Bessemer has all been in melting and casting technology, and we've had tremendous growth over the last 170 years in that. And I was giving you some examples of Chaparral Steel, and here's an example. Let's see if that's, not what I wanted to do. Uh, let's see if I can, I don't want to hit exit because it's liable to kill me, okay fine. Um, okay so here's the ingot that comes off the continuous caster at Chaparral Steel back in the, I don't know time frame of 1995, or maybe early 90s they used to get a rectangular ingot, but then they changed their molds and they would get something that starts to begin to look like an I-beam okay, within about five years.

And actually here's just another picture of a bunch of them. They cut them to length here. Here's a strand coming off the continuous caster, in the background is to just have been cut. Within about five years they perfected that some. Let's see if we can get, this one's pretty dark, uh, yeah for you, um, get the right angle, oh here we go okay. Here's a little bit, I'm gonna have, Gordon Forward gave me these about twenty years ago.  [Tom shows a continuous-cast near-net-shape section.]  Here's the continuous cast part. Now it actually does look like an I-beam right, you can see the end of it there, okay.

And someone says well is the quality, is good. Well it turns out, and these are slides from almost or fifteen years ago, Chaparral Steel, when we were doing the evaluation of them, 1990 one person hours per ton. Net shape casting of structural beams drove down the cost by one-third. As Gordon Forward used to say, he didn't care if the, the Japanese or the Koreans or the Chinese were paying their employees nothing, okay, that everybody said so it's low cut, the advantage of low-cost labor. He says it costs about fifty dollars a ton to ship the product across the ocean, and he was here in the market. The United States is sort of the world's market, everybody wants to dump their product in the United States because we consume so much of everything. So he said if he could make his steel within fifty dollars, okay, excluding labor, of the pri— of the cost that they were making it — and it's raw materials and energy cost — then he could beat them in the marketplace, no matter if they even if they paid people nothing. So if he could drive his costs down, well he drove the cost down by a third, and um by going net shape manufacturing.

It turns out, there's been a competition, I talked about plastic water bottles and you know aluminum bottles cans and things like that. Well there's a competition between steel and concrete. I mean concrete still has steel in it. Here's a reinforcing bar if you want to pass it around, it's galvanized but anyway.  [Tom passes a galvanized reinforcing bar.]  I do have, did have one in my office, we talked about reinforcing bar, and you know they were going slower to roll four times as much, which you know if you went half the speed but you rolled four strands rather than one then you just doubled your productivity on the rolling mill okay. Well, concrete and steel compete for buildings. If you go around the country and look at parking garages as the example I like to give, you can look at parking garages and see if they're made out of steel or if they're made out of concrete. And if you know anything about the relative cost at different points in time of reinforced concrete structures versus steel frame structures, you can almost pinpoint within about a one decade period when that parking garage was built, just on straight economics of which one was more competitive at the time, okay.

I talked about four stand rebar rolling. They had a new facility, is going to drop things, this is like a 1995 slide, and they had $450,000 sales per employee, okay. Well what does that mean? Um well that's one of the metrics that I used to use twenty years ago. If you look at manufacturing companies, you'll find that most of them today have sales per employee in the hundred and fifty to two hundred thousand dollar per year range. If you think about it, you'd better sell two hundred thousand dollars worth of product in order to pay employees a hundred thousand dollars a year, because with overhead and everything else it's 130 and that only leaves you seventy thousand dollars to buy the materials and other stuff. So um, to me, when I would look at a company I would just, if I looked at a balance sheet I would say okay what are their gross sales, divide by the number of employees, see what the sales are per employee. Back when this slide was, when I made this slide, typical value was like a hundred thousand dollars an employee. And uh, you know so $450,000 per employee of sales is pretty good. I mean you're way out there in the bell curve and you can be profitable at that rate. 
 §3 — The Boeing door anecdote

Well it turns out, I had a student back in the 90s working at Boeing at the door product center okay, is where, it's a completely deterministic manufacturing business. Takes three years to deliver an airplane from laying the keel beam to flying it away. And it turns out that uh, the door product center, it takes about one year to produce the doors that go in the fuselage. You know you walk through the door when you get on an airplane right. And it turns out they know exactly how many doors they have to produce, because they know they got these airplanes up in the Everett facility or wherever, that are being, the fuselages are being built, and they know how many doors and there's exit doors, there's cargo doors. So you have doors that are not much bigger than someone to crawl through, you have a door someone can walk through, and you have things they can take pallets and you know like a double garage door or something, in big 747s and stuff. So there's all kinds of doors, but they have a door product center uh in south of Seattle, I think it's in Tacoma, whatever wherever it is.

And so I asked him, I said, uh I was getting the tour of the plant and I said well how much does a door cost? The guy said I don't know because it's all internal sales okay. I mean they only sell to Boeing right, at the door product center, and they know exactly how many they have to sell uh that year, make that year. And I said well how many employees you have? He said 750. I said let's see if I get this right, he says 200, yeah 750 employees. I said how many doors do you make a year? He says about 250. I said oh well, did I get this right? Yeah, I said then your average door costs about fifty thousand dollars, because at that time I was fighting Boeing's a little bit better, maybe $150,000 sales per employee okay.

And he said well I don't know if that's true or not. So a little bit later I asked his boss, and his boss, and I told him how I estimated about fifty thousand dollars a door. So that door you walk through is about a fifty thousand dollar door. Now today it's probably a hundred thousand because that was almost twenty years ago, but nonetheless, that, you know, that's one way to estimate things on a very high level, it's actually pretty accurate. His boss actually says yeah well that's probably about right, but they didn't even know. I mean the accountants hadn't figured out for them what it cost to make a door. But I can tell you, they had to put a drill by hand for every rivet hole in that door, uh, mechanic, and these mechanics are making about forty or fifty bucks an hour at Boeing okay, actually today they're probably making sixty or seventy. And with the Boeing overhead that means like 150 bucks an hour you know for their cost and stuff. A mechanic has to take a drill and put it through that hole about four times. You have to rough drill the hole, you have to size the hole, you have to ream the hole, and there were, I can't remember all the things they had to do, but for every hole they had to put a different drill through about four times. And there's lots of rivets on the door. So you start looking at this and you find, so what's expensive? Well, I think you know compared to my door or my home, that's an expensive door, but there's a lot more labor goes in that aircraft door okay. 
 §4 — Hydrogen cracking demo and Chaparral rolled beams

This is another thing we can pass around. I talked about transformation of steel to martensite, austenitic steel to martensite. This is a fiber wear part, one of the other lectures that's on online, you can, I'll tell the whole story but you can feel by taking this neodymium magnet, almost non-magnetic down here, and you get up to the top it gets very magnetic. It's got cracks in it, these are hydrogen cracks because it transformed to the type of steel that's susceptible to hydrogen cracking.  [Tom hands around a fiber-wear part with a neodymium magnet.]  Okay, so that's four strand rebar rolling out and stuff.

The other slide that goes to Chaparral rolled steel beams. They had 41 percent imports to the U.S. prior to their new mill in the mid-90s. Currently at that time Chaparral, there were, they dropped the imports to the United States to zero, because they could beat them in the marketplace, and they exported twenty percent of the product outside North America. So the new wide flange mill, because you're starting out with the net shape casting, 75 percent energy savings. In-line reheat — it comes out, it used to be in the steel mills you know they'd have this continuous caster and you'd have this red hot band of steel that you take an oxygen jet and you flame cut it with pure oxygen, uh because it's already hot enough to oxidize, and then you let it sit down in there and cool. Well people said that's silly to let all that waste energy, so they basically now have things that goes directly from the casting machine into a reheat furnace to get it uniform in temperature, and then it goes directly into the rolling mill. So there's not standing aside and reheating. So twenty-eight minutes total. I mean the processing time goes from days down to twenty-eight minutes.

You end up because you're doing all this stuff faster and whatnot, and essentially you can do it at lower temperature, or you can roll at lower temp, the steel at lower temperatures, you get finer grain. All chill casts, higher tensile and toughness. And it turns out if you look at the, if you're a civil engineer, they used to make most of, steel bridges and buildings and stuff was 36 ksi yield, A36 steel. A higher grade was 50 ksi. Turns out with the fine grain size and the good toughness — because grains fine grain size gives you both strength and toughness — they were actually rolling compositions that was a 36 composition but they get 50 ksi yield. And so they didn't have to inventory the product. By 1995 or 1998, you order A36 from Chaparral they'd ship you out of this pile. You order 50 ksi they'd ship you out of the same pile. Had both of them, had equivalent weldability, just as easy to weld as the lower strength A36. But you could get 50 ksi, and if you were smart enough you could order 36 ksi and get 50 ksi for free. Okay they would get 50 ksi as a premium. Actually you couldn't do that because you have to have certifications for the building people and everything else that all meets that, but in fact they got to the point where it was just as easy to make 50 ksi material as it was to make 36 ksi material, and the toughness was off the charts. 
 §5 — Gordon Forward and the Chaparral culture
Student:  Yep, who was the guy that was behind all of this?

Well actually that's another story in and of itself. Gordon Forward was, MIT PhD, went off to work for, he's a Canadian, I think he was working for a Canadian steel company, and one of the big ones, Stelco or Dofasco. And he and other people kind of looked at it, and I told you the story, they, you could buy scrap iron for a hundred dollars a ton but it cost you two hundred dollars a ton to make cast iron. And if you want the electric furnace route as opposed to the basic oxygen furnace to melt your steel, a basic oxygen furnace required 70 virgin iron ore blast for, you know, iron blast furnace type of hot melt. Electric furnace you could take all scrap and you could melt it, but you'd always have impurities, residual elements, and people thought well you could never make anything better than rebar. So back in the early 70s you know people like Bethlehem Steel when I was working for it, you know, that's garbage for a variety of stuff, we don't want that, slow, low premium, low markup.

And then they learned, they, but Gordon Forward and Ken Iverson was the guy who started a company called Nucor [New Core] Steel which became the biggest of the mini mills. And it wasn't just one mill that, we did build new steel mills after Bethlehem Steel's Burns Harbor plant which was built in 1965, but by the 1970s not the steel companies but people like Ken Iverson who started out in a strip mall in Charlotte, North Carolina, okay, to build a steel mill in South Carolina just over the border. And Gordon Forward who found some investors, they built a mini mill in Midlothian, Texas okay, just outside of Dallas. They built mini mills that had one twentieth the capacity. They just had a big electric furnace, and at that time electric furnaces could only melt 50 ton heats. Well those same electric furnaces, they get up to like 165 ton heats, they're almost as big as the BOF you know shops it'll cost you a billion dollars. And these guys were paying you know twenty-five million dollars or fifty million dollars for an electric furnace shop, and they just kept on, they started water cooling everything and putting in bigger transformers, and just, they could melt steel just almost as fast as the big guys in their billion dollar facility, but they were doing it with a 50 or 100 million dollar facility okay. Tremendous capital gain savings or capital cost savings.

But they also had a different uh philosophy. I wouldn't plan on spending this much time on steel, um, Steve Wheelwright and I went down there and we were doing this evaluation of why good product development and bad product development at different companies, and we were doing Chaparral and they had some failures, I won't go through those, but on the first day of the first day I said well, they're telling us about one of the failures, I said well who gets the blame? And the people acting like what do you mean blame? And I didn't realize until the second day: you don't get blamed if you try something different at Chaparral. You get blamed if you don't try something new okay. So there is blame, but the blame is not for trying something different and failing. It's for not doing something new this year. If you just keep doing the same old thing at Chaparral, you're a loser.

Also, if you go into every one of those shops, on the bulletin board they will have the weekly profit of the company, and it's a profit sharing company. Every employee there could tell you exactly how much money they made the week before, because they posted the weekly profits and they knew how many shares they had okay. So the people had an incentive, and you know they would jury rig things and figure out cheaper way to do things. So it wasn't Gordon Forward, it was the culture that Gordon Forward put forward — I mean put it forward on Gordon Forward — but anyway. At Bethlehem Steel, at the Taj Mahal research labs that we had, they had an executive dining room. I told you about the strawberries the size of, you know, bigger than golf balls that I had never seen in 1975. Yeah you can get them now, but I'd never seen them before. And you weren't allowed in the executive dining room. We had a beautiful dining room looked over the mountain you know and everything, but it wasn't as nice as the executive dining room.

Uh, there's great stories about these Taj Mahal dining rooms. I mean there's a story about Lee Iacocca wanted to know once when he was president of Ford why uh, one of the Ford's, chairman of the company I don't remember which Ford it was at the time, said, he was saying he loved hamburgers, and he said I never get any hamburger as good as the one here at the Ford executive dining room. So Lee Iacocca goes in to see the chef. He says uh, so why are your hamburgers so good? And he says I'll show you. And he goes and he gets a sirloin steak out of the freezer, prime, puts it in the grinder and said here. So hey, Henry Ford can afford it anyway.

So at Chaparral, the executive diet — as Gordon Forward used to call it — the executive dining room was a folding table, and they would bring in barbecue and we ate with plastic knives and forks out of foam containers. That was the executive dining room at Chaparral. As opposed to Bethlehem or Ford Motor Company or Kodak or all these other places where they treated the managers like royalty. At Chaparral everyone was equal. If you go back and read my leadership management education article at MIT, there's actually that same theme in there okay, about, you know, leadership is treating people equally, and my little sound bite is leaders seek to help others, manage or seek to control others.

So Bethlehem Steel they just wanted to control others. I mean at Bethlehem Steel they had, we had a manual that thick that told me who I could write a letter to within the company okay. I could like write one la— one level up or one level down within my own research organization, or I could write at the same level to some person in another organization at Bethlehem Steel, but the manual was that thick on who I could write a letter to okay. And they had rules about who could have carpeting on the floor, who could have drapes on the windows. So one of my colleagues in his office was looking at x-rays, and he took some black cloth and he covered up the light from the windows. And about a month later some manager came by, saw the cloth on the window, says what gives you the right to have the drapes? Okay, well that's what the managers were worried about, you know, this guy had drapes and he was just an engineer okay. It's a good thing he didn't put a towel to mop up something on the floor, they'd say. Anyway, so this is one of the reasons I work at a university. Not that we don't have the same type of stupid administrative bureaucracy, but with tenure you can thumb your nose at them okay. But you got to get tenure first okay, but I got it so I can anyway.

Okay so that's all on steel. Anybody have any questions? This I didn't plan on going through that but hey, anybody have another question? 
 §6 — Glass as a structural material: bullseye and plate

Okay so what I'd plan on doing today was take another industry and just show you that I'm not negative about everything. I want to talk about glass technology. I haven't told you, I told you all the bad things about glass — it's brittle, it's not a structural material — but in fact it is a structural material, and it has a history. If you go to the web you can read about Sugar [Sleepy] Hollow Glass Company, and they make nice artistic glass. They will actually sell you what's called bullseye glass. Anybody know what bullseye glass is? Yeah that's it right there. What? No you mean the little, this little thing in the corner, that's right. And there's a history of bullseye glass in the United States. Uh, remember taxa— had no taxation without representation type stuff you know, and things the British were trying to tax us.

Well, glass used to be a very labor intensive industry, because they were, the way they made glass at least into the 18th century in England was to, just like we do down the glass lab, you take a blow pipe with just a steel tube, you take some glass out of the furnace and stick it on there and you get it to the right temperature and you blow through the pipe, and you blow up and make a little glass beaker or whatever, you can shape it, you can form it. Eventually you can cut a hole in it and keep on spinning it in the furnace and you can make a disc of glass. And if you make that disc of glass, if you're clever about it — I thought I had a picture, I did have a picture, except that's not the picture — if you're clever about it you can make relatively flat squares, rectangles of glass, not very big. I don't see it right now, I'll come across it later, unless I, anyway.

But at the center of this thing you're going to end up with something that's got all kinds of distortion and stuff. You actually break it off the blowpipe by putting a little, taking a little file, go down there and watch it in the glass lab, you put a little file mark on it and then you kind of hit it quickly and it breaks off, and you end up with a piece of bullseye glass. And people would put this over the lentils [lintels] of the doors okay, and the reason they would do it is cause glass was expensive. People like, didn't have electric lights back in the 18th century, people wanted some light in their house. So over the door they would put glass to let the light in. But bullseye glass didn't have a tax because it was considered scrap. It distorted everything, but what do you care, you just want light to come through, you're not trying to look out the window here. Now looking out the window required one of the pieces of flat glass that was taxed, and people didn't put a lot of windows in their houses because they were drafty and they also cost a lot of money.
Student:  Yep, they cast the [plate?] glass —

I'm going to talk about that. Okay so this is the way they made glass, they just blow it, make a big circle, cut rectangles out of the circle, throw away the center, and so the cheapest stuff was the bullseye glass. However, if you go to — I got things out of order somewhere here — if you go today and you go to Sleepy Hollow Glass, they'll sell you one of these little bullseye things, six inches square, for fifty-five dollars okay, or eight inches square for like ninety dollars. Well that's pretty pricey, but now it's art okay. People put this over there, from the doors of their home still, so they can look like they're an 80 or a 200 year old home or something right. Be careful of the sharp edges, so that's why you keep it up top anyway.

So plate glass manufacturer on the other hand, which is what you were asking about, was invented about 1688 by Abraham Thievart [Thévart], and that became the Saint-Gobain company. Anybody ever heard of Saint-Gobain? Saint-Gobain's got a lot of contacts with us, with this department, in part because uh one of my former doctoral students, Kapoor, was head of their research center here in Northborough, and he started, you know, the MadMec and all this other stuff, they fund those things. But Saint-Gobain in 1688, this guy Abraham Thévart learned to pour glass onto a metal table, spreading it with rollers, annealing, grinding and polishing okay. That was the beginning of Saint-Gobain.

If you want to see a picture, probably from the 19th century, here's a picture of making plate glass. You start with a metal glass— glass, you pour it on a slightly inclined table — that was an invention in the 1800s, to use an incline table — and you, here's your steel roll, and they're going to take this molten stuff and they're just going to roll it out flat okay. The problem is, there are inhomogeneities in the glass, and that type of plate glass, unless you ground it and polished it, and even if you did grind and polish it, was not, still had a lot of distortion okay. And this is a window, an old window in Jena, Germany. And here's a piece of modern glass — and which is not plate glass, it's actually what we call float glass, I'm going to talk about that — and you can see the reflection of a tree in that glass. Here is some of the old plate glass in the rest of this window, and you can sort of see the black outlines of the tree but it's sort of been distorted right okay, in there. But they had, someone broke the glass up here and they had to replace it. 
 §7 — Float glass and the Pilkington process

Steel and glass don't like each other, it'll come off anyway. Plus as it cools down thermal expansion causes them to separate at the interface. But you, it's a problem to try to bond glass to steel — we can do it but we have to put an inner layer like titanium or something reactive in there okay, so far as that goes um.

So in any case, I still haven't found my other slides to some of these things, but continuous ribbon con— production. So plate glass — well plate glass, they would roll it out on these big plates, and a company like, you ever heard of Pittsburgh Plate Glass, PPG okay is what they're called now, they had them, as I'm told or I've read, around the turn of the beginning of the 20th century, in the night or early 1900s, they had a facility in Pittsburgh that was a mile long building. Nice and straight, at one end they would cast the plate glass and they would move it straight, no turning or anything, because glass is brittle, and they would grind it and polish it to where it was fairly smooth. And that's what we call plate glass, and typically might be a half an inch thick or even thicker. We call it plate glass because it's thick, because hey, you roll it out and if you make it too thin you have these great big sheets of it, you're gonna break them. So it tends to be thicker.

So you ever heard of Libbey-Owens-Ford? Okay glass used to have a little LOF on most of the Ford cars. It turns out continuous ribbon production of glass was invented at the Ford Motor Company in 1920, and by 1926 the production was achieved by flowing glass from a tank furnace over a weir. Weir's just a little ceramic brick work, and just like going over a waterfall, this is a controlled waterfall. You just have this thick viscous glass going over the weir, and you pull it over that weir onto a table and let it cool, and then you do the plate glass process. Hey, why did Henry Ford need that? Because he was making lots of windshields for Model T's and Model A's and whatnot. Pilkington Brothers put that into production, and they developed a continuous grinding and polishing process by 1925.

However, I don't know exactly when, but by probably the 1940s, Pilkington developed their own process called the Pilkington process, which is the float glass process. And basically you have a blending and melting furnace — so this is called the batch house — and then the furnace which you melt it. Let me tell you, go through one of these plants, and I have been through a float glass plant in Ohio, uh, and you're walking by this furnace at 1550 C that's about half the size of a football field, and it's hot okay. A lot of radiate, radiant heat even though it's insulated and everything anyway. They pull it over the weir and then they float it on a bath, a molten tin. Here's the molten tin bath okay. Not a very deep bath, molten tin probably only a couple of inches, but it's probably 15 feet wide, and now you can pull off stuff that's an eighth of an inch thick, three-sixteenths, quarter of an inch thick okay. And you take that and you anneal it, because glass can have serious problems if it's not, if it's got residual stresses in it, and you cut it to size and you ship it okay. It's not a mile long building, might be a couple hundred yards, but it's not a mile okay.
Now in these furnaces by the way, yeah —
Student:  So do you still have any [inhomogeneity in this] process?

Well the inhomogeneities originally came from, they were just taking the sand and the limestone and all these different components, they're putting it into a furnace. It was in the 1800s that they learned to stir the bath okay. Glass is very thick okay, very viscous, and the reason you, that Jena window, a lot of those inhomogeneities were not surface irregularities, they were chemical inhomogeneity. It's possible to have plate glass manufacturing — yeah since the last 200 years yeah, but I mean if you go back, that's why they had to go to Jena, Germany to find that window okay, because that's 200 year old technology. It was, in fact if I look at my little history of plate glass, he says in 1884 to 87, uh no, the mechanical stirring of molten glass was introduced, was not introduced until 1798 by Guinand, and was perfected in 1805.

It turns out France kept this as a trade secret. The British didn't get it until about their late 1700s early 1800s. So the first hundred years France sort of controlled the world's glass manufacturing, and it was mostly for mirrors okay. So the, and in fact Saint-Gobain made all the windows and mirrors in the Versailles Palace. If you actually look up Saint-Gobain you'll find they're very proud of the fact that they go back to Versailles okay. They had the technology to make big glass plates, the British didn't, for 100 years. But the British learned to stir the bath okay, and get more uniform mixtures. Then Pittsburgh Plate Glass comes along — a mile long building, very expensive, lots of hand labor, grinding and polishing. And then Pilkington comes along, and the night after World War II comes up with the float glass process. And that, is, probably — that's actually plate glass probably, if it's the original things from this building, but if it's not original, if it's been replaced, broken and replaced, which is fair chance that it was, it's going to be float glass. Float glass, you know, I don't know that you see a half inch thick float glass. So plate glass processing is still around. 
 §8 — Glass compositions and the LCD stack

The float glass process you want to keep it relatively thin, so you know, get move stuff across that bath fairly quickly. In any case, what happened is they were having a shortage of wood, and the revolution of necessity that this book talks about is basically the fact they had to start using coal because they couldn't use wood. And they would first go along just along the ocean, and you could pick up what they called sea coal. So wherever the waves had come up against some coal seam, you'd have sea coal on the beaches. And it turns out that ended up leading to, believe it or not, the science of thermodynamics, okay, and James Watt and steam engines and things like that. So the science came out of the revolution of necessity.

If you wanted to have iron to build hinges or nails or build cannons for warships, if you wanted to have wood for other applications, or if you wanted to have something so you could make glass, which you need a clean fuel to make glass — you have to have something that burns cleanly. How did they make nails going about thousands of years ago? Well, it turns out I have a little history here of cut nails in America. But back in the old days, if you didn't have anything to do in the winter, you might just sit there and forge nails. And it turns out a ten-penny-weight nail was a size nail that you could get ten pennies for 100 nails. An eight-penny nail was a smaller nail that only cost eight pennies for — anyway. But they were hand-forged from before the Christian era to, you know, the 1600s. They were forging individual nails, okay.

They would burn down barns or houses and sift through the ashes to recover the nails, because it was about one person-year per ton to produce this. And what's the productivity today? Well, the productivity today to make nails or steel is about 20 minutes per person ton, okay. Now that's a pretty high increase in productivity, and as a result you can buy a ton of steel today, if you just want to buy garden variety steel, for four or five hundred dollars a ton, okay. The equivalent price back in the 1600s — nails were a valuable commodity, as were hinges or anything else.

And so if you want to learn more about nails, you can go to Trayma Train — it's supposed to be Tremont Nail Company — it's right down here in Weymouth, Massachusetts or something, but they've been making nails for almost 200 years.
