cluster_id: Sea Wolf submarine weld cracking (SSN-21)
content: Sea Wolf submarine weld cracking (SSN-21) The weld metal ran 30–40% higher strength than intended because of carbon and alloy content; toughness dropped; 1 mm microscopic flaws formed that the original inspection wasn't looking for; a grinder noticed magnetized swarf aligning with the cracks, an inspector was called, and every weld in the sub had to be cut out. 18% of the ship had been built. Cost the Navy $2 billion.

id: case:Persian Gulf destroyer brass valve stress corrosion cracking (Second Gulf War)
cluster_id: Persian Gulf destroyer brass valve stress corrosion cracking (Second Gulf War)
content: Persian Gulf destroyer brass valve stress corrosion cracking (Second Gulf War) A destroyer in the Persian Gulf lost its 3,000 psi air system mid-attack; root cause was stress corrosion cracking in a brass valve made of the wrong alloy. Discovered at the Naval Supply Center in Philadelphia that twenty-some percent of brass valves in inventory were the wrong alloy. Two students in the same cohort had worked on different parts of the failure.

cluster_id: Dan Rather CBS building collapse
content: Dan Rather CBS building collapse Six-story Manhattan building under construction for CBS, early 1980s. Concrete beams with steel rebar; rebars were tack-welded where they crossed; high-carbon rebar at the tack-weld became brittle, fracture toughness dropped by a factor of eight, fifth-floor beam failed in bending tension, dominoed all the beams. $50 million loss, one workman's leg broken. The Steinway Piano factory tour (CBS-owned at the time) is a coda.

id: case:Boeing 747-400 titanium catalytic converter / air tubing
cluster_id: Boeing 747-400 titanium catalytic converter / air tubing
content: Boeing 747-400 titanium catalytic converter / air tubing Air tubing switched from stainless steel to titanium to save weight for the extended-range 747-400; Engelhard built the catalytic converters for ozone scrubbing in the cabin air system. Introduced here mainly as a vehicle for the aircraft-range discussion (10,000 → 13,000 mile aircraft) rather than as a developed failure case. Tom flags it as a long story not fully told.

id: case:Upstate New York brewery (1975 consulting job)
cluster_id: Upstate New York brewery (1975 consulting job)
content: Upstate New York brewery (1975 consulting job)

id: case:Air Force probability of detection inspection studies (1980s)
cluster_id: Air Force probability of detection inspection studies (1980s)
content: Air Force probability of detection inspection studies (1980s) Cited as the source of the curve: 95% probability of detection at ⅛", 50% at 1/16", very low in the mm range. Used to anchor the Sea Wolf inspection-gap story.

cluster_id: Cruise missile graphite engine
content: Cruise missile graphite engine Cited as the existence proof that brittle-material jet engines can be built — when the engine only has to last an hour, the inspection problem becomes tractable. Graphite is tougher than most ceramics; coatings prevent burn-up. Cited in passing as another "limited-life engine, hour-and-a-half service" parallel to NASCAR magnesium use. Cruise missile rocket motors made of carbon composites because life requirement is short. Designed to last only 2 hours because the missile is then destroyed; carbon composite engine that would oxidize away in 10 hours but only needs to fly 2.

cluster_id: Harvard Stadium reinforced concrete (1910)
content: Harvard Stadium reinforced concrete (1910) Cited as the oldest reinforced concrete structure in the country, used to illustrate that concrete continues to harden over years and decades — "you have to have a hammer drill with a carbide tip" to drill it now. named 1983 National Historical Landmark, one of the first major reinforced concrete structures in the US, c. 1900.

cluster_id: CH-53/MH-53 helicopter washer corrosion problem
content: CH-53/MH-53 helicopter washer corrosion problem Referenced as the parallel Sikorsky engineering group that had already discovered the T6 stress corrosion problem and ordered fleet-wide washer replacement before the Black Hawk accident. Sikorsky's earlier encounter with the same washer corrosion problem on a different helicopter line, which they fixed by switching from T6 to T7 over-aged heat treatment. Tom uses this to set up the indictment: Sikorsky knew the fix and failed to apply it to the Blackhawk part.

id: case:New England Aquarium exterior panel corrosion
cluster_id: New England Aquarium exterior panel corrosion
content: New England Aquarium exterior panel corrosion Analogy for "bought it in the right condition then transformed it." Stainless steel exterior panels purchased in passivated condition, then mechanically abraded for texture, which removed the passivation. Passivation defeated by post-passivation mechanical abrasion. Mill-passivated 304 panels were ground to create fish-scale texture, which removed the protective chrome oxide. In marine environment (Boston Harbor chlorides), the oxide could not reform. Rust appeared along grinding marks and along bumper scrapes at the loading dock. Tom tested citric acid and Diet Coke (phosphoric acid) as environmentally acceptable cleaning agents. Fish-scale facade specified as passivated stainless but ground for texture, leaving active surface; rust in grinding marks within a year. Tested citric/phosphoric acid/Coke/naval jelly for in-place re-passivation.

id: case:Aircraft landing gear and turbine engine shaft vacuum arc melting
cluster_id: Aircraft landing gear and turbine engine shaft vacuum arc melting
content: Aircraft landing gear and turbine engine shaft vacuum arc melting How 250 ksi yield landing gear is made without hydrogen cracking — triple vacuum melting gets hydrogen below half a part per million. Commercial aircraft landing gear and engine rotors/shafts are double vacuum arc remelted to bring inclusions below 10 microns, since at 250 ksi yield, 100-micron flaws threaten fatigue life. Triple vacuum arc remelting as the standard for aircraft crankshafts, landing gear, transmission shafts, and turbine engine shafts. Used to illustrate why inclusion control matters for fatigue-critical components.

id: case:U.S. Air Force net-shape manufacturing initiative
cluster_id: U.S. Air Force net-shape manufacturing initiative
content: U.S. Air Force net-shape manufacturing initiative Billion-dollar 1980s program to reduce buy-to-fly ratios. Referenced as the funding driver for the buy-to-fly reduction. "The Air Force spent billions of dollars in the '90s on what we call near net shape manufacturing." Frames the lecture's subsequent treatment of near-net-shape continuous casting at Chaparral.

id: case:Electric Boat welding humidity specification violation
cluster_id: Electric Boat welding humidity specification violation
content: Electric Boat welding humidity specification violation Newport News bay-doors-closed humidity practice. Navy spec prohibits welding above 80% humidity; shipyards keep doors closed even in temperate weather to control atmospheric moisture exposure.

cluster_id: HY-80 and HY-100 steel development
content: HY-80 and HY-100 steel development Cost of qualifying new pressure vessel steels — $50M in 1960s money for HY80/HY100 development; today hundreds of millions. Referenced as benchmark for DoE's stalled 9% nickel / Ni-1Mo qualification effort. Passed around as $2–3/lb benchmark to contrast with $12,000/lb X-33 composite. Manufactured at Electric Boat, Groton. HY-100 noted as same composition as HY-80, different heat treatment. HY steels framed as the achievement of the 1950s–60s Navy-funded weldability research. Tom holds up his own 30-year-old HY80 weld at §7.p1 to show the heat-affected zone. At §10.p2 he discusses a 100 ksi quenched-and-tempered plate (HY100-class chemistry but lower) that failed Charpy.

id: case:Department of Energy 9% nickel steel qualification effort
cluster_id: Department of Energy 9% nickel steel qualification effort
content: Department of Energy 9% nickel steel qualification effort 40-year stalled qualification of nickel-1-molybdenum (Tom corrects "9% nickel") for higher-temperature nuclear reactor service.

cluster_id: Boomer Submarine Trident Tube Retrofits
content: Boomer Submarine Trident Tube Retrofits Navy built full-size 30-foot HY100 sections for boomers in the 90s for welding experience before committing to an all-HY100 hull. Brief mention. The Electric Boat–trained welder whose shop took the Millstone contract was simultaneously doing SSGN conversion work — inserting clusters of ~19 non-nuclear warhead tubes inside former Trident tubes as part of SALT-era nuclear arsenal reductions. Used to establish the welder's credentials.

id: case:SSN-21 Sea Wolf hull cracking problem
cluster_id: SSN-21 Sea Wolf hull cracking problem
content: SSN-21 Sea Wolf hull cracking problem Even with prototype experience, Sea Wolf hull welding had major problems. In §7 the case is developed: they thought they had HY100 filler but got HY80-equivalent due to property scatter, hydrogen control inadequate, 18% of the ship welded with undermatched filler. A grinder smoothing welds on the first Seawolf-class submarine noticed grinding swarf lining up in lines under a sixteenth of an inch — a flaw size below anything the specification had ever required inspectors to find. Destructive sampling revealed clusters of micro-cracks throughout the welds; 18% of the hull had been completed. Tom contributed to the investigation report and identifies the weld-wire chemistry being on the high side as a contributing factor. Repair costs Tom heard ranged from half a billion to ~$2 billion — comparable to building a new boat. Two Seawolves were built before the program was canceled with the end of the Cold War. Tom uses the case to dramatize how improvements in measurement capability create disputes about flaws the original specification never contemplated. Brief reference. Source of lessons on welding high-strength steels. Used as a parallel to the Thresher in Petroski's framing of "we learn from failure."

cluster_id: Magnesium anode nickel contamination failure
content: Magnesium anode nickel contamination failure Hot-water-tank sacrificial anode. Nickel solubility in magnesium is ~7 ppm; excess nickel forms precipitates that cause local galvanic self-consumption — anode disappears in hours without protecting the steel vessel. Spine of the corrosion thread. The anode's high-purity magnesium spec (<7 ppm nickel) used to teach concentration-cell corrosion; the Juarez fabrication line used to teach how design accommodates real-world coating defects.

id: case:Massachusetts Supreme Court ICC bumper jack failure case
cluster_id: Massachusetts Supreme Court ICC bumper jack failure case
content: Massachusetts Supreme Court ICC bumper jack failure case Case law on expert testimony scope. Man jacking truck by ICC bumper, bumper welds broke without frame deformation. Tom's testimony (defective welds based on Lincoln Electric reference) was challenged at the Massachusetts Supreme Court; ruling established what a welding expert may say in MA courts.

cluster_id: Portsmouth submarine fire investigation
content: Portsmouth submarine fire investigation Called by a former student (then commander at Portsmouth) to help assess fire damage to submarine steel. The point of the anecdote: he couldn't get David Taylor to pay attention without going around them.

cluster_id: Egon Orowan dislocation discovery (rug anecdote)
content: Egon Orowan dislocation discovery (rug anecdote) Origin of the dislocation concept in 1930s Hungary; Orowan watching a maid kick a dislocation across an oriental rug. Used to introduce the concept of dislocations as one-atom-row-at-a-time deformation. Hungarian cleaning lady, working in Orowan's office, moves a Persian rug across the floor by introducing a small fold and kicking it across the room. Orowan watches and recognizes the principle of an edge dislocation. Tom physically tears a sheet of paper to demonstrate.

cluster_id: Iron whiskers (1950s screw dislocation studies)
content: Iron whiskers (1950s screw dislocation studies) 1940s iron whiskers with axial screw dislocations measured at 2 million PSI when pulled along the screw axis. Used to establish that theoretical strengths are achievable only in idealized geometries. Counter-example to the "defects destroy strength" rule — iron whiskers grown as single crystals with one axial screw dislocation achieved 2.2 million psi because the dislocation was not loaded. 1950s growth of single-crystal iron whiskers containing only a screw dislocation along the axis. Pulled to 2 million PSI experimental strength — the theoretical strength of perfect crystal steel. Used to argue that physicists' claims about carbon nanotube strength (the "rope to the moon") are decades behind what materials scientists already demonstrated and refuted. Single-crystal iron whiskers grown in the 1950s with only a screw dislocation (no edge dislocations), measured at ~1.2 million PSI — close to the theoretical Lennard-Jones prediction of ~2 million PSI. Used to validate the dislocation theory of weakening.

id: case:High-temperature superconductor critical current density problem
cluster_id: High-temperature superconductor critical current density problem
content: High-temperature superconductor critical current density problem The scaling argument: pinning-site size scales inversely with critical temperature, so 40-70 K superconductors need pinning sites smaller than an electron — impossible.

id: case:High-temperature superconductor critical current measurement error
cluster_id: High-temperature superconductor critical current measurement error
content: High-temperature superconductor critical current measurement error Papers in *Science* magazine around 1990 measuring critical current with field parallel to current (zero J-cross-B force), reporting fantastic values that would never apply to a wound magnet where J and B are perpendicular. Seven orders of magnitude difference. *Science* magazine papers reporting critical currents two orders of magnitude above Tom's thesis values — measured with conductor parallel to the magnetic field, which is physically meaningless (J×B = 0). The peer reviewers didn't catch it. "One of the problems when there's lots of money, you bring out all the people who don't know what they're doing."

id: case:Niobium-titanium superconductor development for high-energy physics
cluster_id: Niobium-titanium superconductor development for high-energy physics
content: Niobium-titanium superconductor development for high-energy physics John Wulff's work; critical temperature ~9 K, fields ~6 Tesla. The 1970s workhorse superconductor. GE niobium-tin and other manufacturers' niobium-titanium magnets, ~1960, for physics. Establishes the pre-1986 commercial baseline against which high-Tc was hyped.

id: case:Niobium-3.5tin superconductor with zirconium oxide pinning precipitates
cluster_id: Niobium-3.5tin superconductor with zirconium oxide pinning precipitates
content: Niobium-3.5tin superconductor with zirconium oxide pinning precipitates Mark Benz at GE Research; 1% zirconium internally oxidized to form 20-30 nm zirconium oxide precipitates spaced ~100 nm apart, providing the pinning sites that gave good critical field. The case Tom was originally going to lecture on.

id: case:Wire drawing thesis project on superconducting wire production
cluster_id: Wire drawing thesis project on superconducting wire production
content: Wire drawing thesis project on superconducting wire production Tom's house tutor's doctoral thesis on severely deformed niobium as a superconductor; the wavy-slip picture in Backofen. Tom's undergraduate thesis: $1,000 worth of diamond dies bought in 5% increments, which Tom now identifies as the wrong approach — should have used 30–50% draws to avoid high-delta operations and centerline cracking.

cluster_id: American Superconductor commercial viability (1995–present)
content: American Superconductor commercial viability (1995–present) MIT spin-off founded by Greg Yurek (with Vander Sande and Yet-Ming Chiang) using silver internal-oxidation route to HTSC ceramics. Twenty-some years on: limping, Chinese theft of wind-turbine software, some New York City transmission lines installed. The downstream consequence Tom predicted. Greg Yurek's 1989 departure from MIT to found American Superconductor; company has never made money but draws hundreds of millions in research grants on the promise.

cluster_id: DC transmission line in Manhattan
content: DC transmission line in Manhattan Brief mention as one of American Superconductor's deployments. Not developed.

id: case:US Navy SQUID magnetic anomaly detection program
cluster_id: US Navy SQUID magnetic anomaly detection program
content: US Navy SQUID magnetic anomaly detection program Late 1980s Navy concern that Soviet satellites equipped with HTSC-based SQUID detectors would render steel-hulled submarines visible from orbit. The applied motivation for both titanium and stainless-steel submarine programs.

id: case:Ford Taurus aluminum body cost analysis
cluster_id: Ford Taurus aluminum body cost analysis
content: Ford Taurus aluminum body cost analysis Joel Clark's student's doctoral thesis (early 1990s, later Harvard Business School assistant professor): $500 steel unibody vs $1,000 aluminum unibody, before fabrication. Tom's critique: the thesis ignored that aluminum can't be resistance spot welded like steel. Tom recounts his disagreement with Professor (Joel) Clark's student's thesis, which concluded an aluminum Taurus would cost only $500 more. Tom challenged the analysis on fabricability grounds; the student rewrote a page but, in Tom's telling, missed the point. "Any fool can make an all-aluminum hundred-thousand-dollar car." The $20K Taurus as the target benchmark. Quick numeric anchor — "$25,000 car, $500 of steel" — to make the 5%-material-cost point. Engine and seats called out as the two most expensive subsystems.

cluster_id: All-aluminum automobile body cost analysis (early 1990s)
content: All-aluminum automobile body cost analysis (early 1990s) The broader case of which Joel Clark's student's thesis is one instance. Tom's prediction in the early 90s that mass-market all-aluminum vehicles were twenty years out. Ford looked at an all-aluminum Taurus — $25,000 car becomes $35,000 car.

id: case:Kim Clark Harvard Business School career arc
cluster_id: Kim Clark Harvard Business School career arc
content: Kim Clark Harvard Business School career arc Tom's contemporary at Harvard (he was at HBS while Tom was at MIT). Cub Scout father (built the bad Pinewood Derby track). Paid honoraria by AISI to advise on decisions, including the Armco case which he characterized as a "good decision." Eventually Dean of HBS. The personal-history anchor for Tom's MIT-vs-HBS thesis.

cluster_id: Morris Chang / Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing
content:
Morris Chang / Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Tom's student Nun-Sen Tsai (welding heat flow thesis) becoming one of Chang's right hands at TSMC, but losing the succession to a Stanford materials-and-business student. Used as the closing example of MIT producing technicians-to-leaders rather than leaders.

## Figures referenced (not cases)

cluster_id: Navy Tributyltin (TBT) paint environmental damage
content: Navy Tributyltin (TBT) paint environmental damage Example of the Navy justifying environmentally damaging practices on national security grounds until Congressional intervention (~20–25 years prior to 2013). Used to illustrate the limit of DoD national-security override of civilian regulation. Navy used TBT in hull paint for barnacle prevention; parts per trillion wiped out mollusk populations in every US harbor; Congress overrode the Navy in the 1990s.

id: case:Aberdeen Proving Ground RDX soil contamination
cluster_id: Aberdeen Proving Ground RDX soil contamination
content: Aberdeen Proving Ground RDX soil contamination Environmental contamination of former JP Morgan hunting reserve turned Army firing range. Used to make a point about military environmental legacy.

id: case:Newport News Shipyard carbide shack incident
cluster_id: Newport News Shipyard carbide shack incident
content: Newport News Shipyard carbide shack incident Welding engineer racing fire department to a carbide shack fire to prevent water-based suppression (which would generate more acetylene). Illustrates acetylene-from-calcium-carbide on-site generation.

cluster_id: Thomas Wilson calcium carbide discovery
content: Thomas Wilson calcium carbide discovery Spray, North Carolina, early 1900s. Wilson trying to synthesize metals in an arc furnace with carbon and limestone, ended up with calcium carbide, ignited it accidentally in the Neuse River. Origin of industrial acetylene production.

id: case:Acetylene cylinder explosion hazard (early acetylene storage)
cluster_id: Acetylene cylinder explosion hazard (early acetylene storage)
content: Acetylene cylinder explosion hazard (early acetylene storage) PC Avery, James Allison, Carl Fisher and the 1904 origin of Prest-O-Lite/Union Carbide acetone-dissolved acetylene cylinders. B cylinders for bus headlights. 1950s calcium silicate binder development.

cluster_id: MIT undergraduate mercury fulminate fly-catcher
content: MIT undergraduate mercury fulminate fly-catcher Tom's personal undergraduate-era anecdote. Contact-explosive demonstration. Personal/biographical reference.

id: case:Plumber MAPP gas torch facial injury incident
cluster_id: Plumber MAPP gas torch facial injury incident
content: Plumber MAPP gas torch facial injury incident Plumber soldering copper pipe while holding cell phone and smoking cigar, using lit MAP torch as a hammer, split the neck, woman walking by saw 8-foot flame shoot into his face.

id: case:Southern California MAP cylinder misuse federal lawsuit
cluster_id: Southern California MAP cylinder misuse federal lawsuit
content: Southern California MAP cylinder misuse federal lawsuit Federal lawsuit settled month before this lecture (~May 2013) after judge threw out plaintiff's case for perjury. Tom and colleague were going to testify that plaintiff was smoking methamphetamines and MAP cylinder failure resulted from being thrown/abused, not from manufacturing defect. References Mount Shasta burn testing.

id: case:Mount Shasta MAP and acetylene burn testing study
cluster_id: Mount Shasta MAP and acetylene burn testing study
content: Mount Shasta MAP and acetylene burn testing study Field tests measuring duration and intensity of MAP cylinder release fires. 3–5 second burns; 75% body-area burn risk if standing in the stream.

cluster_id: MIT titanium flame-cutting environmental incident
content: MIT titanium flame-cutting environmental incident Late 1970s. Tom's first research project at MIT. Technician Bruce flame-cutting titanium, smoke escaped from welding lab into hallway, thesis advisor's secretary called environmental police, who came and asked "what kind of lab is this?" Lab = welding lab. Anecdote about the laxer environmental enforcement era. Tom's welding lab cutting titanium ~25–30 years before the lecture (so ~1985); the secretary across the hall complained to MIT environmental health; investigator concluded that a welding lab is expected to produce smoke.

id: case:Tank explosion at Pennzoil Oil City refinery
cluster_id: Tank explosion at Pennzoil Oil City refinery
content: Tank explosion at Pennzoil Oil City refinery ~1998 (15 years before 2013). Old riveted 1920s tank exploded killing a welder, blowing her across the river. Facility had 80 years of oil-soaked gravel; Tom realized the plant stayed open to defer EPA cleanup obligations. Includes reference to 1859 Drake well (corrected from Tom's "1856" slip) and Titusville-to-Oil-City riverine oil transport. Forensic consulting case ca. 1995. 1920s riveted storage tanks, oil-saturated tank farm ground. Tom figures out at breakfast that Pennzoil keeps the refinery running not for production economics but because shutting it would trigger EPA cleanup assessment. Used to illustrate economic externalities.

id: case:Belmont elementary school oil tank leak
cluster_id: Belmont elementary school oil tank leak
content: Belmont elementary school oil tank leak Newton's rings on a clay pit pond noticed by a high school student; traced to corroded number-6 bunker oil heating pipes at an elementary school a third of a mile uphill. $1.5 million repair. Tom's hometown. Contrast case to Pennzoil — same hazard class (heating oil leak) under modern environmental regulation cost the town of Belmont two million dollars in cleanup. Used to make the point that the rules have changed since 1900.

cluster_id: Ship dismantling in Bangladesh
content: Ship dismantling in Bangladesh Decommissioned commercial ships beached and cut up for scrap by workers earning ~50 cents/day with acetylene torches; average occupational lifespan ~5 years. Used as illustration of disposal end-of-life problem analogous to aircraft parked in Arizona desert. Workers cut up beached ships with acetylene torches, exposed to asbestos and residual chemicals; reported life expectancy of three years for workers. Tom notes "we export our environmental problems."

cluster_id: Navy nuclear reactor disposal practices
content: Navy nuclear reactor disposal practices Brief Q&A with student. Tom believed reactors were buried in the Atlantic off Norfolk; student corrects to Washington State (Hanford).

cluster_id: Liquid copper jet cutting research
content: Liquid copper jet cutting research Anonymized company developing superheated molten copper laminar jet cutting at 10× plasma cutting speed. Worked at 10-foot lab scale; ceramic nozzle lifetime was the limiting factor.

cluster_id: Alabama aluminum foundry freeze-up
content: Alabama aluminum foundry freeze-up Phone call to Tom as junior faculty (~1978). Foundry's 2-foot deep aluminum melting pot froze after a day-long power outage; Tom couldn't help. Alabama foundry loses power for a day; holding pot solidifies 2 feet of aluminum; can't be flame-cut due to protective oxide. Years later Tom learns from Alcoa's Peter O'Brien that the standard remedy is to call a specialist in Pittsburgh who blows it out with explosive charges.

id: case:Alcoa aluminum potline freeze-up explosive demolition
cluster_id: Alcoa aluminum potline freeze-up explosive demolition
content: Alcoa aluminum potline freeze-up explosive demolition Dinner conversation ~15 years after the Alabama call with Alcoa senior VP "Peter." Steel mills cut breakouts with oxyacetylene; aluminum can't be flame-cut, so Alcoa called a Pittsburgh specialist who drilled holes, set explosive charges, and blew the frozen aluminum apart — sometimes destroying the potline in the process. Same incident; the resolution side via Alcoa's Pittsburgh specialist who drills holes, places charges, and breaks up frozen aluminum masses.

id: case:Red Adair oil well blowout firefighting
cluster_id: Red Adair oil well blowout firefighting
content:
Red Adair oil well blowout firefighting Contextual aside positioning the Pittsburgh aluminum-explosives specialist as a Red-Adair-equivalent for potline freeze-ups. References first Gulf War (Kuwaiti oil fires) as the moment Red Adair's techniques became widely known.

## Figures referenced (not cases)

cluster_id: America's Cup 4340 welding procedure development
content: America's Cup 4340 welding procedure development Used to introduce the hardenability concept. A four-inch-thick keel beam couldn't be made from HY-130 (too soft, plastically deforming in trials) so they wanted 4340, but didn't know how to weld it in that section thickness. Tom showed them how.

cluster_id: Sub-Zero refrigerator hinge failure
content: Sub-Zero refrigerator hinge failure Illustrates the consequence of 303 vs. 304 mix-up. Manufacturer used 303 (sulfur-bearing, non-weldable) instead of 304 for a pin-to-plate weld. Cracked at the weld, plated over, doors fell off in service. ~$7M in repairs. Tom's consulting case. Sub-Zero (twelve-thousand-dollar refrigerators) had a TIG-welded hinge pin made by a subcontractor from free-machining sulfur-bearing steel; sulfur formed iron sulfide and the welds cracked. ~3000 units repaired in the field at ~$7 million. Used as the headline example of the design/fab/field 1:10:100:1000 cost-of-failure escalation, and the example that wealthy customers are litigious. Physical sample (the hinge from his son's $11,000 refrigerator). Used to illustrate the low-value-per-pound end of the materials market — plain carbon steel.

id: case:316 stainless steel heat exchanger tube pitting failure (Fenway Frank application)
cluster_id: 316 stainless steel heat exchanger tube pitting failure (Fenway Frank application)
content: 316 stainless steel heat exchanger tube pitting failure (Fenway Frank application) Dramatic 304-vs-316 substitution case. Original 316 cooker ran 10-20 years with no problems. Replacement parts mis-specified as 304 cracked and rusted within weeks in the high-salt steam environment.

cluster_id: Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) process development
content: Argon oxygen decarbonization (AOD) process development Closing case of the lecture. MIT doctoral student Krivsky, working under John Chipman in the Building 8 basement, doing basic carbon-monoxide-reaction research. Discovered low oxygen potential of argon would pull carbon and oxygen out of molten steel. Not patented at MIT; Krivsky commercialized it at a company. Now used for virtually all stainless steel and most nickel superalloys worldwide. Tom estimates ~$1B/year value to the world steel industry. The case Tom uses to illustrate "MIT lost the patent" lessons elsewhere in the corpus. Discovered in MIT Building 8 basement; Chipman's [Chapman's] student William Krivsky takes it to a small NY State steel company; AOD enables low-ppm carbon in stainless steel, drops stainless price by ~3X. Now used for essentially all stainless steel and aerospace alloys (with VOD for the latter). "Christy" (Chipman doctoral student, 1950s) studied the carbon-monoxide reaction in steel melts using argon-diluted oxygen. The technique went from MIT thesis to Crucible Steel + Union Carbide commercial process. All 5M tons of stainless steel today made by AOD; price reduced to one-third of 1950s value. Born in basement of Building 8 from a John Chipman graduate student (Krivsky [?]) doing basic carbon-burnout chemistry; commercialized at a small steel company because the majors wouldn't risk it. Dropped stainless steel price by 5–10×, enabled <0.03% C for weldability and corrosion resistance, recovered chromium from slag. AOD reduces carbon from 300 ppm to 30 ppm by argon blowing. Basic science done at MIT under John Chipman by Krivsky in the 1950s; process invented when Krivsky moved to a small steel company. 99% of stainless steel today made by AOD. Tom identifies AOD as an MIT-originated process (basic research in the basement of Building 8) that today accounts for ~98% of world stainless-steel production. By bubbling argon through the molten bath, the partial pressure of CO in the gas bubbles is suppressed by ~100×, allowing the equilibrium C·O activity product to drive carbon down below 300 ppm even at high chromium content. The economic consequence: cost of stainless steel roughly halved per ton since the 1960s.

cluster_id: Infinium magnesium extraction process development
content: Infinium magnesium extraction process development Forward-reference to Adam Powell's upcoming guest lecture. Spinoff from MIT via Boston University; ~$10-20M in funding for an environmentally clean metals extraction process.

cluster_id: Japanese steel soda cans
content: Japanese steel soda cans Policy-protected industrial choice — Japanese government protected domestic steel by keeping vending-machine soda in steel cans rather than aluminum, since Japan has no indigenous aluminum industry. Aluminum has now displaced steel as the protection eased. Used as the lecture-opening illustration of how non-technical factors drive materials selection.

id: case:Steel vs. aluminum auto markets US vs. Europe
cluster_id: Steel vs. aluminum auto markets US vs. Europe
content: Steel vs. aluminum auto markets US vs. Europe Fuel-price economics would favor aluminum cars in Europe, but European manufacturers must build for the US market where fuel prices favor steel. Illustrates how exporting drives materials selection.

cluster_id: Hadfield's manganese steel (prison bars application)
content:
Hadfield's manganese steel (prison bars application) 12-13% Mn steel that work-hardens during machining, making it nearly impossible to saw or file. Used historically for prison bars. Distinct alloy class from the 200-series stainless steels Tom is discussing.

id: case:Hugh Nibley "Leaders to Managers: The Fatal Shift" (framing text)
cluster_id: Hugh Nibley "Leaders to Managers: The Fatal Shift" (framing text)
content: Hugh Nibley "Leaders to Managers: The Fatal Shift" (framing text) Provides the leader-vs-manager dichotomy that structures the second half of the lecture. The German General Staff anecdote at §7.p1 is drawn from Nibley's text.

id: case:Pacific Gas and Electric pumped-storage hydroelectric project
cluster_id: Pacific Gas and Electric pumped-storage hydroelectric project
content: Pacific Gas and Electric pumped-storage hydroelectric project Slocum's proposal — combined pumped-water storage and reverse-osmosis desalinization for regions where ocean meets mountain. Used to introduce Slocum's upcoming guest lecture; positions complex multi-system engineering design.

cluster_id: Early steamboat boiler explosions (Ohio River)
content: Early steamboat boiler explosions (Ohio River) The first federal research contract (1836, Franklin Institute) — origin of materials engineering science. Used to establish the deep-historical lineage of pressure vessel safety regulation.

cluster_id: Boston Big Dig
content: Boston Big Dig Tom's consulting role on the galvanized bolt corrosion question, before the ceiling collapse that killed a motorist. Used to demonstrate the engineering-judgment clause of the code: a non-conformance (out-of-sequence galvanizing) didn't have to mean uninstalling all the bolts; comparative analysis of zinc throwing power between hot-dip and electro-galvanized coatings showed the disputed bolts were safer than the as-built electrical hardware adjacent to them. Tom's 2001 tour. Used to illustrate cable-stay tensioning precision — strands must match length within a quarter inch or stress concentration causes cascade failure.

id: case:Alberta transmission tower steel contract dispute
cluster_id: Alberta transmission tower steel contract dispute
content: Alberta transmission tower steel contract dispute A $50M contract dispute between buyer (Canadian utility) and seller (Indian steel mill) over 100,000 tons of steel for 111 towers (~1000 tons each at ~$1.5M steel cost per tower). Tom's quoting code section 6.5 (inspection responsibilities). Used to ground the abstract code-citation discussion in current consulting work, and at §9.p5 to illustrate the financial stakes of weight savings from LRFD design.

id: case:Johnson & Johnson medical device manufacturing defect
cluster_id: Johnson & Johnson medical device manufacturing defect
content: Johnson & Johnson medical device manufacturing defect Generic reference to Tom's consulting role advising J&J on manufacturing-hiccup waivers — whether half-million-dollar lots could be saved or had to be scrapped. Used to illustrate the engineer-as-judgment-arbiter point.

id: case:Private Mach 2.5 aircraft crash and wing flutter failure
cluster_id: Private Mach 2.5 aircraft crash and wing flutter failure
content: Private Mach 2.5 aircraft crash and wing flutter failure Reno-based homebuilt-loophole aircraft program: $10M deposit aircraft, second test pilot (the owner) killed at Mach 2 / 40,000 ft over Nevada desert. Tom's forensic finding: inadequate adhesive joint on the lead-weight damper at wingtip — wing flutter went unstable and ripped the wing off. Wreckage spread over 50 miles. Tom's signature observation: "Why they didn't put a screw in there to join the lead to the aluminum is beyond me."

cluster_id: Private jet friction-welded titanium startup
content: Private jet friction-welded titanium startup Brief mention as another example of speculative private-aircraft scams — $1M down before design existed; all friction-stir-welded titanium-skin Cessna-class plane. Failed venture used to illustrate friction-welding limits above aluminum (mandrel wear with reactive titanium).

id: case:1849-1850 Royal Commission bridge safety factor study
cluster_id: 1849-1850 Royal Commission bridge safety factor study
content: 1849-1850 Royal Commission bridge safety factor study The Commission asked Charles Fox and other bridge designers what safety factor to use; answers ranged from 3 to 7; the Commission chose 6. Used to anchor the 150-year safety-factor trajectory (6 → 1.67) at the section's pivot to modern practice.

cluster_id: New Orleans Canal Levee Failure
content: New Orleans Canal Levee Failure Reported post-Katrina safety factor of 1.3 — the lowest Tom knows of in a structural application. Personal connection: Tom's great-grandfather, a civil engineer, worked on the levees around 1880. Safety factor 1.3. Tom emphasizes the levees did not fail by strength — they were overtopped. Personal note: Tom's grandfather built levees in New Orleans in the 1880s.

cluster_id: Cincinnati Red Stadium I-beam collapse
content: Cincinnati Red Stadium I-beam collapse Roy McCauley (head of welding at Ohio State, deceased) showed the contractor how to flame-straighten a 30°-bent giant I-beam after a crane cable broke during erection of the Cincinnati Reds Stadium roof in the Pete Rose era. Replacement lead time was 18 months from the mill; flame straightening saved the schedule. Tom uses it as the canonical demonstration that residual stress always pulls in the opposite direction of the applied heat expansion.

cluster_id: USS Iowa gun turret explosion
content: USS Iowa gun turret explosion Tom recalls the 1989 Iowa turret explosion (attributed at the time to a sailor in a failed relationship lighting off a powder charge inside a 16-inch gun). In 1985 Tom spent summers at David Taylor in Annapolis, where the Navy was trying to figure out how to repair the turret — but no one in 1985 knew how to make the welds being made in 1945. The repair was abandoned and all battleships decommissioned within five years. 1989 turret explosion. Navy could not repair because they had lost the heavy-section peening technology for 14-inch armor steel welds; the turret was abandoned rather than repaired. Used to teach the disappearance of mid-century heavy-section welding expertise.

cluster_id: Three-tank RPG penetration test (1985)
content: Three-tank RPG penetration test (1985) One of Tom's students worked for the Army in the mid-1980s. The Army developed improved sabots that could penetrate multiple armor layers; a field demonstration with three old tanks lined up showed the round going through all six armor layers. The general present reportedly vomited at the implication for tank crews.

id: case:1991 Gulf War M1 Abrams vs T-72 tank engagement
cluster_id: 1991 Gulf War M1 Abrams vs T-72 tank engagement
content: 1991 Gulf War M1 Abrams vs T-72 tank engagement Tom recounts the episode from Tom Clancy's *Armored Cav* of a stuck-in-mud M1 Abrams that defeated three successive T-72s — the first two firing rounds that bounced off; the third trying to hide behind a sand berm and being killed through the berm via infrared sighting. Tom uses it as the bookend of meaningful tank warfare; he frames tank battles since the 1973 Suez War (2.5-minute average lifetime) as anachronistic in the helicopter-RPG era.

id: case:Western Massachusetts laser cutting machine factory fire
cluster_id: Western Massachusetts laser cutting machine factory fire
content: Western Massachusetts laser cutting machine factory fire A $2–3M oxygen-assist laser cutting machine running lights-out in a Western Massachusetts factory caught fire and was destroyed. The plaintiffs hypothesized that metal-powder accumulation under the machine ignited. Tom (called in after another fire investigator) noted that with oxygen-assist cutting, the powders are already iron oxide — "you can't burn wood twice." Plaintiffs withdrew the suit at mediation.

id: case:Tom Eagar LNG welding sunburn incident
cluster_id: Tom Eagar LNG welding sunburn incident
content: Tom Eagar LNG welding sunburn incident En route to a New Orleans conference in the early 1980s, Tom stopped at Alcoa in Pittsburgh, where they were developing a 600-amp gas tungsten arc process for welding 4–8 inch aluminum on LNG ship spheres. Holding the torch ungloved for 15–20 seconds gave Tom a UV sunburn on the exposed lower half of his hand (the torch shielded the upper half) — a vivid demonstration of arc radiation losses and aluminum's reflectivity.

cluster_id: Civil War cannonball drop towers
content: Civil War cannonball drop towers Embedded within the Alpha submarine arc as a Watertown Arsenal origin story. During the Civil War the Arsenal pursued a research program to drop molten cast iron from towers to form spherical cannonballs. Without knowledge of heat transfer or dimensionless numbers (chemical engineering wasn't invented until the 1880s, at MIT), they needed a ~50-mile-tall tower; surface-tension/gravity ratio also required drops below 3 mm. The program produced only splats. Tom uses it as a contrast to Watertown's eventual post-WWII success developing Ti-6Al-4V.

id: case:SSN-21 Sea Wolf submarine hull cracking problem
cluster_id: SSN-21 Sea Wolf submarine hull cracking problem
content: SSN-21 Sea Wolf submarine hull cracking problem Brief closing reference: Captain Millard Firebaugh (a graduate of MIT's program) was designing the SSN-21 in the mid-1980s when Congress zeroed the next year's budget, saying they wouldn't build another steel sub while the Soviets had titanium subs — and that the U.S. should leapfrog to composite submarines. Tom mentions attending a four-day workshop on composite subs which he calls "a laughing mess." Setup for a future lecture.

id: case:Aluminum casting aircraft engine repair consulting case
cluster_id: Aluminum casting aircraft engine repair consulting case
content: Aluminum casting aircraft engine repair consulting case Recent (Jan 24, 2014) consulting question from "Chuck," chief engineer at an FAA-approved aircraft piston engine crankcase repair shop. Customer's 3/8" stud stripped at 204 inch-pounds in a 4043-filler weld repair. Tom walks through SAE/AMS specifications, Aluminum Association filler metal recommendations (4043, 4145, 4009, 4010, 4011, 4047), and the reasoning for matching vs. over-matching vs. under-matching filler metal selection. Foreshadow only — Tom announces the case will be developed in detail on Friday. The shop is one of the only FAA-authorized aluminum casting weld repair operations in the US; they had been using 4043 filler metal since 1976 and were criticized in a Canadian Aviation Authority report following a crash investigation. Used to set up a filler-metal-selection case study.

id: case:Canadian Transportation Board filler metal composition criticism
cluster_id: Canadian Transportation Board filler metal composition criticism
content: Canadian Transportation Board filler metal composition criticism Prior (fall 2013) accident investigation in Canada where the Canadian Transportation Safety Board concluded the under-matching 4043 filler metal caused a fatigue crack. Tom helped the client respond. Reused in §5 as an example of how failure analysts mistake difference for cause.

id: case:Johnson & Johnson laser surgery instrument coating
cluster_id: Johnson & Johnson laser surgery instrument coating
content: Johnson & Johnson laser surgery instrument coating Early-1980s consulting case. J&J's surgical instruments division wanted laser-cutting hand tools (scissors, drills, reamers) that wouldn't reflect the laser onto unintended tissue. Tom recommended anodized aluminum (oxide layer for absorption + aluminum substrate for thermal diffusion), helped them design the experiment with 4/6/8/10-micron anodized discs, and confirmed the 6–10 micron optimum. Patent and held-harmless arrangement. Tom developed an anti-reflective surface coating for J&J laser surgical instruments to prevent burn injury from reflected laser energy. Took six months of J&J legal department to issue a hold-harmless letter.

id: case:Independent consultant patent liability and indemnification
cluster_id: Independent consultant patent liability and indemnification
content: Independent consultant patent liability and indemnification Tom's request to J&J for indemnification on the two patents bearing his name. Pedagogical use: warning to students who may become independent consultants that named-inventor liability persists for decades after the work.

cluster_id: General Aviation Revitalization Act (1992) — statute, not a case

id: case:Aircraft piston engine crankcase 30-year repair defect pattern
cluster_id: Aircraft piston engine crankcase 30-year repair defect pattern
content: Aircraft piston engine crankcase 30-year repair defect pattern Tom's observation that for thirty years, periodic investigators have flagged the under-matching 4043 weld as the cause of failure, despite ~100,000 successful repairs over forty years. Used to make the methodological point that failure analysts mistake difference for cause.

cluster_id: FAA aircraft parts certification case
content: FAA aircraft parts certification case General reference to the FAA repair-station authorization regime and counterfeit-parts problem; turbine blade notching practice cited.

cluster_id: post-1965 greenfield steel mills
content: post-1965 greenfield steel mills Burns Harbor as the last green-field steel mill built in the U.S., framing the magnitude of capital investment required for primary materials production and why only nation-states (not companies) now build them.

cluster_id: Boeing 747 C-5A competition
content: Boeing 747 C-5A competition Tom's anecdote about the 747 being Boeing's losing C-5A military transport design, repurposed as a commercial jetliner — used to illustrate the bet-your-company scale of aerospace capital investment. Tokyo Narita anecdote of forty-seven 747s on the ground. Origin story of the 747. Boeing lost the four-or-five-billion-dollar C-5A military airlift contract to Lockheed (Marietta, Georgia); used their sunk investment to pitch the 747 as a commercial transport. Used to teach the magnitude of bet-your-company aerospace programs.

cluster_id: Copper-bearing carbon steel railroad application
content: Copper-bearing carbon steel railroad application 1880s discovery that small copper additions (<0.2%) doubled atmospheric corrosion resistance in railroad steels. Used to motivate why "carbon steels" carry more than just carbon.

id: case:America's Cup yacht center board (Jerry Milgram consulting)
cluster_id: America's Cup yacht center board (Jerry Milgram consulting)
content: America's Cup yacht center board (Jerry Milgram consulting) Twenty-years-ago consulting call from MIT Professor Jerry Milgram (Course 13, now 2N): a six-inch-thick HY-80 (or HY-130) center board bent on first sea trials. Tom consulted on the move to 4340 and the 600°F preheat needed to weld it. Used to introduce both the high-end of alloy steel hardenability and the consequences (preheat protocols) for welding.

cluster_id: HSLA 65 carrier weight-reduction study
content: HSLA 65 carrier weight-reduction study NAVSEA-funded million-dollar Newport News study finding 2,000-ton weight savings possible by substituting HSLA-65 for 50 ksi steel on Nimitz-class carriers. Tom's punchline: his "10× material cost" rule of thumb predicts the same answer. Also frames the broader Nimitz weight-creep problem (250 tons/year) and the $50M cost of designing a new hull. Million-dollar study Newport News did for the Navy on substituting 65 ksi HSLA steel for traditional 36/50 ksi. Tom's example of the "materials are 10% of manufactured cost" rule playing out in a Navy procurement study.

id: case:US Navy Japan steel mill visit and HSLA technology transfer
cluster_id: US Navy Japan steel mill visit and HSLA technology transfer
content: US Navy Japan steel mill visit and HSLA technology transfer Tom's trip to Japan to study HSLA accelerated-cooling technology for Navy and Japanese steel companies. Background to the HSLA-65 story.

cluster_id: Single-crystal turbine blades (GE/Pratt & Whitney)
content: Single-crystal turbine blades (GE/Pratt & Whitney) Student-driven aside on why we don't grow single-crystal structural metal. Tom explains creep resistance motivation, growth rate (~1-2 mm/hour), $7,000 per blade, Pratt & Whitney / GE Christmas-tree casting trees vs. Rolls-Royce's small-furnace approach. The $6,000 single-crystal blade as the showcase application of investment casting. Tom walks the full chain: ceramic-shell mold → polycrystalline cast → temperature-gradient furnace → pigtail seed-crystal selection → CAT-scan wall-thickness inspection. Used to teach how casting can produce the most thermodynamically demanding part in modern engineering. Physical demonstration. A 20-year-old single-crystal turbine blade ("no grain boundaries"), worth $6,000–$7,000, ~100 per wheel. Used to motivate the grain-boundary discussion that frames Backofen vs. Grant's research programs. $6,000/blade × 100 blades/disc = $600K replacement; engine companies make 40% of profit on 20% of volume from blades/vanes.

id: case:Polycrystalline silicon solar cell grain boundary efficiency
cluster_id: Polycrystalline silicon solar cell grain boundary efficiency
content: Polycrystalline silicon solar cell grain boundary efficiency Personal-anecdote pedagogy — Tom's solar-powered outdoor lights have visibly inch-across silicon grains, illustrating the grain-boundary efficiency loss that motivates single-crystal silicon in higher-end cells.

id: case:Charles Street MBTA station welding specifications case
cluster_id: Charles Street MBTA station welding specifications case
content: Charles Street MBTA station welding specifications case Architectural welding firm consulting Tom on welding to unspecified 1910-era steel during MBTA station rehab. Tom looks up the procedure in Stout and Doty in five minutes for $500. Used to illustrate the practical value of weldability tables.

cluster_id: Seawolf HY-100 hydrogen cracking
content: Seawolf HY-100 hydrogen cracking The lecture's centerpiece case. Tom's consulting role on the Seawolf HY-100 cracking investigation. Key elements: high-side wire from Lincoln Electric meeting spec but at the upper alloy bound (producing 130-140 ksi weld metal); 5-15 ppm hydrogen vs. the 2-3 ppm tolerable at that strength; Tom's drawing-lubricant hypothesis based on hydrogen scaling with wire surface-to-volume ratio (1/R); the Crystal City meeting with two Navy captains; in-his-head fracture mechanics calculation showing critical flaw size >> existing sub-eighth-inch flaws, leading to "don't derate, do more inspection" recommendation.

cluster_id: de Havilland Comet
content: de Havilland Comet Brief contrast to Aloha — the 1950s British Comet's square windows caused stress-concentration fatigue cracks leading to mid-Atlantic disappearances. Reason airliners no longer have square windows. Square windows as stress concentrators. Alan Wells worked out the cause. Used to anchor stress-concentration intuition immediately after Griffith's equation. Mid-1950s mid-Atlantic breakups. Alan Wells (British Welding Institute) identified square window stress concentration. Water-filled pressure tank reproduced the cracking. Tom uses it to introduce stress concentration around a hole in a plate (3-sigma result, 1883).

cluster_id: Cape Air Cessna fleet consulting
content: Cape Air Cessna fleet consulting Tom's ongoing forensic consulting relationship with Cape Air's head of maintenance — Cape Air is the Cessna fatigue leader; cracks unfamiliar to Cessna show up there first. Tom's one-page letters get forwarded to Cessna and the Burlington, MA FAA office. Same outlier-leader pattern as Aloha.

id: case:Professor Reggie Pelloux MIT fatigue and fracture mentorship
cluster_id: Professor Reggie Pelloux MIT fatigue and fracture mentorship
content:
Professor Reggie Pelloux MIT fatigue and fracture mentorship Tom credits Pelloux (ScD MIT, then Boeing, then MIT faculty) as his fatigue-and-fracture teacher. Frames Boeing's fracture-mechanics culture.

## Figures referenced (recurring numeric anchors, not cases)

cluster_id: Howard Hughes pressurized aircraft development
content: Howard Hughes pressurized aircraft development Used to anchor the calculation of how much water is in the atmosphere — Hughes pioneered flying above the clouds, which is why we know cloud-layer thicknesses. Sets up the "one percent times 10,000 feet" rough-magnitude estimation.

cluster_id: US Army materials study
content: US Army materials study Million-dollar Army study to identify which material the Army would purchase most over the next 20-30 years. Answer: steel. Tom's example of waste in government materials research — he could have told them for free. Million-dollar study, ~mid-1990s, asking what the material of the future for the Army would be. Conclusion: steel. Used as the punchline of the cost-strength-toughness Ashby argument.

id: case:National Academy of Sciences 2002-2003 Defense Department materials research committee
cluster_id: National Academy of Sciences 2002-2003 Defense Department materials research committee
content: National Academy of Sciences 2002-2003 Defense Department materials research committee The committee on which Tom served and to which he contributed the appendix that is the source of the handout used throughout the lecture. Used to frame the entire materials-cost discussion that follows.

id: case:Westbrook 1962 General Electric structural materials price-vs-volume plot
cluster_id: Westbrook 1962 General Electric structural materials price-vs-volume plot
content: Westbrook 1962 General Electric structural materials price-vs-volume plot The classic plot Tom uses to introduce the price/volume relationship in structural materials. Source: Jack Westbrook, internal GE memo, 1962. Notable as a corpus-recurring figure.

id: case:General Electric synthetic diamond development (Tracy Hall)
cluster_id: General Electric synthetic diamond development (Tracy Hall)
content: General Electric synthetic diamond development (Tracy Hall) Aside to explain why diamond appears on Westbrook's structural-materials plot — GE had a near-monopoly on synthetic diamonds at the time of the 1962 plot.

id: case:Boeing aircraft disc weight savings analysis (1990 LGO study)
cluster_id: Boeing aircraft disc weight savings analysis (1990 LGO study)
content: Boeing aircraft disc weight savings analysis (1990 LGO study) First LGO thesis student went to Boeing, recovered the proprietary $188/lb value-of-a-pound-saved figure that confirmed Tom's $200/lb rule of thumb. 1990 MIT LGO students at Boeing found the actual value of weight saved on a commercial aircraft was $188/lb — the source of Tom's "round to $200/lb" figure.

id: case:Peter Bridenbaugh Alcoa aluminum vehicle economics communication (October 2001)
cluster_id: Peter Bridenbaugh Alcoa aluminum vehicle economics communication (October 2001)
content: Peter Bridenbaugh Alcoa aluminum vehicle economics communication (October 2001) Personal communication, October 11, 2001. Tom hedged his "all-aluminum vehicles need $4/gal gas" claim to avoid offending Bridenbaugh, who at the break confirmed Tom's actual $2/lb working figure.

cluster_id: Nimitz-class carrier weight creep
content: Nimitz-class carrier weight creep Carriers gain 250 tons/year, growing from ~60-65K tons at class introduction to ~90K tons 60 years later, mostly at the top of the ship. The economic driver for the HSLA-65 feasibility study that follows. Nimitz-class carriers gain 250 tons per year over the hull life, mostly topside. Drove the HSLA-60 investigation: Newport News estimated 2,000 tons savings if HSLA-60 substituted for lower-strength components. 250 tons/year weight gain across the class from the early 1960s through 2000, used to motivate the structural lightweighting program.

id: case:Soviet scandium aluminum alloys / aluminum baseball bats
cluster_id: Soviet scandium aluminum alloys / aluminum baseball bats
content: Soviet scandium aluminum alloys / aluminum baseball bats Worldwide scandium production is only 2,000 tons/year. The high-strength aluminum alloys for baseball bats derive from Soviet aluminum-scandium research.

cluster_id: Tom Eagar 80-year-old home renovation (Spring 2016)
content: Tom Eagar 80-year-old home renovation (Spring 2016) Personal anecdote, surfaces twice. In §5 it anchors the electric-vehicle infrastructure cost discussion (three driveway outlets being wired during a down-to-the-studs renovation). In §7 it anchors the cast-iron sewer pipe corrosion-replacement point and the plastic-vs-cast-iron longevity comparison. Real-time during this lecture: "they just started digging out the basement."

cluster_id: Wright Brothers aircraft engine
content: Wright Brothers aircraft engine First aerospace use of aluminum-copper alloy (engine housing, 1903). Used to anchor the historical depth of the 2000-series aerospace alloys. Used to push back on the framing of aluminum as a "new" structural material.

cluster_id: Coca-Cola can manufacturing
content: Coca-Cola can manufacturing 3004 is "thirty or forty percent of all the aluminum made" — one of the largest-tonnage alloys, work-hardened, lightly alloyed with manganese and magnesium. Used to illustrate multi-stage deep drawing plus ironing in one stroke, with five-micron die tolerances and supercomputer design.

id: case:Werner Ladder Company extrusion temper case
cluster_id: Werner Ladder Company extrusion temper case
content: Werner Ladder Company extrusion temper case Used to illustrate T1 temper — extrusion heat itself serves as the solutionizing treatment; the ladder rail ages naturally as it cools in the plant. A teaching scenario rather than a documented failure case.

cluster_id: Upstate New York brewery (1975)
content: Upstate New York brewery (1975)

cluster_id: GTD-111 superalloy patent dispute
content: GTD-111 superalloy patent dispute GE developed GTD-111 in early 1980s but couldn't patent the composition (too overlapped); patent office denied the heat-treatment patent for 18 years, then granted it after competitors had adopted the alloy. Royalty windfall. Chromalloy rejuvenation work on GTD-111 blades via HIP ties the case to §4. The central developed case of the lecture. GE files a heat-treatment patent in ~1986; the patent office rejects; the industry adopts the alloy; ~2001-2006 the patent issues; everyone is suddenly infringing. Tom's master's-thesis student finds a HIP-based rejuvenation workaround for an engine-refurbishment company.

cluster_id: Caroline Joseph corrosion testing project
content: Caroline Joseph corrosion testing project Student LGO internship at a Houston oil company. Corrosion analysis correctly recommended clad pipe, but the project was canceled for external reasons: host-country offset requirements and local-worker employment quotas.

id: case:Evanston Wyoming hydrogen sulfide gas field operations
cluster_id: Evanston Wyoming hydrogen sulfide gas field operations
content: Evanston Wyoming hydrogen sulfide gas field operations Tom's visit to the sour-gas dome at Evanston, including the "Danger, toxic gases" roadside signs and the two competing approaches (Chevron heated sulfur pipeline vs. Amoco's 10-mile sulfur-trucking road) to handling the H2S byproduct. Sets up sulfide stress corrosion cracking as a hydrogen-cracking variant.

id: case:Japan-US Oil and Steel Embargo (World War II)
cluster_id: Japan-US Oil and Steel Embargo (World War II)
content: Japan-US Oil and Steel Embargo (World War II) US 1930s cutoff of scrap steel shipments to Japan as one cause of Pacific War; framed in context of attempted appeasement re: Nanking. Externalities as military precipitant. US scrap iron/steel withholding and oil cutoff to Japan triggered Pearl Harbor — compared to modern North Korea and Iran sanctions. Military externality. The 1941 embargo of oil (Long Beach) and scrap iron to Japan in response to atrocities in China is presented as the proximate cause of Pearl Harbor. Tom develops the case through Japanese carrier strategy (four-carrier strike force aimed at U.S. carriers, which were at sea).

cluster_id: U.S. copper tubing manufacturing
content: U.S. copper tubing manufacturing

id: case:Sweden cadmium electrical switch fire hazard
cluster_id: Sweden cadmium electrical switch fire hazard
content: Sweden cadmium electrical switch fire hazard 1970s-80s Swedish environmental policy outlawed Cd in electrical components. Within three years, house fires from inadequate arc-suppression in <15A switches forced reversal. Teaching point: 0.1% CdO in Ag contacts raises arc-suppression rating from ~7A to 15A. Sweden outlawed cadmium ~30 years ago (i.e., ~1982 from a 2012 lecture). Light switches without cadmium oxide arc-suppression burned down houses; standard relaxed for electrical switches.

cluster_id: Norwegian chlorine elimination proposal
content: Norwegian chlorine elimination proposal Bob Rose's periodic-table-with-chlorine-X'd-out gift to Tom — Norwegians proposed banning an element. Used as setup for the Congress-DNA-oxygen punchline.

cluster_id: Congressional DNA-destruction material ban proposal
content: Congressional DNA-destruction material ban proposal Congress nearly passed a law banning anything that destroys DNA; would have outlawed oxygen. Used as the punchline for "politicians taking over science."

id: case:Chinese aluminum overproduction and market displacement
cluster_id: Chinese aluminum overproduction and market displacement
content: Chinese aluminum overproduction and market displacement Tom redirects to China's 250% aluminum capacity increase over six years. Framed as China selling aluminum cheap to export coal-derived energy, hurting global aluminum producers.

cluster_id: 1980s-1990s Wyoming coal mining operations
content: 1980s-1990s Wyoming coal mining operations Tom's first Alberta tar sands consulting case (when oil was ~$30/bbl and extraction cost ~$30/bbl); contrasted with current (2014) state ($50/bbl extraction, $100/bbl market price). Used to make the point that "running out of oil" really means running out of $2/bbl oil — heavy oil reserves remain enormous.

cluster_id: Molten Metal Technologies
content: Molten Metal Technologies Extended case study of an MIT-licensed startup (1989–1997) that used molten steel baths for toxic waste processing. Tom narrates: the technology origin (Chris Nagel, ex-US Steel); MIT's John Preston as licensing officer with conflicting financial interest; venture promotion through Vic Gatto, Al Gore, Maurice Strong, Michael Porter; the technical failures (refractory destruction by sodium/chlorine, phosgene formation, dioxin/furan production, bismuth/antimony steel contamination); MIT institutional conflicts of interest; bankruptcy in 1997; Preston's later fraud conviction. Tom's central conflict-of-interest case. Chemical engineer at US Steel research proposes using molten iron as a universal high-temperature solvent for environmental waste; US Steel declines to patent. Founder partners with John Preston (head of MIT TLO) to start Molten Metal Technology; both worth $30M each before building a plant. Fall River, MA induction-melting facility. Claims to make radioactive waste non-radioactive (Wall Street Journal front page). Al Gore presidential-campaign technology roundtable at Kresge, organized by Preston, who included his own 30%-owned company without disclosure. MIT VPR informed of the conflict; declined to act. Preston eventually resigns from TLO in disgrace following Justice Department interest.

cluster_id: A Civil Action (Woburn chemical spill)
content: A Civil Action (Woburn chemical spill) Tom invokes the Duvall/Travolta exchange to make his point that legal advocacy displaces truth-seeking. Used as a rhetorical frame for the MMT ethics narrative.

cluster_id: Molten Metal Technology tenure case
content: Molten Metal Technology tenure case A junior MIT materials faculty member receiving MMT research funding from Nagel was denied tenure after Tom (as department head) refused to suppress his publication. Tom alleges his predecessor as department head, who was on MMT's scientific advisory board, polluted the tenure case by influencing external letters (notably from Professor Fuwa of Tohoku University). The professor was later denied tenure at MIT and became a tenured full professor at Boston University.

id: case:Doc Edgerton stroboscope and EG&G founding
cluster_id: Doc Edgerton stroboscope and EG&G founding
content: Doc Edgerton stroboscope and EG&G founding Parallel case to MMT origin. GE funded Edgerton's stroboscope research at MIT, didn't see commercial value, let him keep the IP; Edgerton became wealthy, founded EG&G, funded the Boston Science Museum. Tom uses the parallel to set up the US Steel / Nagel handoff at §2.p6.

id: case:Al Gore MIT commencement buzzword bingo hack
cluster_id: Al Gore MIT commencement buzzword bingo hack
content: Al Gore MIT commencement buzzword bingo hack Brief MIT-culture anecdote in the middle of the MMT hype narrative; characterizes Gore's relationship to MIT technology promotion. Sloan students distributed buzzword bingo cards as graduates entered; Secret Service tipped off Gore.

id: case:Nashua Corporation board collapse and acquisition failure
cluster_id: Nashua Corporation board collapse and acquisition failure
content: Nashua Corporation board collapse and acquisition failure Tom's personal experience on the Nashua Corporation board (1993 onward). A new CEO took the half-billion-dollar company to a quarter-billion in one year; pushed for a twenty-five-million-dollar European acquisition; twelve other board members voted yes despite all twelve having articulated reasons against. Tom abstained. He was later given a Steuben glass mountain lion sculpture as a parting gift — the "mountain lion ready to pounce" — and a consulting retainer. Used as the closing demonstration of the lecture's lesson about going along with the crowd. Used to make the "balance professional and personal" point. New CEO's spouse wanted to stay in California; CEO failed within a year. Charlie Clough's regret about not interviewing the spouse.

id: case:General Electric boiling water reactor stress corrosion cracking
cluster_id: General Electric boiling water reactor stress corrosion cracking
content: General Electric boiling water reactor stress corrosion cracking Cited as the exemplar of attacking a problem across all three of Tom's circles (metallurgy / mechanical / corrosion) rather than just the metallurgist's circle. GE's discovery thirty years prior that 304 stainless reactor components were cracking on solidification, traced to trace sulfur. Motivated the development of the Varestraint test at RPI. Sensitization of stainless steel welds in BWR safe ends cost GE "a couple billion dollars" in the 1970s. Westinghouse PWRs avoided it by using Inconel (10× the cost) for higher temperatures. The teaching consequence of the John Wulff sensitization patent and the broader carbon-control rationale. GE's response to in-reactor sensitization-driven SCC, via the 304→304L→ultra-low-carbon→LN-grade (low-carbon, nitrogen-strengthened) sequence. Tom uses it to motivate the AOD-driven cost collapse for low-carbon stainless production. Tom's marquee case for sensitization in service. GE built 1970s boiling water reactors using 304 stainless steel and incurred a two-billion-dollar worldwide problem from stress corrosion cracking in ultra-pure water with parts-per-million chlorine and oxygen. Motivated industry-wide move to 304L and 304LN.

cluster_id: Los Angeles class submarine life extension hull evaluation
content: Los Angeles class submarine life extension hull evaluation Brief reference. Hull condition is good; lifetime limited by internal components and rate of technological advance.

content: Three interacting circles (metallurgy / mechanical / corrosion) Tom's framework for thinking about welding-related failures. Each problem can be attacked by shrinking any of the three circles; the metallurgy-only orientation of US welding practice is named as a limitation.
