Rensselaer Hydrogen Diffusion Experiments (1950s–1960s) RPI experiment from "back in the 1970s" — polished, stressed, cracked steel specimen immersed in water under microscope; bubbles observed at the crack tip increasing with applied stress. Used to motivate the energy argument for why hydrogen migrates to crack tips. Notched-tensile specimens showing hydrogen bubbles diffusing to the advancing crack tip under microscopy. Tom recalls a researcher (rendered by captioner as "Apollo Tiffany" — identity unconfirmed).

## Figures and framing statistics referenced (not cases)

cluster_id: Electroplated bicycle tube fatality
content: Electroplated bicycle tube fatality Brief callback ("we talked about electroplating of bicycle tubes") used to anchor the 375°F bake-out rule. If the tube had been baked within an hour of plating, no hydrogen crack would have formed, no fatigue propagation, no paraplegia.

id: case:Nautilus submarine hydrogen cracking during construction
cluster_id: Nautilus submarine hydrogen cracking during construction
content: Nautilus submarine hydrogen cracking during construction Centerpiece historical case of the lecture. Mid-1950s Nautilus mockup construction with HY-80; egg-crate stiffener welds made during the day; cracks audible as rifle-shot reports during the night shift — delayed hydrogen cracking, 8-hour diffusion timescale to crack tip. Workaround: switch to austenitic stainless steel electrodes (FCC structure, higher H solubility, lower cracking susceptibility) at the cost of undermatched strength.

id: case:Seawolf submarine welding hydrogen embrittlement failures
cluster_id: Seawolf submarine welding hydrogen embrittlement failures
content: Seawolf submarine welding hydrogen embrittlement failures One-sentence flag — "I can tell you a story about welding of the Seawolf submarine, and I tracked it down in my opinion to lubricants." Tom does not develop the case here. The hydrocarbon-as-hydrogen-source point is what's being illustrated.

id: case:Groton Connecticut submarine welding hydrogen embrittlement failures
cluster_id: Groton Connecticut submarine welding hydrogen embrittlement failures
content: Groton Connecticut submarine welding hydrogen embrittlement failures Operational practice case — New London / Groton shipyard electrode-issuance and stub-return protocols. 20 electrodes at a time, 2-hour exposure limit, insulated canisters, mandatory stub return. Also: 85% relative humidity prohibition violated ~200 days/year at east-coast shipyards.

cluster_id: ESAB founding from muddy-electrode discovery (Gothenburg ~1910)
content: ESAB founding from muddy-electrode discovery (Gothenburg ~1910) Origin story for mineral-coated electrodes. Welder in Gothenburg dipped bar electrode in mud, found mineral coating excluded atmospheric nitrogen and eliminated porosity. Became basis of ESAB, now one of the world's largest welding companies. Also: contemporary discovery of cellulosic coatings from paper-wrapped electrodes.

cluster_id: Henry Bessemer converter development (1856)
content: Henry Bessemer converter development (1856) Bessemer figures out how to make tons of steel rather than hundreds of pounds; ~10 years of process perfection; the inflection point Tom uses to mark "the Iron Age." Note: a related but distinct entry exists in the canon ("Basic oxygen furnace introduction in Austria"); Bessemer's converter is the prior generation.

id: case:Andrew Carnegie and US Steel founding
cluster_id: Andrew Carnegie and US Steel founding
content: Andrew Carnegie and US Steel founding Carnegie scales Bessemer's process to economies of scale, becoming the richest man in the world; sells to JP Morgan for $480M; US Steel later represents the establishment that fails to adopt BOF and continuous casting.

cluster_id: US Steel basic open hearth (early 1970s)
content: US Steel basic open hearth (early 1970s) Tom's central indictment of US Steel management: in the early 1970s, after BOF had been proven for a decade, US Steel built the last large open hearths (450-ton capacity) at ~$1B cost. "Billion-dollar dinosaurs."

cluster_id: Bao Steel government-funded growth
content: Bao Steel government-funded growth Current (2016) world's largest steel company; Chinese government funded.

id: case:Lakshmi Mittal steel mill acquisition strategy
cluster_id: Lakshmi Mittal steel mill acquisition strategy
content: Lakshmi Mittal steel mill acquisition strategy "They buy plants at ten cents on the dollar when the great managers run them into the ground." Acquired Burns Harbor from bankrupt Bethlehem. Mittal buying up distressed steel companies at two cents on the dollar in the late '80s and early '90s; ArcelorMittal as proof that the future-of-metals thesis was right. "This guy in India" bought up unprofitable steel companies for a song; ArcelorMittal became the second largest steel company in the world. Used to illustrate that Wall Street misread steel's productivity-driven margin collapse as industry decline. "Goes around buying up steel companies for a song" — the case that vindicates Tom's "steel isn't dead" thesis against Wall Street and Ned Thomas. Mittal recognized in the 1980s that worldwide steel excess capacity was temporary; bought up cheap steel companies (ten cents on the dollar); by 2005 sitting on a fortune as capacity caught up with demand. ArcelorMittal as conglomerate of ~15 pre-1970 firms. Mittal bought distressed steel mills worldwide at ~10¢ on the dollar while Wall Street dumped them; became multi-billionaire as overcapacity worked out. Arcelor Mittal (Luxembourg-based) is the largest European steelmaker; the Thyssen Krupp merger discussion (2017) would make them #2 worldwide after Baosteel. Mittal bought distressed US steel mills at ten cents on the dollar in the late 1980s while Wall Street pronounced steel dead. Used to illustrate the productivity-disguised-as-decline pattern: US steel halved employment 1980–1990 with constant output, doubling productivity at 6–7%/year vs. 1% economy-wide. Closing case. Indian industrialist bought distressed U.S. and European mills at ten cents on the dollar in the 1980s–90s when Wall Street wrote off steel as a dying industry. Became multi-billionaire when overcapacity worked itself out.

cluster_id: 1991 future-of-metals Welding Journal article
content: 1991 future-of-metals Welding Journal article Tom's published argument that metals were not dying, presented against the ceramics/composites/superconductor hype of the late 1980s. Returned to throughout §1 and §2 as the framing device for the productivity argument.

cluster_id: US Steel Price Rollback
content: US Steel Price Rollback President Kennedy forces U.S. Steel to roll back a price increase in 1962. Steel-industry executives cite this as the moment they lost profitability; Tom uses it to make the point that steel was the commodity controlling the global economy before the 1973 oil embargo.

id: case:MIT basement stainless steel carbon control technology
cluster_id: MIT basement stainless steel carbon control technology
content: MIT basement stainless steel carbon control technology Low-carbon stainless steel technology invented in the basement of Building 8 in the 1950s; John Chipman as the materials department head (1945–1962) who taught the world how to make reproducible-chemistry steel. The graduate-student-to-industry pipeline that lowered stainless steel costs.

id: case:Cyril Smith humanities course on materials history
cluster_id: Cyril Smith humanities course on materials history
content: Cyril Smith humanities course on materials history Tom's junior-year humanities paper on the hardening of steel, taught by Cyril Smith (former University of Chicago metallurgist who became MIT institute professor in humanities, archaeology of materials).

cluster_id: Medieval sword tempering practice
content: Medieval sword tempering practice Meteoric iron as the first usable steel; the discovery that hammering, heating, quenching, and tempering produce hardness and ductility. The Crusades-era legend of quenching hot steel by running it through a living slave.

id: case:Eagar manganese deposition expert witness testimony
cluster_id: Eagar manganese deposition expert witness testimony
content: Eagar manganese deposition expert witness testimony The full arc — sulfur as a 1870s–1880s European problem, Spiegeleisen as the manganese-bearing solution, manganese's essentiality for health, the 1980s–1990s welding-industry litigation, Tom's testimony in Danville, Illinois, the box-of-raisins comparison, the "objection your honor" courtroom moment. Most developed teaching unit in the lecture.

cluster_id: Welding industry manganese litigation
content: Welding industry manganese litigation The class-action wave against the welding industry on manganese-Parkinson's claims; $100M+ in legal defense costs; the eventual scientific resolution that manganism attacks a different part of the brain than Parkinson's; plaintiffs' attorneys migrating from asbestos to welding.

id: case:General Motors Linden New Jersey locating pin failure
cluster_id: General Motors Linden New Jersey locating pin failure
content: General Motors Linden New Jersey locating pin failure Recap from a prior session. Used as the canonical TPM example — a two-dollar pin that a maintenance engineer never replaced caused several percent scrap. Setup for the broader discussion of acceptable-defect thresholds. Former LFM student Bill Fonte called Tom in to diagnose welding defects at GM's Linden, NJ plant. On-site walkthrough revealed (a) oil contamination preventing electrical ground, (b) a worn hardened-steel locating pin causing fixture slippage, (c) unnecessary galvanizing on an interior hinge causing frosty welds. Each defect was a "hundred dollar bill on the floor" visible to anyone who would walk the line.

cluster_id: Toyota supplier quality crisis (1990s)
content: Toyota supplier quality crisis (1990s) 1990s Columbus, Ohio. A Tier-1 supplier to Honda/GM/Ford/Chrysler arrived 45 minutes late to a dinner because Toyota had summoned him to fix a parts problem same-day. Used to contrast Japanese collaborative supplier management with GM's adversarial "fix it by 9 AM or we sue" approach.

cluster_id: 1973 Honda Civic corrosion failure
content: 1973 Honda Civic corrosion failure Early 1970s Honda Civics rusting within 12 months of purchase. Used to illustrate Japanese cultural response to quality embarrassment — they were mortified and fixed it, leading to the modern reputation for reliability. Quality-reputation case. Honda's 1973 Civic rusted through in a year; their response built the modern Honda body-engineering reputation. Honda Civics rusting within twelve months in the mid-1970s as origin story for Honda's modern quality culture. "The Japanese don't like to be embarrassed."

id: case:Raytheon Aegis missile part aluminum bending incident
cluster_id: Raytheon Aegis missile part aluminum bending incident
content: Raytheon Aegis missile part aluminum bending incident Early 1980s. A worker straightened a bent aluminum bar with a handheld torch — destroying the heat treatment. Navy inspector caught the lack of procedure, shut down the 400-worker plant. Tom (after Mortensen begged off) called it a tempest in a teapot, wrote up the analysis, and the plant was back in operation by Friday. Used to illustrate Navy SUBSAFE-era documented-procedure enforcement. Used to illustrate the role of resident DOD inspectors and the cost of procedure gaps. Navy inspector halts thousand-employee plant for several days; Tom's consulting letter reopens production within 48 hours. Illustration of ISO 9000's "everything must have a written procedure" requirement. Navy inspector found a worker putting a torch to heat-treated aluminum with no documented procedure; plant shut down for three days.

id: case:Upton Sinclair meatpacking industry exposure and Food and Drug Act
cluster_id: Upton Sinclair meatpacking industry exposure and Food and Drug Act
content: Upton Sinclair meatpacking industry exposure and Food and Drug Act Brief historical anchor for FDA authority — Upton Sinclair's 1906 book about the meat industry led to the Food and Drug Act. Used to root current FDA Good Manufacturing Practice regulation in a century-old legislative response.

id: case:Government helicopter design approval and manufacturer liability protection
cluster_id: Government helicopter design approval and manufacturer liability protection
content: Government helicopter design approval and manufacturer liability protection Early 1990s Supreme Court decision (referenced but not named — likely Boyle v. United Technologies). Once the government accepts a contractor's design in writing, the contractor cannot be sued on a design-defect theory. Rationale: cutting-edge defense systems will make mistakes, and Congress chose to absorb that risk. Tom uses this to extend the design-freeze concept from ISO 9000 to defense procurement.

id: case:Frederick Fish patent attorney (Wright Brothers, Alexander Graham Bell)
cluster_id: Frederick Fish patent attorney (Wright Brothers, Alexander Graham Bell)

id: case:Thixotropic/semi-solid casting patent suppression at MIT
cluster_id: Thixotropic/semi-solid casting patent suppression at MIT
content: Thixotropic/semi-solid casting patent suppression at MIT The rheocast / thixocast / thixomolding family of processes, developed by Flemings' student in 1970, licensed by MIT to a company that sat on it 10–15 years to suppress competition. Used to teach (a) the physical principle (extracting half the heat of fusion before injection) and (b) the institutional consequence — MIT's march-in-rights patent reform.

id: case:Modern single-crystal turbine blade casting (core shift defect)
cluster_id: Modern single-crystal turbine blade casting (core shift defect)
content: Modern single-crystal turbine blade casting (core shift defect) 15-thousandths-inch walls with ceramic-core shift up to 5–10 thou leaving zero wall remaining; 100% CAT-scan inspection at a half-million-dollar machine; <30% scrap rate the production target.

id: case:NASA deep-space mission plutonium-fueled thermoelectric generators with iridium containment
cluster_id: NASA deep-space mission plutonium-fueled thermoelectric generators with iridium containment
content: NASA deep-space mission plutonium-fueled thermoelectric generators with iridium containment Tom's worked example of why iridium would be the perfect jet-engine material (3000°C melting point) but is impossible at scale (100 oz/year world production). Pivots into the actual deployed application: iridium spheres containing plutonium-238 for RTGs on deep-space probes, with the safety concern that a launch failure scatters nuclear-warhead material into the Atlantic. Used as an example of an exotic welding application (iridium) — about once every 25 years there is a real need to weld iridium spheres around plutonium for deep-space spacecraft RTGs.

id: case:US Army M16 firing pin semi-solid steel injection molding program
cluster_id: US Army M16 firing pin semi-solid steel injection molding program
content: US Army M16 firing pin semi-solid steel injection molding program 1970s Army program that gave Flemings' group millions to injection-mold semisolid steel firing pins. Failed because no mold material could withstand the temperatures; 100 parts per $100,000 mold. Used to mark the limit of the semisolid process for steel.

cluster_id: Vancouver World's Fair gold coin
content: Vancouver World's Fair gold coin 36-inch-diameter, 3/4-inch-thick 14-karat gold display coin Tom welded together from cast bars without distortion. ~$4–5M of gold, recovered after the fair.

id: case:Reading Pennsylvania copper plant deoxidation process
cluster_id: Reading Pennsylvania copper plant deoxidation process
content: Reading Pennsylvania copper plant deoxidation process Green tree trunks thrown into molten copper baths to deoxidize — "poling the bath." Tom proposes (uncertain) that "electrolytic tough pitch" copper's name derives from the pitch resins in the trunk.

id: case:Continuous casting of steel strip (50-year unsolved challenge)
cluster_id: Continuous casting of steel strip (50-year unsolved challenge)
content: Continuous casting of steel strip (50-year unsolved challenge) Hazelett's attempt to extend their copper-on-steel-band process to steel strip. Failure mode: steel-on-steel has no thermal conductivity advantage; bands wear out. The "billion-dollar-if-you-solve-it" framing.

id: case:Amtrak New Haven to Boston trolley wire / Amtrak catenary wire procurement fraud case
cluster_id: Amtrak New Haven to Boston trolley wire / Amtrak catenary wire procurement fraud case
content: Amtrak New Haven to Boston trolley wire / Amtrak catenary wire procurement fraud case Tom's forensic case. British supplier's caster couldn't deliver enough cross-sectional-area reduction; large grains → rough surface → arcing at 100 mph. Tom rejects $6M of wire on two days' notice; British firm sues; counter-investigation by US federal authorities reveals sole-source procurement fraud (Phelps Dodge had been kept out of the bid). Wire is replaced with Phelps Dodge material via the Conform redundant-deformation process. The Providence test-track 6-mile arcing demonstration is the dispositive forensic evidence.

cluster_id: Conform process development
content:
Conform process development Mentioned as the redundant-deformation process Phelps Dodge used to win the replacement contract; also as the process the Army is now evaluating for magnesium armors. British lab origin.

## Cases mentioned in passing British severe-plastic-deformation extrusion process from ~30 years ago, in which metal is squeezed through a 90° die at 30× normal extrusion energy, yielding extreme strength and ductility. Tom's Phelps Dodge trolley-wire procurement for the New Hampshire–Boston rail connection used Conform-made wire.

cluster_id: Ingot-cast rim steel surface purity
content: Ingot-cast rim steel surface purity Why ingot-cast rim steel gave the best sheet properties — first stuff to solidify on the mold wall is the purest iron. Used to argue that the casting method has to be chosen for the product (sheet vs. plate).

id: case:1985 Ford Aerostar rear axle fatigue failures
cluster_id: 1985 Ford Aerostar rear axle fatigue failures
content: 1985 Ford Aerostar rear axle fatigue failures The shock to Ford when high-strength steel substitution for fuel-economy weight reduction failed in fatigue — Ford's design engineers didn't know what bridge engineers had known for forty years, that welded joints get no fatigue benefit from higher strength steels. Welded rear axle of HSLA steel, designed assuming fatigue strength proportional to tensile strength. Brackets welded onto axle; field failures in first six months. Big product recall. Triggered industry-wide work on fatigue of welded HSLA sheet.

cluster_id: Cement truck case
content: Cement truck case Brief mention. Aluminum water tanks on cement trucks with saddle arrangements — change in stiffness at the saddle creates a fatigue crack location from sloshing liquid.

cluster_id: Caterpillar earthmoving machinery fatigue study
content: Caterpillar earthmoving machinery fatigue study Caterpillar's multi-decade, multi-hundred-million-dollar program to develop welding procedures (torch angle, weave pattern, pulse current, robotic consistency) that produce weld profiles good enough to gain fatigue benefit from higher-strength steels (50 ksi → 60–70 ksi HSLA). Tom consulted briefly; most work is proprietary.

cluster_id: Guthrie weld toe fatigue research
content: Guthrie weld toe fatigue research Guthrie's career at the British Welding Institute developing TIG dressing, full-penetration welds, and machined toe profiles to recover the strength-fatigue benefit lost in as-welded fillet joints.

id: case:Coast Guard cutter bracket undermatching case
cluster_id: Coast Guard cutter bracket undermatching case
content: Coast Guard cutter bracket undermatching case Brief reference. Undermatching filler metal acceptable here because the brackets had ample weld area, the substrate was high-strength for deflection (not strength) reasons, and undermatching gave better corrosion resistance and toughness.

id: case:Navy PH stainless steel hydrofoil rudder/propeller
cluster_id: Navy PH stainless steel hydrofoil rudder/propeller
content: Navy PH stainless steel hydrofoil rudder/propeller Navy used precipitation-hardened stainless on hydrofoil rudders or propellers — high strength, lightweight, 180 ksi. Aluminum hull, PH stainless in the drive end. "We created a few problems back there" — implies a welding consulting episode not developed here.

cluster_id: US Navy superaustenitic submarine material evaluation
content: US Navy superaustenitic submarine material evaluation Brief reference. Navy considered replacing HY-100 with super-austenitic stainless (zero ferrite, non-magnetic, no acoustic signature) ten or fifteen years prior. Rejected as overpriced and unnecessary given the threat environment.

content: Either `Farberware cooking pot thermal warping` or `Farberware stainless steel cookware pot cracking` (one of several Farberware entries) Brief reference. Tom's pot had varying ferrite content from bottom to top — 5–10% ferrite at the bottom, ~80–90% martensite (transformed by deformation) at the top, making the top magnetic. id: case:Fiberglass truck bed trial at coal mine
cluster_id: Fiberglass truck bed trial at coal mine
content: Fiberglass truck bed trial at coal mine Joel Clark, working with Ford, supplied resin-molded composite truck beds to a coal mining operation for a six-month wear test alongside steel beds. The mine refused to return the composite beds because they didn't crack. Used to show composites can win on durability where cost is acceptable.

cluster_id: Longfellow Bridge guardrail perforation
content: Longfellow Bridge guardrail perforation Hundred-year-old Longfellow Bridge handrails are rusted through, perforated, where snow (pH 5.5 frozen acid rain) accumulates and melts. Used to teach atmospheric corrosion rate (~4 mil/year) and the square-root-of-time scaling.

id: case:New England highway bridge rebar corrosion
cluster_id: New England highway bridge rebar corrosion
content: New England highway bridge rebar corrosion Rebar corrosion expands the steel, blows out concrete, creates highway potholes; full bridge-deck rebuilds required every ~20 years. Used to set up corrosion as steel's Achilles heel and motivate galvanized / stainless / nickel-base rebar substitution attempts.

id: case:Black iron pipe corrosion rate field observation
cluster_id: Black iron pipe corrosion rate field observation
content: Black iron pipe corrosion rate field observation Physical-object demonstration. Tom produces black iron pipe to teach that the magnetite (Fe3O4) scale formed at hot-rolling temperatures adheres to steel because its CTE matches, in contrast to hematite rust which spalls off. Tom holds up a Home Depot pipe nipple as a physical-object demonstration. Magnetite (Fe₃O₄) coating from mill heat treatment provides practical nobility. Teaching numbers: 0.002–0.010 inches/year corrosion rate; ~25-year shipboard piping lifetime — the historical naval ship life until NAVSEA mandated 50-year lifetime, forcing the move to cupro-nickel, Monel, and titanium.

id: case:Steel-toe boot heat treating tank stress corrosion cracking / hydrogen embrittlement
cluster_id: Steel-toe boot heat treating tank stress corrosion cracking / hydrogen embrittlement
content: Steel-toe boot heat treating tank stress corrosion cracking / hydrogen embrittlement Heat-treating shop near Boston airport built a large welded steel tank for sodium nitrate quench bath of steel-toe boot toes. Tank cracked at the welds. Literature said sodium nitrate causes stress corrosion cracking; Tom's U-bend test with anodic polarization wouldn't crack the specimen, but reversing the polarity (cathodic) cracked it within 24 hours. The real mechanism was hydrogen embrittlement, not SCC.

id: case:USS Sea Wolf submarine hull cracking
cluster_id: USS Sea Wolf submarine hull cracking
content: USS Sea Wolf submarine hull cracking Around 1992 at Groton (Electric Boat), the Navy moved from HY-80 to HY-100 for the Sea Wolf hull. A grinder noticed swarf lining up along sub-eighth-inch cracks in completed welds. Re-inspection found all welds (18% of hull complete) full of microscopic hydrogen cracks. Required scrapping the completed portion, delaying the program a year and costing ~$2 billion. Fix: preheat the steel to 400°F, with welders working in recirculated-liquid blue jelly suits inside heated submarine compartments.

id: case:Nuclear submarine welding hydrogen embrittlement cracks
cluster_id: Nuclear submarine welding hydrogen embrittlement cracks
content: Nuclear submarine welding hydrogen embrittlement cracks General reference to Groton submarine welding: if hydrogen isn't controlled, night-shift welders hear cracks running through the steel like rifle shots. Sets up the Sea Wolf case at §5.p7.

cluster_id: Bolt hydrogen embrittlement cracking dispute
content: Bolt hydrogen embrittlement cracking dispute A cracked bolt that Dr. Ballinger circulated in class. Tom and Ballinger are still debating whether the mechanism is hydrogen embrittlement (cathodic) or stress corrosion cracking (anodic). Used to introduce the anode/cathode distinction between the two mechanisms.

cluster_id: USS Seawolf hydrogen cracking
content: USS Seawolf hydrogen cracking Tom's role as one of five outside experts brought in by the Navy in 1991–92 to advise on the Electric Boat HY-100 weld failures. His report uniquely concluded the cause was dirty welding wire (drawing-lubricant contamination, worse on smaller-diameter wire due to higher surface-to-volume ratio). Eighteen percent of the hull was riddled with sixteenth-inch under-bead cracks in weld metal, discovered when a grinder noticed swarf aligning magnetically.

content: Davenport Iowa aluminum plate mechanical stress relief Boeing/Alcoa aircraft wing plate, up to 50 ft long and 4 in. thick, mechanically stress-relieved by a multi-million-pound hydraulic stretcher that elongates the plate three percent in plastic deformation.

cluster_id: Submarine first-deep-dive mechanical stress relief
content: Submarine first-deep-dive mechanical stress relief The hull welds of a new submarine are plastically deformed and stress-relieved on the first deep dive, on which the shipyard managers themselves are aboard — a quality-control incentive structure Tom highlights as exemplary.

cluster_id: Bonal Technologies / vibratory stress relief
content: Bonal Technologies / vibratory stress relief Fifty-year story of Bonal Technologies of Columbus, Ohio, selling piezoelectric vibratory stress relief. US Navy spent over $1M evaluating it; British Welding Institute spent several million on behalf of oil companies; neither uses it. Closes with a recent email inquiry from a $10B/year aluminum company asking Tom's opinion.

id: case:JG Sylvester and Associates consulting apprenticeship
cluster_id: JG Sylvester and Associates consulting apprenticeship
content: JG Sylvester and Associates consulting apprenticeship How Tom learned failure analysis. Returning to MIT from Bethlehem Steel in 1976 with a one-third pay cut and a growing family, Tom needed consulting income. Bruce Sylvester (who ran his late father's metallurgical/NDT firm south of Boston) hired Tom on the side. Sylvester wanted to expand into diving and nuclear failure analysis; his prior staff metallurgist had been Dave Holt, a former MIT junior faculty member who'd gone into the ministry after being denied tenure. Bruce Sylvester turned out to be embezzling from his mother's company via fake invoices, caught ~1983; he embezzled half a million dollars and disappeared, leaving his mother to mortgage her home.

Tom's visiting committee anecdote: NIST staff claimed to be "the National Laboratory for competitiveness" and couldn't distinguish productivity (labor hours/ton, internal) from competitiveness (exchange rates, regulations, external). id: case:1952 T2 tanker fracture off Cape Cod
cluster_id: 1952 T2 tanker fracture off Cape Cod
content: 1952 T2 tanker fracture off Cape Cod Seven- or eight-year-old T2 tanker broke completely in two off Cape Cod in 1952; most of the crew survived. Tom references the Hollywood adaptation *The Finest Hours*. Not developed; T2 tankers are mentioned only to clarify that the 4,694-vessel figure is not all Liberty ships.

id: case:North Andover hot isostatic press explosion
cluster_id: North Andover hot isostatic press explosion
content: North Andover hot isostatic press explosion 10-inch-thick pressure vessel designed for 12-inch critical flaw size; manufacturing errors reduced critical flaw size to half an inch. Catastrophic failure ejected a 16-ton piece a quarter mile, landing in an industrial area at 2 a.m. with no injuries. World's largest HIP vessel (200 tons; 17-inch top, 10-inch wall) ruptured at night ~15 years before lecture. 16-ton fragment thrown a quarter mile. Tom and Travelers Insurance investigator first two into the pit by crane. Replacement unit was already 3 months from commissioning — averted a 3-year global gap in capacity for 60-inch aircraft engine rotors. **Cause discussion deferred to next lecture session.**

cluster_id: Rail steel derailments
content: Rail steel derailments Rail steel specifications, developed circa 1900–1920, still lack fracture-toughness requirements; rail companies have not been forced to modernize. Example of code lag.

id: case:Bell Helicopter rotor blade corrosion fatigue failure (Brazil)
cluster_id: Bell Helicopter rotor blade corrosion fatigue failure (Brazil)
content: Bell Helicopter rotor blade corrosion fatigue failure (Brazil) Helicopter rotor spar failed in Brazil. Initial diagnosis blamed surface sanding scratches; Tom's fracture-mechanics calculation four years later showed grinding scratches were too shallow to explain failure. Reread the photos: stress corrosion cracking under inadequate paint repair produced a 3 mm crack that did fit fracture mechanics. Tom's deposition led to the manufacturer withdrawing its alert service bulletin. Operators avoiding Bell-authorized service center costs ground down rotor dings without proper repainting. Stress-corrosion-assisted fatigue from poor paint coverage propagated cracks until the blade flew off, killing several. Tom's fracture-mechanics analysis showed the initial flaw was too small for the proposed pitting-only mechanism; stress-corrosion fatigue was required.

id: case:Aluminum automotive applications (1990s Ford Taurus vs. Toyota Camry)

content: Aluminum automotive applications (1990s Ford Taurus vs. Toyota Camry) The break-even argument: aluminum body-in-white costs roughly twice steel ($4,000 vs. $2,000), unaffordable on a $20,000 car but invisible on a $40,000 Audi. Anchors the broader pricing-by-market-segment argument.

cluster_id: Audi-Alcoa aluminum vehicle development partnership
content: Audi-Alcoa aluminum vehicle development partnership Peter Bridenbaugh anecdote. Tom and Bridenbaugh (then SVP at Alcoa) at a metallurgical conference; Bridenbaugh confirms the break-even point is $4 a pound, not $3. Establishes that the Alcoa-Audi partnership was bounded by aluminum's premium-segment economics. Brief aside — Audi's high-volume all-aluminum vehicle production hit problems that the historical J.P. Morgan low-volume aluminum cars (1930s, hand-repairable) had not exposed. Used as a learning-curve example.

cluster_id: Visby-class corvette (Swedish composite frigate)
content: Visby-class corvette (Swedish composite frigate) Cited as example of low-stiffness structural materials (aluminum, composites) failing as "beam between waves" in heavy seas — modulus argument: aluminum is ~10 Msi vs. steel's ~30 Msi. World's largest composite ship; usable only in good weather. Cautionary tale against Navy composite-hull aspirations. All-composite corvette. Insufficient modulus → flexed in North Sea conditions → cracked within ~3 years. Tom's anchor case for "modulus matters, not just weight." Paired with Admiral Grace Hopper's "ship in harbor is safe" line.

content: Lithography semiconductor machining precision problem Used to motivate why stress relief matters before precision machining — heat-treated material walks during stock removal, an issue Tom describes as a "20-billion-dollar problem" for the semiconductor industry. Continuation of the lithography case — at sub-wavelength feature sizes, photolithography gives way to UV / electron-beam patterning, with chips patterned in sections matched together because tolerance can't be held over a centimeter.

cluster_id: Vietnam-era Naval jet engine crashes and rebuilds
content: Vietnam-era Naval jet engine crashes and rebuilds 1969 Norfolk VA, Tom as freshman/sophomore engineering intern. Chief engineer designs a pneumatic peening tool to avoid disassembly; Tom witnesses Almen-gauge testing, signs the certification under threat of "you'll be in jail within 24 hours" if the plane goes down. The teaching point: "sometimes you just have to take risk" — but not without knowledge.

content: Tekken test development for Japanese railways Japanese small-coupon weldability test (double bevel on one plate, single on the other, weld in the joint, look for cracks). Tom translates "Tekken" as "railroad" and ties the test to Japanese railway construction of the 1970s–80s.

id: case:Lost foam casting invention and commercialization
cluster_id: Lost foam casting invention and commercialization
content: Lost foam casting invention and commercialization Origin story — a Boston-area sculptor (name uncertain on tape) brings a styrofoam-based casting idea to Professor Flemings at MIT around 1960; MIT perfects the fluid-flow analysis; the technique is now used industrially for GM cast iron engine blocks.

id: case:Turbine blade casting development at Pratt & Whitney
cluster_id: Turbine blade casting development at Pratt & Whitney
content: Turbine blade casting development at Pratt & Whitney Investment casting of cooled turbine blades perfected by Bud Schenck, formerly MIT professor, at Pratt & Whitney in the 1960s. The ceramic insert supplier is also an MIT ceramist grad.

id: case:General Electric CF6-6 engine fan rotor failure
cluster_id: General Electric CF6-6 engine fan rotor failure
content: General Electric CF6-6 engine fan rotor failure Referenced implicitly via the Sioux City discussion and GE's 99.75% reliability statistic. Frames the cost economics: turbine blades are 20% of GE revenue but 40% of profit.

id: case:Electric arc furnace water-cooled pipe rupture and molten steel explosion
cluster_id: Electric arc furnace water-cooled pipe rupture and molten steel explosion
content: Electric arc furnace water-cooled pipe rupture and molten steel explosion Introduces the case that continues into chunk 2 — modern 150 MW electric arc furnaces (scaled up from 50 MW since the 1970s) require water-cooled walls because radiant heat tripled with the power increase; water leaks into molten steel cause explosions. Tom describes getting consulting calls that begin "we had an explosion in our casting facility."

id: case:Edison, New Jersey gas pipeline explosion
cluster_id: Edison, New Jersey gas pipeline explosion
content: Edison, New Jersey gas pipeline explosion Brief mention as a counterpart to molten-metal hazards — 1,000 PSI / 42-inch pipeline failure producing 600-foot flames over Edison NJ at midnight. Cited to make the point that high-energy industrial failures are rare but dramatic. 42-inch diameter pipeline, 1000 psi, laid in 1960s through then-farmland. Let go in the 1990s after suburban buildup. Flames 600 ft in the air; radiant heat melted neighboring roofs. Tom's consulting case 15–20 years prior. Backhoe damage 1/4" deep, fatigue crack grew over years, catastrophic release produced a 600-foot flame at 11 PM; radiant heat melted apartment building roof next door.

id: case:MIT Lincoln Lab Quadulan radar dome bogie replacement
cluster_id: MIT Lincoln Lab Quadulan radar dome bogie replacement
content: MIT Lincoln Lab Quadulan radar dome bogie replacement Tom's 1970s consulting case. Kwajalein radar dome (football-field-size dish, scientific instrument repurposed for monitoring Soviet boost-phase satellite launches) needed a bogie casting replaced; one-year casting lead time was unacceptable for a classified Cold War asset operating at 3000% of design life. Specifying NDT for a machined-from-plate substitute exposed the ASM standard that any defect fitting within a 12-inch circle is acceptable in plate above six inches — Tom's anchor for "defect size scales with casting size."

id: case:Caltech rapid solidification metallic ribbon research
cluster_id: Caltech rapid solidification metallic ribbon research
content: Caltech rapid solidification metallic ribbon research Pol Duwez's 1960s discovery: pouring iron-boron brazing-alloy melts onto a spinning copper wheel produces paper-thin ribbons at million-degree-per-second solidification rates, yielding amorphous metals with 500 ksi strength and stainless-grade corrosion resistance without chromium. DoD/NSF spent hundreds of millions in the 1970s–80s on this research line. Used as the prototype "great properties, can't make it bulk" cautionary case. 1960s Caltech work spreading nickel-boron liquid on a 60-mph-surface-speed water-cooled spinning copper drum, achieving ~10⁶ °C/s cooling and producing paper-thin amorphous foils. Triggered the 1970s rapid-solidification powder/foil research wave.

cluster_id: Bulk metallic glass commercialization effort
content: Bulk metallic glass commercialization effort Bill Johnson (Caltech, Duwez's student) developed iron-beryllium and other bulk metallic glass alloys in the late 1980s — golf-ball-sized amorphous parts achievable at 100 °C/sec cooling. Fifteen-year-old company; the only commercial product is golf-club metal woods, which fail at about 50 shots. Used to land Tom's "you can sell anything to a golfer" line and his broader skepticism about scaling research-grade materials.

cluster_id: Bulk metallic glass golf clubs
content: Bulk metallic glass golf clubs Same case-cluster as the BMG commercialization above; cited specifically as a fatigue-life and high-margin-niche case. About 50 shots before fracture. Bill Johnson (Duwez student, now Caltech professor) succeeded in casting 2–3 mm bulk metallic glasses with ~500 ksi strength and excellent corrosion resistance, but the only commercial product in 15–20 years has been golf clubs — which crack after ~100 shots. Service temperature limited to 300–400°F before recrystallization. Tom's running line: "you can sell anything to a golfer."

cluster_id: Army wonder armor scaling failure
content: Army wonder armor scaling failure Army using Conform-process lightweight alloy to make armor rods with extraordinary properties. Tom raised the consolidation-to-plate question at the program review; was told "we'll worry about that later." His response: this is the same failure mode as 1980s rapid-solidification powder consolidation. Santayana quote follows.

id: case:Depleted uranium armor penetrators and Gulf War environmental contamination
cluster_id: Depleted uranium armor penetrators and Gulf War environmental contamination
content: Depleted uranium armor penetrators and Gulf War environmental contamination Cited in passing — DU contamination of Kuwait and southern Iraq during First Gulf War led the Army (not the Navy) to discontinue DU rounds on environmental grounds. Depleted-uranium kinetic-energy penetrators left radioactive shell debris across Kuwait; Pakistani and Bangladeshi laborers were sent into the desert to retrieve them. Tom has personally seen a uranium penetrator drive through three feet of steel.

cluster_id: NYC titanium heat exchanger fire
content: NYC titanium heat exchanger fire Detailed teaching unit — workers flame-cutting a titanium heat exchanger in a Manhattan basement post-9/11, generating hydrogen when garden-hosed, leading to small hydrogen explosion and subsequent lawsuit against the fire department. Backward-reference to a previously-discussed case. Cited to make the point that water spray on burning titanium generates hydrogen and amplifies the fire. Post-9/11 skyscraper in NYC; titanium heat exchanger took on East River silt through a misopened valve; under-deposit corrosion; non-English-speaking workers brought in with oxy-acetylene torches. Used to demonstrate that titanium *can* corrode and *can* burn when its protective oxide is breached.

cluster_id: Barge machine turnings fire
content: Barge machine turnings fire Passing reference — Professor Szekely consulted on metal-powder fire aboard a scrap-laden barge en route to a steel mill.

id: case:Air Force titanium powder prototype facility (Wyman Gordon)
cluster_id: Air Force titanium powder prototype facility (Wyman Gordon)
content: Air Force titanium powder prototype facility (Wyman Gordon) $10 million Air Force prototype for clean titanium powder production via electron-beam surface melting on water-cooled copper hearth, with preferential vaporization of ceramic inclusions. Located at Wyman-Gordon, Worcester, MA, about 20 years before lecture date.

id: case:Navy 25 kilowatt laser welder at Naval Research Laboratory
cluster_id: Navy 25 kilowatt laser welder at Naval Research Laboratory
content: Navy 25 kilowatt laser welder at Naval Research Laboratory Largest commercially available laser of the 1970s; baseline for inferring Air Force classified laser power levels.

id: case:Hot isostatic pressing development at Battelle Memorial Institute
cluster_id: Hot isostatic pressing development at Battelle Memorial Institute
content: Hot isostatic pressing development at Battelle Memorial Institute First HIP unit developed at Battelle post-WWII; second unit installed circa 1950 in the MIT room that later housed Tom's 1985 HIP, in Nick Grant's powder metallurgy lab. Used to demonstrate the practical importance of knowing gas-vs-condensed-phase density ratios. The world's first HIP press at Battelle, the second at MIT (4-131). 2,000°C, 2,000 atmospheres argon, squeezing pores out of powder-metallurgy turbine discs.

id: case:Phelps Dodge / Boston-New Hampshire trolley wire procurement (from chunk 2)
cluster_id: Phelps Dodge / Boston-New Hampshire trolley wire procurement (from chunk 2)
content: Phelps Dodge / Boston-New Hampshire trolley wire procurement (from chunk 2) Brief reference within §12.p1; cited as an application of the Conform process. The specific role here is to anchor "Conform produces real industrial product, not just research curio."

id: case:Nuclear Metals (Concord MA) rotating electrode process and depleted uranium extrusion
cluster_id: Nuclear Metals (Concord MA) rotating electrode process and depleted uranium extrusion
content: Nuclear Metals (Concord MA) rotating electrode process and depleted uranium extrusion MIT Mech-E spinoff in Concord, MA; manufactured all US depleted-uranium kinetic-energy penetrator rounds by extrusion. About 20 years before lecture date, they developed the rotating electrode process: a spinning machined ingot of homogeneous alloy is melted at its tip by a plasma torch and centrifugally atomized into clean powder. Yields aerospace-quality superalloy powders for jet-engine rotors.

id: case:Air Force 50-megawatt laser weapon classified power inference
cluster_id: Air Force 50-megawatt laser weapon classified power inference
content: Air Force 50-megawatt laser weapon classified power inference Tom's three-method inference from open literature (superconducting generator program, Bowen's halide glass window project, Rockwell engineer's space-shuttle-cargo-bay confirmation) deducing the classified laser weapon power and the rationale for sizing the Space Shuttle cargo bay.

id: case:MP35N cold-worked cobalt-nickel alloy section-size limitation
cluster_id: MP35N cold-worked cobalt-nickel alloy section-size limitation
content: MP35N cold-worked cobalt-nickel alloy section-size limitation Continuation from prior session. Annealed yield 60 ksi; with 65% cold work plus aging, up to 290–300 ksi tensile with 10% elongation and 48% RA — better than aircraft landing gear steel. But cannot be made in plates or in diameters much above 2 inches because cold-working tools fail. Available only as wire or sheet. Tom returns to it as the "if you could afford it and could make it thick" submarine hull thought experiment.

cluster_id: Velcro invention (serendipitous discovery)
content: Velcro invention (serendipitous discovery) Origin anecdote — Swiss inventor walking in the Alps observing cockle-burs on wool pants, microscopy revealing hooks and loops, plastic translation.

cluster_id: Morgrip propeller bolt single-use replacement
content: Morgrip propeller bolt single-use replacement Student-recalled shipyard experience confirms Tom's general rule: high-strength bolts (propellers, aircraft, bridges, racing cars) are one-time-article use because reuse degrades thread fit-up via micro-yielding and shifts torque-vs-preload calibration.

id: case:High-strength bolt reuse in aviation accidents
cluster_id: High-strength bolt reuse in aviation accidents
content: High-strength bolt reuse in aviation accidents Tom mentions investigating multiple aviation accidents where reused bolts lost fatigue strength due to lost clamp-up.

id: case:Westbrook pounds-per-year vs. dollars-per-pound structural-materials correlation
cluster_id: Westbrook pounds-per-year vs. dollars-per-pound structural-materials correlation
content: Westbrook pounds-per-year vs. dollars-per-pound structural-materials correlation Tom credits Jack Westbrook (MIT alum, GE 1960s) for the log-log plot showing that halving material cost quadruples consumption — slope steeper than iso-market-size.

cluster_id: Atlantic-coast cement barging distribution model
content: Atlantic-coast cement barging distribution model Tom's father worked for a cement company that manufactured at Vinea (likely Ravena), NY and barged to Atlantic-coast depots (Chesapeake VA, Baltimore/Philadelphia). 500–1,000-mile truck-rail limit for low-value-per-pound materials. Cement is the largest manufactured-material volume in the world at ~2B tons/yr.

cluster_id: Kinik brazed-diamond CMP pad conditioner
content: Kinik brazed-diamond CMP pad conditioner Tom passes around a brazed-diamond pad conditioner used to dress chemical-mechanical-polish pads in semiconductor planarization (200–400 processing steps per chip). Functions as structural abrasive plus high-thermal-conductivity substrate.

cluster_id: MIT engineering department founding chronology
content: MIT engineering department founding chronology Origin of "civil engineering" via 1823 Rensselaer (Erie Canal needs) distinguishing from West Point military engineering. MIT 1865 course numbering: 1 Civil, 2 Mechanical, 3 Mining (→ Metallurgy 1888 → Materials 1974), 4 Architecture, 5 Chemistry, 6 (→ EE 1890s). Elihu Thompson and Edison as GE co-founders. Sloan's 1950 gift removing management from the School of Engineering. Tom's role in the 1996 report creating the Engineering Systems Division — originally drafted as "Division of Engineering Management," renamed to evade Sloan School's M-word ownership. Bioengineering as planned outgrowth of the same perpendicular-structure mechanism.

cluster_id: Bismuth-telluride thermoelectric remote-pipeline sensor power
content: Bismuth-telluride thermoelectric remote-pipeline sensor power Hand-passed module: ~20°C ΔT yields 5V across plasma-sprayed aluminum / polymer-insulated Bi₂Te₃ array. Used on remote gas pipelines, heat supplied by a platinized catalytic Coleman-lantern-style mantle oxidizing pipeline gas.

id: case:Langmuir GE vaporization studies and tungsten filament burnout
cluster_id: Langmuir GE vaporization studies and tungsten filament burnout
content: Langmuir GE vaporization studies and tungsten filament burnout Tom credits Irving Langmuir (GE Research Labs, ~100 years ago, Nobel laureate) with founding surface-vaporization science motivated by tungsten light-bulb filament failure. The "Langmuir" unit (~10⁻⁸ atm·s for one monolayer at unity sticking) anchors the vapor-deposition rate argument.

id: case:Army gun barrel erosion and coating programs
cluster_id: Army gun barrel erosion and coating programs
content: Army gun barrel erosion and coating programs Long-running Army effort to deposit structural coatings on gun-barrel interiors to combat propellant-driven erosion. Current production solution is electroplated chromium ("they know there are better materials but nothing as cheap"); vapor-deposition routes all tried.

id: case:Lockheed Skunk Works X-33 spaceplane composite tank (rapid prototyping redesign)
cluster_id: Lockheed Skunk Works X-33 spaceplane composite tank (rapid prototyping redesign)
content: Lockheed Skunk Works X-33 spaceplane composite tank (rapid prototyping redesign) Geographic-political context: the X-33 LH₂ tank was built in the same Palmdale top-secret hangar that produced the F-117. NASA used the Skunk Works specifically to escape conventional defense-contractor schedule/budget overruns — and got them anyway.

cluster_id: Strategic Defense Initiative materials-fantasy critique
content: Strategic Defense Initiative materials-fantasy critique Cited as exemplar of "defense department thinking … when you're not limited by science or physics or chemistry."

id: case:ALVIN submarine pressure hull cost overrun
cluster_id: ALVIN submarine pressure hull cost overrun
content: ALVIN submarine pressure hull cost overrun Tom's role on the 2003–04 National Academy of Sciences study estimating the cost of a new Alvin submersible. Woods Hole's $6.5M estimate; Tom's $16M revised estimate; final actual cost ~$40M. Pressure hull fabrication identified as the dominant cost risk. The specific cost-estimation episode. Woods Hole estimated $6.5M ($193/lb); Tom estimated $16M ($400/lb plus margin); actual cost ~$37M ($~1,000/lb). Used to teach the discrepancy between Jason 2 cost-per-pound ($320/lb tethered unmanned) and Woods Hole's optimistic projection for a manned untethered vehicle.

id: case:Submerged arc welding of titanium flux economics
cluster_id: Submerged arc welding of titanium flux economics
content: Submerged arc welding of titanium flux economics Tom's first research contract as a young professor, ~1977–78. Calcium fluoride flux at $100/lb, hygroscopic and contamination-prone, with 1.5 lb of flux per lb of titanium weld metal — an order of magnitude worse than steel submerged arc economics.

id: case:B1 bomber program titanium surplus repurposing
cluster_id: B1 bomber program titanium surplus repurposing
content: B1 bomber program titanium surplus repurposing Air Force cancellation of the B-1 left thousands of tons of titanium 6-4 in pre-ordered shapes. Navy convinced the Air Force to transfer the stockpile to David Taylor, which used four-inch plate to fabricate welding tables in lieu of buying new ones.

cluster_id: Titanium heat exchanger corrosion failure
content: Titanium heat exchanger corrosion failure Under-deposit corrosion attack on titanium heat exchanger tubes where river silt accumulated; replacement of the entire heat exchanger. Cautionary case against the assumption that "titanium won't corrode."

id: case:NIST F1 atomic clock as measurement standard
cluster_id: NIST F1 atomic clock as measurement standard
content: NIST F1 atomic clock as measurement standard One part in 10¹⁵ accuracy — one second in 30 million years. Returns at end of lecture as the time-measurement upper bound.

cluster_id: Cow magnet ingestion in livestock
content: Cow magnet ingestion in livestock Aside during the ball-identification exercise — Tom uses 400-series stainless steel cow magnets as the magnet props. Explains the livestock-medicine origin. Physical demonstration. Stainless-steel magnet swallowed by dairy cattle to capture stray ferrous wire and protect the udders. Used as an aside off the guide-wire topic. Stainless-steel magnet swallowed by cattle to capture ingested metal in the stomach.

id: case:Fire assay gold analysis (MIT historical curriculum)
cluster_id: Fire assay gold analysis (MIT historical curriculum)
content: Fire assay gold analysis (MIT historical curriculum) Tom's account of the centuries-old gravimetric technique still standard for referee gold analysis: digest in lead bath, oxidize off base metals, separate gold-silver button, dissolve silver in nitric, weigh refined gold. One part in 5,000 accuracy. Tom notes he was tasked 25–30 years ago with developing a replacement; inductively coupled plasma is finally getting close.

cluster_id: Aluminum silicon carbide brake calipers
content: Aluminum silicon carbide brake calipers Example of a sufficiently narrow presentation topic, and substantive failure mode (brake fade from aluminum creep under high temperature). Mid-80s automotive industry attempt to replace cast iron brake calipers with Al-SiC metal matrix composite. Star Wars era. Failed initially because aluminum creeps and the calipers sprung open after two or three hard brake applications — brake fade. Tom has heard the problem has since been solved.

id: case:Manganese aluminum bronze electron-beam 3D printing trial
cluster_id: Manganese aluminum bronze electron-beam 3D printing trial
content: Manganese aluminum bronze electron-beam 3D printing trial Better-wetting alloy, deposited in circles with electron beam. Shows acceleration humps at scan reversals (Newton's laws) and residual-stress problems despite better surface-tension balance.

id: case:US Air Force turbine vane repair program (DAABER)
cluster_id: US Air Force turbine vane repair program (DAABER)
content: US Air Force turbine vane repair program (DAABER) The "dabber" — arc welding machine to rebuild worn turbine vane tips. Five-hundred-dollar vane, couple hundred dollars repair, three thousand more hours of life. Ten-million-dollar automated machine in Oklahoma City repair facility making fifty million on the blades. Used to argue that we have been doing additive manufacturing for eighty years on high-value-added parts.

id: case:General Motors 1980s automation and competitive decline
cluster_id: General Motors 1980s automation and competitive decline
content: General Motors 1980s automation and competitive decline GM VP big on robotics, spent fifty billion in the 1980s automating — same fifty billion that could have purchased Toyota if Japanese law had allowed it.

id: case:Speaker's home gas service sleeving (three-quarter inch pipe)
cluster_id: Speaker's home gas service sleeving (three-quarter inch pipe)
content: Speaker's home gas service sleeving (three-quarter inch pipe) Continuation of the neighbor anecdote — Tom's house and another nearby flagged with high soil gas concentrations; service sleeved with plastic pipe inside the original steel. Tom alludes to a "another story" (gas accumulation in the house) but does not develop it. The plastic-to-steel transition leak that nearly flooded the speaker's home with gas; the lost Boston Gas work order; speaker's escalation to state regulators.

id: case:Gas pipe corrosion and home explosions
cluster_id: Gas pipe corrosion and home explosions
content: Gas pipe corrosion and home explosions Framing case for why the polyethylene pipe was developed — sixty-year-old steel pipe corroding through, century-old cast iron pipe failing.

id: case:Cape Cod sailboat anodized aluminum corrosion failure
cluster_id: Cape Cod sailboat anodized aluminum corrosion failure
content: Cape Cod sailboat anodized aluminum corrosion failure Tom's first Cape Cod consulting visit. A 40-foot sailboat owner had aluminum rails pitting because the anodizer failed to seal the porous coating. Illustration of the trade-off between anodizing-for-bonding (leave porous) and anodizing-for-corrosion-resistance (seal in boiling water).

id: case:Cold bonding of integrated circuits and transistors
cluster_id: Cold bonding of integrated circuits and transistors
content: Cold bonding of integrated circuits and transistors Indium bead used to cold-bond the metal can to the silicon-chip base on early discrete transistors. Illustration of why oxide-to-metal hardness ratio matters in practice. Thermocompression gold-wire bonding in microelectronic packaging. Kulicke and Soffa (NW Pennsylvania) makes ~90% of the world's wire-bonders. ~50 trillion bonds/year worldwide; 7 bonds/second per machine; 1-mil gold wire; bond geometry has a central "dead zone" with shear bond in the wings. Limited to ~4-mil pitch by head stiffness.

id: case:Single transistor hermetic packaging with indium cold bonds
cluster_id: Single transistor hermetic packaging with indium cold bonds
content: Single transistor hermetic packaging with indium cold bonds Same anecdote as above; the corpus aggregate carries it under both cluster names. Tom uses it as a single beat.

cluster_id: Brewery filling line consulting project
content: Brewery filling line consulting project Thirty-year-old observation of bottling-line throughput (20 bottles/sec, 24 cans/sec), the foam-rejection dumpster, beer cost of 16 cents/gallon. Used to motivate why label adhesives have to be low viscosity.

id: case:Welch's grape juice packaging versus beer
cluster_id: Welch's grape juice packaging versus beer
content:
Welch's grape juice packaging versus beer Counterpoint to brewery — Welch's grape juice at $9/gallon vs. beer at 16¢/gallon. Used to make the point that adhesive economics scale with product value; advertising is what makes beer expensive.

They went through seven tons of gold per year. His consulting project ended after an inventory shortfall in the early 1990s.

cluster_id: Platinum jewelry laser cutting adoption
content: Platinum jewelry laser cutting adoption Second-largest jeweler in the world (also Attleboro). They slice thick-walled platinum tube and turn down rings on screw machines. Switched from mechanical cutting (0.8 mm kerf) to high-power laser cutting (1/4 the kerf), $3–4M laser paid back in two months. Carrying cost on raw materials drives processing decisions in this industry.

cluster_id: Eagar wife's engagement ring (electron-beam-melted platinum-iridium)
content: Eagar wife's engagement ring (electron-beam-melted platinum-iridium) Tom made his wife's engagement ring himself, electron-beam-melting platinum-iridium on the 4th floor of MIT Building 8 with an old radar power supply, nearly electrocuting himself. Used as illustration of unique vs. high-volume manufacturing.

cluster_id: Tanyon laminated silver wedding band
content: Tanyon laminated silver wedding band Colleague Mike Tanyon made his wedding band by diffusion-bonding/laminating layers of sterling silver and silver, rolling and twisting and machining. Companion example to Tom's own ring for unique-object manufacturing.

id: case:German superplasticity research (1938, lost in WWII)
cluster_id: German superplasticity research (1938, lost in WWII)
content: German superplasticity research (1938, lost in WWII) Companion to the Backofen case. Original superplasticity measurement on fine-grain material in a 1938 German paper, lost in the war.

cluster_id: Honeywell aircraft brake leasing economics
content: Honeywell aircraft brake leasing economics Symbiotic incentive structure — the brake manufacturer bears replacement cost, so it has incentive to develop longer-lasting brakes; airline pays a fixed per-landing fee.

cluster_id: aircraft engine power-by-the-hour leasing model
content: aircraft engine power-by-the-hour leasing model Engines leased from GE / Rolls-Royce; lessor maintains, airline pays per operating hour. Same incentive structure as brakes.

id: case:Corrugated stainless steel gas tubing lightning strike fires
cluster_id: Corrugated stainless steel gas tubing lightning strike fires
content: Corrugated stainless steel gas tubing lightning strike fires Physical demonstration of the lightning-perforation failure. Six billion feet installed in US homes; manufacturing flaw + high-voltage discharge → perforation of the steel through the plastic jacket.

id: case:Boeing composite wing lightning strike internship project
cluster_id: Boeing composite wing lightning strike internship project
content: Boeing composite wing lightning strike internship project Painted aluminum vs bare aluminum vs composite wing response to lightning; Tom's student internship at Boeing on composite-wing lightning strikes. Connects to the §2.p3 stainless-steel-tubing case through shared failure physics.

id: case:Tungsten carbide and sintered diamond asphalt milling bit optimization
cluster_id: Tungsten carbide and sintered diamond asphalt milling bit optimization
content: Tungsten carbide and sintered diamond asphalt milling bit optimization Highway-reclamation milling bits wear out in 3–4 hours with tungsten carbide tips; sintered diamond extends life past an 8-hour shift. Tom consulted on whether to acquire the company; verdict was technologically superior but too expensive.

cluster_id: Rongeur (orthopedic surgical pliers) consulting work
content: Rongeur (orthopedic surgical pliers) consulting work Tom's ~1982 consulting case for a Johnson & Johnson medical-instruments division south of Boston. They wanted a stiffer material than steel for arthroscopic rongeurs; Tom proposed single-crystal sapphire (twice the stiffness of steel, behind diamond on hardness, can be color-tinted as ruby for surgeon-preference marketing). Client rejected without explanation.

cluster_id: Surgical scissors (medical liability premium)
content: Surgical scissors (medical liability premium) $300 (1980s) / $600–700 (present) stainless steel scissors with cobalt-alloy brazed cutting edge, gold-plated handles, 100% hardness check. DeBakey color-preference anecdote. Used to motivate the sapphire/ruby marketing pitch in §5.p9.

id: case:Sachs polycrystalline silicon ribbon solar cell venture
cluster_id: Sachs polycrystalline silicon ribbon solar cell venture
content: Sachs polycrystalline silicon ribbon solar cell venture Emanuel Sachs (MIT, co-coiner of "3D printing") founded a company that pulled silicon ribbon directly from the melt using carbon-fiber wires for solar-cell manufacture. Was projected to take over the solar-cell market 25 years ago; company subsequently bankrupt.

cluster_id: Spruce Goose
content: Spruce Goose World's largest aircraft, built of spruce by Howard Hughes. Used to motivate the "wood as a strength-to-weight material" point on the Ashby strength-density plot. Currently displayed at an aviation museum in Oregon.

id: case:Aluminum baseball bat *(adjacent — this is wood-bat context for the bat material discussion)*
cluster_id: Aluminum baseball bat *(adjacent — this is wood-bat context for the bat material discussion)*
content: Aluminum baseball bat *(adjacent — this is wood-bat context for the bat material discussion)* Ash chosen for bats because it's the strongest wood on the Ashby plot; Kentucky ash availability is part of why Louisville is the bat-manufacturing center. Student question on maple goes unanswered.

cluster_id: Boston Edison stainless steel corrosion
content: Boston Edison stainless steel corrosion John Wolff (Tom's freshman adviser) diagnoses overnight failure of all stainless steel in the Boston Edison plant after their first shipment of Venezuelan oil arrives post-WWII. Vanadium in the oil forms an oxide that strips the protective chromium oxide off stainless steel. Wolff charges $5,000 (≈$200–300K today) for the one-sentence answer. Frames Tom's broader theme of expert knowledge as economic asset. Setup only — the case is introduced (Boston Edison stainless steel falls apart overnight; Wulff demands $5,000 fee in advance; identifies the new Venezuelan oil shipment as the cause) but the recording cuts off before Tom finishes the story of why the Venezuelan oil caused the corrosion.

id: case:Cambridge water main floods from cast iron pipe failure
cluster_id: Cambridge water main floods from cast iron pipe failure
content: Cambridge water main floods from cast iron pipe failure Tom describes water main repair crews shattering 100-year-old cast iron mains with a sledgehammer — illustrating both cast iron brittleness and the longevity of legacy infrastructure. Connects to recurring corpus theme of aging Boston/Cambridge buried infrastructure.

id: case:Alcoa Tennessee lead-contaminated aluminum beverage can recycling failure
cluster_id: Alcoa Tennessee lead-contaminated aluminum beverage can recycling failure
content: Alcoa Tennessee lead-contaminated aluminum beverage can recycling failure Early 1990s. Alcoa Tennessee can-stock production fouled by lead from Mexican aluminum scrap. Initially suspected slugging (lead weights for price-by-weight fraud). Root cause: leaded-gasoline exhaust deposited on roadside cans collected by informal Mexican scavengers; lead concentration dropped sharply within 200 feet of highway edge. Alcoa stopped buying Mexican aluminum scrap. ~30 years prior (~mid-1980s). Alcoa Tennessee finding lead-contaminated Mexican aluminum can scrap. Initial hypothesis (slugging with lead) ruled out by x-ray. Actual cause: leaded gasoline exhaust deposition on highway-discarded cans, no Mexican deposit law. Alcoa's solution: stop buying Mexican scrap.

id: case:US Steel price control by President Kennedy (1962)
cluster_id: US Steel price control by President Kennedy (1962)
content:
US Steel price control by President Kennedy (1962) Cited as a contributing factor to the US steel industry's inability to reinvest in modern capacity through the 1970s–80s.

## Figures referenced Kennedy forced US Steel to back down from a 10% price increase to avoid global inflation; US Steel later blamed this decision for its decline. Used to mark the transition from steel to energy as the world's price-setting commodity. Tom at age 12 reading about Kennedy forcing US Steel to roll back 10% price increase. Used to set up the post-WWII US steel dominance story (75% world capacity) and the management-arrogance thesis. Some industry observers blame this for decline; Tom disagrees.

content: IBM mainframe and salaried workforce restructuring The TQM challenge week at the IBM executive training facility on the Hudson, ~1990. IBM's reduction of salaried staff by ~45,000 without touching hourly workers, and the executive's admission that fewer problems rose to the surface afterward. content: Baosteel and Chinese steel industry dominance Baosteel as world's largest steel company today, producing 2× US total. Used to set up the tragedy-of-the-commons argument about state-subsidized steel exports.

id: case:Reagan Star Wars and Japanese financing of US debt

content: Reagan Star Wars and Japanese financing of US debt Reagan's SDI funded via Japanese loans; yen appreciation from 240 to 100 per dollar meant US repaid at ~40 cents on the dollar. Tom's economics-of-currency lesson.

cluster_id: Honda Civic rust failure (1970s)
content: Honda Civic rust failure (1970s) 1975 Honda Civic as joke product (rusty within twelve months); Japanese response was to engineer the rust-free Civic of today. Example of being "embarrassed into" quality improvement.

id: case:SUBSAFE program and Navy origins of TQM
cluster_id: SUBSAFE program and Navy origins of TQM
content: SUBSAFE program and Navy origins of TQM Three-year submarine production shutdown post-*Thresher*; SUBSAFE instituted with Deming's involvement; redesigned joints for what would later be called Six Sigma quality. Tom claims the Navy coined "total quality management" terminology in mid-1980s memos.

cluster_id: MIT International Motor Vehicle Program and the origin of lean
content: MIT International Motor Vehicle Program and the origin of lean $5M, five-year MIT study (Womack, Jones, Roos) on the future of the automobile; origin of the term "lean manufacturing." Toyota beating GM/Ford/Chrysler on quality.

cluster_id: MIT Materials Processing Center vs. LMP turf war (1980s)

Tom announces this story will continue next lecture.

cluster_id: Mississippi pressure vessel explosion
content: Mississippi pressure vessel explosion 4-ft diameter, 2-inch-thick steel pressure vessel hydrotested with nitrogen at 2200 psi (1.5× the 1500 psi operating pressure). Door blew off, weighed 4000 lb, found half a mile away. One worker killed, one sandblasted and going blind. Used here as the setup for Charpy testing and cup-cone fracture samples.

id: case:Gas compressor station failure in Texas
cluster_id: Gas compressor station failure in Texas
content: Gas compressor station failure in Texas Distinct from the Mississippi case — gas distribution line where a failed check valve caused the pressurizing turbine to run in reverse. Cup-cone tensile fractures and Charpy bars from this case are passed around the class. Some steels tested were so brittle they snapped without deformation; others so tough they exceeded the 300 ft-lb capacity of the test machine.

id: case:New Jersey prison elevator bearing failure
cluster_id: New Jersey prison elevator bearing failure
content: New Jersey prison elevator bearing failure Elevator pulley bearing failed; safety brakes engaged at 1.6 G. Guard transporting three prisoners (one a former NY Giants lineman) was on the floor with a slipped disc when the surveillance camera came back on after 10–15 seconds of obstruction. Court awarded $1.6M because jury could not be told what likely happened during the blackout.

cluster_id: Elevator cable brittle fracture investigation
content: Elevator cable brittle fracture investigation Recent consulting query — investigator saw brittle wire failures in an elevator cable but couldn't find intergranular fracture, so was reluctant to call it hydrogen embrittlement. Tom's point: piano-wire-class wire has been deformed so much the grains are wavy, so intergranular fracture is not the diagnostic indicator it normally is.

cluster_id: Classified aircraft hydrogen embrittlement case
content: Classified aircraft hydrogen embrittlement case Companion case to the elevator wire — Tom can't name it but notes it involved a very high strength steel similar to aircraft landing gear material. Same diagnostic confusion (no intergranular fracture despite hydrogen embrittlement).

content: California texting and driving fatal collision Closing aside. Woman texting at 70 mph rear-ended a stopped vehicle; the other driver died in the fire. Two months later the same woman was stopped again by state police for texting. Judge sentenced her to 5 years.

Used to close the lecture on the theme that engineers from different disciplines describe the same phenomenon in different vocabularies.

id: case:Cement truck pressure vessel explosion (Pennsylvania) — full case
cluster_id: Cement truck pressure vessel explosion (Pennsylvania) — full case
content: Cement truck pressure vessel explosion (Pennsylvania) — full case Aluminum 200-gallon water tanks for cement trucks built by an Iowa subsidiary of a large defense contractor. Designed by a lawyer using exclusions in the boiler and pressure vessel code and a D.O.T. opinion to skip doubler plates around port holes. Two failures recounted: (1) Iowa hydrotest explosion that took a worker's legs off when the tanks were new; (2) Pennsylvania field failure during overpressurized weld-repair testing (100 psi shop air instead of 5 psi) that killed the welder, found in four pieces. Used to illustrate (a) doubler plate requirements at stress concentrations, (b) the National Board inspection regime under state law, (c) the cost of replacing engineering with legal interpretation. The Connecticut steering-failure embedded anecdote (§4.p3) is a sub-story illustrating muriatic acid corrosion, not a separate case.

cluster_id: Connecticut cement truck steering failure
content: Connecticut cement truck steering failure Cement truck driver lost steering on a Connecticut bridge after muriatic acid (carried on the truck for cement cleanup) leaked through seals and corroded the steering gears. Truck and driver fell ~100 feet. Used as a tangent inside the cement truck case to motivate why cement trucks carry acid and water.

cluster_id: Tree stand aluminum turnbuckle lawsuit
content: Tree stand aluminum turnbuckle lawsuit Cast aluminum turnbuckle from a hunting tree stand fractured; plaintiff's expert magnified four pores to basketball size in SEM imagery. Tom's "four ping-pong balls on a desk" analogy at trial conveyed the actual ~2% area loss to the jury. The turnbuckle was also bent — failure cause was bending overload, not porosity. Used to illustrate (a) the proportional strength-loss relationship for porosity in aluminum, (b) how to explain microstructural scale to lay audiences. Forensic case used to illustrate that small amounts of porosity (four or five pores under half a millimeter in a cast aluminum turnbuckle) are not the cause of failure. Tom on the witness stand uses a five-ping-pong-balls-on-a-table analogy to convey the porosity fraction. The actual failure cause was overloading from improper climbing.

content: Cambridge MA water chlorine content Used as a real-world reference point for the Delrin chlorine sensitivity — Cambridge water from Fresh Pond has 5–10 ppm chlorine, ten times the DuPont "corrosion resistant" threshold. cluster_id: Atomic bomb recovery off Spain
content: Atomic bomb recovery off Spain Brief reference. One of the Alvin's military-era missions located a US Air Force atomic bomb dropped off Spain, with Soviet competitors also searching. Briefly cited to explain why the Office of Naval Research wanted deep-sea capability in the early 1960s — an American plane dropped a nuclear warhead in the Atlantic near Spain, and the recovery race against the Soviets drove the Alvin program.

id: case:U.S. Navy titanium submarine welding research (Alvin prototype program)
cluster_id: U.S. Navy titanium submarine welding research (Alvin prototype program)
content: U.S. Navy titanium submarine welding research (Alvin prototype program) Mare Island Naval Shipyard attempted to use GMAW (gas metal arc welding) technology developed at David Taylor / Annapolis to build the Sea Cliff titanium hull. Failed after six months; fell back to GTAW (gas tungsten arc), which took a year to deposit the 2¼" weld at ~4 inches/minute. Used to teach: naval shipyards' lost capability to *build* (vs. repair) vessels, and the cost-of-time tradeoff in titanium welding.

cluster_id: Naval shipyard radiography eye injury incident
