id: case:Liberty ships and welded merchant vessel failures (WWII)
cluster_id: Liberty ships and welded merchant vessel failures (WWII)
content: Liberty ships and welded merchant vessel failures (WWII) Tom reads from the postwar damage report — 4,694 ships, 970 with fracture casualties, 24 complete hull fractures, 26 lives lost. Frames the rest of the lecture as the story of how welding technology had to be invented to support mass-produced welded ships.

id: case:Forging press weld repair (Pennsylvania, 17-inch thick steel)
cluster_id: Forging press weld repair (Pennsylvania, 17-inch thick steel)
content: Forging press weld repair (Pennsylvania, 17-inch thick steel) Stage-direction case — Tom passes around a section of the repair weld to demonstrate the ~100 stick-electrode passes required to weld through 17 inches.

id: case:Nova Scotia sailboat trailer weld failure (Route 24)
cluster_id: Nova Scotia sailboat trailer weld failure (Route 24)
content: Nova Scotia sailboat trailer weld failure (Route 24) A driver from Nova Scotia returning from Newport sailing races on a home-built trailer experienced a slug-welded joint failure — a bolt had been dropped into the angle iron joint and welded over. The boat broke loose at highway speed. Tom uses it as the one slug weld he has personally seen, and as an illustration of why slug welds are unacceptable.

id: case:Quonset Point submarine hull cap fixturing and welding practice
cluster_id: Quonset Point submarine hull cap fixturing and welding practice
content: Quonset Point submarine hull cap fixturing and welding practice Student-led description of automated tractor-welding of pre-triangulated submarine cap heads, ~100 weld passes per joint, back-gouging, inert gas shielding, 3mm defect limit. Tom then adds the secrecy aside about Soviet satellite measurement of hull thickness.

cluster_id: Submarine torpedo tube distortion control
content: Submarine torpedo tube distortion control Tom's first student at Electric Boat developed an in-process distortion-monitoring technique using feeler gauges, allowing real-time compensation by adjusting weld sequence and grinding-and-reweld corrections. Reduced finishing pass from quarter-inch machining to skin pass.

cluster_id: Carrier nuclear piping corrosion repair
content: Carrier nuclear piping corrosion repair Student-side: original construction jacked misaligned pipes into place and welded them, locking in residual stress. Years later, corrosion-driven repair requires refabrication of entire piping systems because the locked-in stress prevents simple cut-and-replace.

cluster_id: Shipyard thermal distortion during construction
content: Shipyard thermal distortion during construction 1 part in 20,000 tolerance for shipbuilding (vs. typical 1 part in 2,000 for general manufacturing) — the precision is so high that solar heating changes the shape of a thousand-foot ship and must be welded around. Student adds Pascagoula sun-shade practice.

id: case:Boeing aircraft rivet hole fit-up specification
cluster_id: Boeing aircraft rivet hole fit-up specification
content: Boeing aircraft rivet hole fit-up specification Boeing general spec: cannot apply more than five pounds of force to bring two parts into registry before riveting, to limit residual stress around rivet holes. Tom uses it to contrast Boeing's fatigue-driven specification with the Navy's looser fit-up tolerance.

cluster_id: Russian submarine hull thickness intelligence
content: Russian submarine hull thickness intelligence A briefly visible curtain flap during commissioning ceremony revealed double-hull construction; subsequently used in computer simulations of weapon-damage scenarios. Tom uses it as illustration of why hull-thickness measurement is classified.

id: case:John Chipman MIT steelmaking research (Manhattan Project era through 1973)
cluster_id: John Chipman MIT steelmaking research (Manhattan Project era through 1973)
content: John Chipman MIT steelmaking research (Manhattan Project era through 1973) Chipman applied physical chemistry to 1500°C steel melts in Building 8 basement, developed the modern iron-carbon phase diagram (1973), worked on the Manhattan Project developing sulfide ceramic crucibles for uranium and plutonium melting. His treatises appear enshrined in Plexiglas in Chinese libraries as the seminal text on steelmaking.

cluster_id: Bessemer converter introduction (1856)
content: Bessemer converter introduction (1856) The counterflow preheating innovation that made it possible to reach 1500°C using hydrocarbon combustion, by preheating incoming air with exiting combustion gases.

cluster_id: Basic open hearth furnace (Carnegie 1880s)
content: Basic open hearth furnace (Carnegie 1880s) Half-football-field-sized brick-lattice regenerative furnace, three-hundred-ton tap per day, the standard process for steel for the first hundred years.

cluster_id: Basic oxygen furnace (postwar Austria)
content: Basic oxygen furnace (postwar Austria) Supersonic-velocity pure-oxygen lance creates froth of steel; 300 tons of cast iron converted to steel in 20 minutes vs. 24 hours in basic open hearth. The shaving-cream-vs-surface-diffusion analogy.

id: case:Pellini and Naval Research Laboratory brittle fracture work
cluster_id: Pellini and Naval Research Laboratory brittle fracture work
content: Pellini and Naval Research Laboratory brittle fracture work One of the three postwar research centers studying weld brittle fracture; Pellini later joined MIT Course 13 as a lecturer in the 1980s before retiring on Cape Cod.

id: case:Morris Cohen MIT postwar brittle fracture research
cluster_id: Morris Cohen MIT postwar brittle fracture research
content: Morris Cohen MIT postwar brittle fracture research Cohen was the postwar Mr. Steel at MIT studying brittle fracture of welded ships; Krauss was his doctoral student and inherited the Mr. Steel title; *Steels* (Krauss's textbook) is Tom's source for the carbon-vs-hardness curve.

cluster_id: Medieval Islamic sword quenching practice
content: Medieval Islamic sword quenching practice Tom's undergraduate history paper material — Muslim swordsmiths during the Middle Ages believed quenching a hot blade through a living person or in blood produced a better edge than quenching in water or oil.

id: case:Allegheny Ludlum Steel—1980s profitability under Dick Simmons
cluster_id: Allegheny Ludlum Steel—1980s profitability under Dick Simmons
content: Allegheny Ludlum Steel—1980s profitability under Dick Simmons The one US steel company that didn't lose money in the 1980s overcapacity crisis. Used to make the "CEOs who understand their industry beat business-school CEOs" point. Dick Simmons (MIT '52) became Allegheny Ludlum president. Two 1980s leveraged buyouts made him a half-billionaire. The only U.S. integrated steel company with no unprofitable quarter in the 1980s. Tom's anecdote about Simmons's private plane. Used to set up the 40%-of-auto-cost-is-health-insurance claim. Simmons's Pittsburgh hospital-board move to control employee health costs is the bridge between steel profitability and material-cost arithmetic. the incumbent that fought back. Allegheny Ludlum, run by Dick Simmons (MIT alumnus, namesake of Simmons Hall), never had an unprofitable quarter during the 1980s steel industry collapse, because its CEO knew how to make steel. Workforce loyalty contrast: workers hated management generally but loved Simmons.

cluster_id: Pittsburgh Reduction Company / Alcoa founding
content: Pittsburgh Reduction Company / Alcoa founding Charles Martin Hall's patent victory over Paul Héroult by hours; founding of Pittsburgh Reduction Company → Alcoa; the trust-busters' breakup of the Alcoa-Boeing-Pratt & Whitney combine.

cluster_id: NSF 1989 superconductor-only funding directive
content: NSF 1989 superconductor-only funding directive NSF announced in 1989 that only high-Tc superconductor proposals would be funded for a year; within one year, half the MIT Materials Science faculty pivoted into the field. Four of the five faculty who had prior superconductor experience stayed out, knowing the critical-current problem was unsolvable.

cluster_id: Nigerian cement shipping crisis
content: Nigerian cement shipping crisis ~25 years before lecture, 200 ships sat full of cement outside Lagos, unloaded for so long that humidity set the concrete in the holds — converted the cargo into junk and consumed a significant fraction of world shipping capacity. Used as the punctuation example for "cement is heavy, transportation cost dominates."

content: MIT Lincoln Lab 300 GHz Radar Dish Structure Air Force wanted to retrofit the old MIT Millstone steel pedestal/bearing with a new 150-foot aluminum radar dish at sub-quarter-inch tolerances. No shop would bid; ex-Electric Boat welding company eventually took the contract and succeeded. cluster_id: Alaska Pipeline Welding Union Control
content: Alaska Pipeline Welding Union Control All field pipeline welding worldwide is controlled by the Tulsa, Oklahoma union. Automated welding technology was available in 1976 for the Alaska Pipeline; it was built manually instead, and remains manual forty years later. Used to make the point that welder availability/scarcity is sometimes political rather than technical — paralleling the technical scarcity case of aluminum welders in §7. Tulsa Oklahoma welders' union controls field welding contracts on pipelines worldwide. Tom's 1970s Alaskan pipeline anecdote: the union told the oil company CEO they would sabotage automatic welding if introduced. Also covers the American-food union contract requirement and the worker-pays-for-rework custom.

Eight-stage forming sequence: shear → size → backward extrude → deepen → flange → punch hole → knurl → thread → plate. Production rate 10–20/sec; phosphate-stearate ("soap") lubrication; deafening noise levels.

cluster_id: Philips Elmet molybdenum rolling mill (Maine)
content: Philips Elmet molybdenum rolling mill (Maine) Tom visits former undergrad Charlie's plant in Maine. Hot rolling Mo plate at ~1800 °C in air; volatile MoO₃ forms a dense white smoke fog and coats the mill walls. Backofen sample (now bisected) shows alligator-style splitting from inhomogeneous deformation; white MoO₃ residue visible in the cracks. Customer in the 1980s: IBM for computer chip interconnects.

cluster_id: Blackhawk helicopter tail-rotor washer failure (Arkansas crash)

First cracks found by the Navy on Seahawks (corrosion leader in the service); first fatality on an Army Blackhawk. Same airframe as presidential helicopters.

## Figures referenced

cluster_id: 1980s refrigerator shelf failures
content: 1980s refrigerator shelf failures Material-substitution case. Manufacturers transitioned to plastic interiors but kept screw-mounted shelves, designing plastic as if it were steel. Plastic's brittleness at stress concentrations caused three-year failure cycles until KitchenAid and others adopted molded slots. Used as opening example of how naïve material substitution (metal → plastic shelving) creates new stress concentrations at dissimilar-material joints. Holman teaches it as a thermal-expansion-mismatch failure.

cluster_id: KitchenAid refrigerator successful design
content: KitchenAid refrigerator successful design Counterpoint to the shelf-failure case — manufacturers who designed *to* the plastic rather than against it.

id: case:Boston hot-work fire-watch regulation and building cost impact
cluster_id: Boston hot-work fire-watch regulation and building cost impact
content: Boston hot-work fire-watch regulation and building cost impact Externality-of-regulation case. The 1978 lead-tin solder ban plus OSHA hot-work rules made plumbing soldering expensive enough to drive adoption of a $800-tool, $30-fitting mechanical seal. Specifically Belmont, MA, where Eagar lives. Used as an externality argument for why swage fittings displaced solder fittings even where the joint quality might be inferior.

cluster_id: Massachusetts lead solder ban
content: Massachusetts lead solder ban Background to the fire-watch case. 1978 ban triggered the cascade. Massachusetts Commonwealth plumbing code change forced transition from lead-tin to tin-silver and then tin-antimony solders for potable water. Sets up Tom's argument that the tin-base replacements don't bridge plumbing-clearance gaps the way lead-tin did. Brief reference — 1978 Massachusetts ban on lead solder in plumbing.

id: case:Pratt & Whitney / General Electric jet engine disc HIP vessel failure
cluster_id: Pratt & Whitney / General Electric jet engine disc HIP vessel failure
content: Pratt & Whitney / General Electric jet engine disc HIP vessel failure Forensic conclusion. Tom analyzes the 200-ton vessel failure as a three-cause convergence — transient thermal stresses (the operator hadn't waited for thermal equilibration; the design hadn't been modeled in finite element because 1982-era computing couldn't), susceptible microstructure (Japan Steelworks delivered material with toughness below specification, and the un-heated corner regions retained the as-rolled properties), and hydrogen from a corrosion-pit-initiated crack on the water-cooled jacket (the inspection company hadn't been checking the outside often enough; the water treatment company was using out-of-date molybdate chemistry). Critical flaw size: half an inch. Three liable parties: Japan Steelworks, operator, water-treatment / inspection company.

content: *ambiguous — possibly* `7000-ton forging press casting weld failure` *or* `Aluminum truck wheel press weld crack` *or a new cluster* Tom produces the ~18-inch-thick, 400–600-pass weld sample. Tells the story: forging press broke after 60 years of service; competent welders, no weld defects, but high residual stress; cracked off the welding platform on first attempt; on second attempt the press cracked the first time they tried to forge an aluminum truck wheel. cluster_id: Nautilus submarine hull material (HY-80) / HY-80 and HY-100 steel development
content: Nautilus submarine hull material (HY-80) / HY-80 and HY-100 steel development HY-80 was developed at U.S. Steel under Navy program, jumping submarine hull yield from ~50 ksi (WWII) to 80 ksi, with corresponding depth-capability gain. Paired with Rickover's nuclear reactor development. Brief mention, framing the postwar payoff of Pellini's brittle-fracture work.

id: case:MIT steam plant pipe cracking during hot-weld repair
cluster_id: MIT steam plant pipe cracking during hot-weld repair
content: MIT steam plant pipe cracking during hot-weld repair Tom's recommendation thirty years ago to leave a crack (with a patch over it) on a winter-active steam line near 100 Memorial Drive, rather than continue trying to hot-weld it while moisture-driven hydrogen kept reopening the crack. Used to illustrate the rare case where the practical answer is "leave the crack."

cluster_id: US Navy 5000-series aluminum superstructure cracking
content: US Navy 5000-series aluminum superstructure cracking Triggered by a Coast Guard / Navy student's report of severe corrosion and fatigue cracking on a 5456 cruiser superstructure. Tom traces the problem to residual stresses in heavy-thickness aluminum welds, plus pitting at 5456's higher alloy content acting as fatigue initiation sites. The Navy is now retreating to 5083 for LCS construction.

cluster_id: Scandium-aluminum baseball bats
content: Scandium-aluminum baseball bats Tom holds up the scandium-microalloyed aluminum bat case as the highest-strength aluminum alloy he knows of — 100 KSI yield from fine grain size achieved by extrusion-quenching. Limited to ~2 mm wall thickness; bats break and must be replaced; $300-400 retail.

content: Westinghouse Bettis crack-acceptance welding code Cited twice as the only welding code Tom knows of that permits leaving small cracks in place, on the basis of detailed fracture mechanics analysis. Used as the exception that proves the rule "all codes say grind out cracks."

content: Steel mill wet scrap incident Magnetic crane lifting rain-soaked scrap into the steel furnace, illustrating the everyday source of 1–3 ppm hydrogen in commercial steel heats.

cluster_id: Sea wall bolt failures
content: Sea wall bolt failures Three or four consulting cases where steel bolt heads broke off after six months in salt water due to corrosion-generated hydrogen. Used to make the point that hydrogen embrittlement does not require welding — corrosion alone can charge the steel.

content: Nine-month delayed hydrogen crack (High Sierras) Forward-referenced as Monday's story — steel component buried in snow that finally cracked nine months later because the cold Sierra environment slowed hydrogen diffusion to a near-stop. Not developed in this lecture.

content: Hydrogen cracking in welded steel Tom's own work at Bethlehem Steel using a three-inch plate with a window cutout to fully restrain a test weld with strain gauges. Pedagogical illustration of how restraint is simulated in the lab.

id: case:Boston Gas Company buried steel pipe corrosion and gas leaks
cluster_id: Boston Gas Company buried steel pipe corrosion and gas leaks
content: Boston Gas Company buried steel pipe corrosion and gas leaks Boston Gas (now NSTAR/National Grid) training facility holds excavated 1880s gas distribution components — cast iron sleeves and bell-and-spigot joints filled with oakum. Extended case. Speaker's own street: a 1930s steel water/gas pipe network full of leaks; mud-sealing as accidental containment; the Boston Gas sniffer survey; speaker's home being sleeved and the plastic-to-steel connection failure (§4.p8–p10).

id: case:Boston wooden gas pipes (1880s street light system)
cluster_id: Boston wooden gas pipes (1880s street light system)
content: Boston wooden gas pipes (1880s street light system) Earliest Boston gas distribution: gun-drilled logs, ~6-inch diameter with 2-inch bore, used for street-light gas. Eventually replaced by cast iron.

cluster_id: Lead-sealed water pipe failures
content: Lead-sealed water pipe failures Student question prompt. Lead sealing arrived ~1900–1910; Tom has worked on lead-sealed water pipe failures from 90 years out.

cluster_id: Cardiac guide wire lawsuit
content: Cardiac guide wire lawsuit Mentioned descriptively rather than as a case study — Tom explains the femoral-artery / fluoroscopy / barium-tipped guide wire / stent procedure. Used as setup for the stiffness discussion. Physical demonstration. Tom passes around a 25-year-old guide wire whose weld tip failed at less than 2.5 lb. 304 stainless, very fine coiled wire. Anchor for lawsuit anecdote (surgeon left 30 inches inside patient).

id: case:Air Force blisk (bladed disc) welding development
cluster_id: Air Force blisk (bladed disc) welding development
content: Air Force blisk (bladed disc) welding development 1980s–1990s Air Force program to weld turbine blades directly to disc, eliminating half the rotating mass that lives in the "tree" mechanical attachment. Tried electron beam, laser, arc, linear friction welding. Economics failed at Six Sigma quality requirement. "Tens, if not hundreds, of millions of dollars" spent trying to figure out how to weld blades to disk. No commercial product yet at large-engine scale. Air Force has spent billions trying to weld blades directly to disc to eliminate Christmas-tree flange weight. 20 lb savings per disc, multiplied by 3–4 discs × 2–4 engines × collateral airframe weight = ~2,000 lb total savings; military aircraft bogey is $1,000/lb saved.

cluster_id: Pratt & Whitney turbine blade
content: Pratt & Whitney turbine blade The physical blade Tom holds up as exemplar of precision-ground "tree" mechanical attachment, Wood's-metal fixturing for the $10M grinding machine. Returns in §8 as the artifact Tom distributed to high-school visitors with the corner-cut / notch quality-control markings to prevent reuse.

id: case:Turbine blade quality control theft risk
cluster_id: Turbine blade quality control theft risk
content: Turbine blade quality control theft risk Tom's anecdote distributing worn/defective Pratt & Whitney blades to ~200 high-school visitors in 1995/96, with care taken about cut-corner and notch markings — at $4,000–$6,000 per blade, defective blades stolen and reinstalled could blow up engines.

cluster_id: Percy Bridgeman high-pressure materials research
content: Percy Bridgeman high-pressure materials research Harvard physicist, Nobel laureate, tetrahedral anvil press at gigapascal pressures, foundation for synthetic diamond manufacture. Used to anchor the "parameter" usage dispute with Hallock Campbell. Extended sketch — Harvard physics professor, Nobel laureate, suicide in Randolph NH 1961. Invented the tetrahedral anvil press, opened up high-pressure materials science (artificial diamond synthesis). Used as the lead-in to the central teaching point: hydrostatic stress suppresses brittle fracture, and at sufficient pressure even steel necks like plasticine. Tom anchors the rock-creep / deep-mine point in Bridgman's framework.

cluster_id: Hallock Campbell AWS definition dispute
content: Hallock Campbell AWS definition dispute Hallock Campbell (Harvard grad, AWS glossary author) wrote to Tom in Japan in 1985 critiquing his use of "parameter" in a Welding Journal title. Tom showed the dictionary cited Bridgman; Campbell's handwritten reply: "Percy, how could you?" Used as launchpad for Tom's "weld defined by properties, not process" reformulation in his keynote address.

cluster_id: H.C. Starck Newton tantalum operations
content: H.C. Starck Newton tantalum operations H.C. Starck (now part of Bayer) operates one of the world's largest tantalum production facilities in residential Newton, MA. Tom traces its founding to post-WWII MIT mechanical engineering vacuum-melting innovation.

cluster_id: Nuclear Metals Concord depleted uranium extrusion
content: Nuclear Metals Concord depleted uranium extrusion Concord, MA company (now largely defunct) that extruded depleted uranium for bullets, and produced tantalum wire by cold-weld die forging. Tom obtained his tantalum cold-weld sample from them.

cluster_id: Titanium-clad steel gasoline refinery vessel production

id: case:Quincy LNG tanker aluminum tank skirts
cluster_id: Quincy LNG tanker aluminum tank skirts
content: Quincy LNG tanker aluminum tank skirts Tom's tenure as a Bethlehem Steel engineer developing weldable steel for the 150-foot-diameter cylindrical skirt supporting the aluminum LNG sphere. Coast Guard required Charpy testing at weld centerline, toe, and 1/3/5 mm into HAZ at 20 ft-lb / −20°F. Sparrows Point steel-making struggled to meet the spec on base plate; shipyard would hunt down high-toughness plates (30 ft-lb outliers) to cherry-pick for runoff tab testing — gaming the Coast Guard reporting. Tom's project welding the steel skirts that supported the aluminum LNG tanks. Coast Guard 20 foot-pound specification at four positions per weld drove the test-plate substitution scheme — the shipyard cut all test plates from the rare 30 foot-pound outlier plate from Sparrows Point.

content: Carbon composite filter for precious metal catalyst recovery Physical-object demonstration. Koch Industries research project. content: Tin-bismuth solder steel recycling contamination 25 years prior (~early 1990s) push to replace lead-tin solder with bismuth-tin. id: case:Continuous casting of steel — Japanese development
cluster_id: Continuous casting of steel — Japanese development
content: Continuous casting of steel — Japanese development Japanese-led commercialization of continuous casting. Ten-story-tall casters; copper molds; 10-foot-high mold zone; horizontal cut-off as the slab moves at centimeters/minute. Yield jumped from 65% (ingot) to 90%+ (continuous). Breakouts (shell rupture) catastrophic — hundreds of tons of liquid on a billion-dollar facility, weeks of shutdown.

cluster_id: Bao Steel — Chinese government-financed integrated steel

cluster_id: Saugus Ironworks — energy-crisis emigration of British iron
content: Saugus Ironworks — energy-crisis emigration of British iron 1600-era. British wood shortage forced iron production to North America. Tom's estimate: 2,000–4,000 person-hours per ton of steel at Saugus. Today: 15 person-minutes per ton. Tom's headline productivity-gain figure.

id: case:Japanese steel manufacturing technology — Tom's 1985 Navy-funded visit
cluster_id: Japanese steel manufacturing technology — Tom's 1985 Navy-funded visit
content: Japanese steel manufacturing technology — Tom's 1985 Navy-funded visit Tom's 1985 sabbatical in Japan; U.S. Navy sent him to learn Japanese steel for better ship construction. Discovery: Japanese were using 1950s/1960s American technology that U.S. firms had never commercialized.

cluster_id: Soviet titanium electro-slag welding technology
content: Soviet titanium electro-slag welding technology Two-pass treatment. First Tom recounts realizing in 1980 that Gurevich's group had used electroslag for the Alpha sub hull. Then he describes returning to MIT and making "probably the first electroslag titanium weld outside of the Soviet Union or France." The Navy classified the result. The technical content Tom was after on the exchange. Paton Institute led the world in electroslag, and Tom's group made the first US electroslag weld on titanium ("just in the room next door") after Gurevich quit publishing. Closes with the inference that the Soviets used electroslag to weld their titanium hulls. During a 1980 visit to the Ukraine with Julian Szekely, Tom learned that half of all Soviet steel was electroslag remelted. Julian's interpretation: Soviet BOP steel was so poor (fist-sized inclusions in ship plate) that ESR was necessary just to reach Western BOP quality. The political driver was Dr. Paton at the Paton Institute in Kiev — a WWII hero for electroslag welding of armor plate — who controlled ~25% of Soviet Ukrainian scientific funding and grew his institute to ~5000 people.

id: case:Army helicopter rotor casting weld repair (early 1980s)
cluster_id: Army helicopter rotor casting weld repair (early 1980s)
content: Army helicopter rotor casting weld repair (early 1980s) Tom's student "Gordon" worked at Watertown Arsenal on whether weld repairs of titanium helicopter rotor castings would be acceptable. Result: welds were better than the base metal because of faster cooling and finer Widmanstätten structure. Used to make the point that in titanium, welds can outperform base material in fatigue strength.

cluster_id: Glomar Explorer (Soviet submarine recovery)
content: Glomar Explorer (Soviet submarine recovery) Howard Hughes's cover for the CIA Glomar Explorer — a multibillion-dollar disguised freighter that lifted a Soviet submarine off the Pacific floor — invoked as the most dramatic example of US deep-sea retrieval capability built up in the same period as the Alvin work.

cluster_id: Beryllium copper spark-free tools (mining application)
content: Beryllium copper spark-free tools (mining application) Tom's own beryllium copper crescent wrench ($130) as a teaching prop. Used in methane-bearing mines because high thermal conductivity prevents the frictional hotspot that would ignite gas. Properties: well over 1 GPa strength, 150–180 ksi, hardness comparable to a steel wrench, but ten times the cost.

cluster_id: HY-80 nuclear submarine steel
content: HY-80 nuclear submarine steel Used as the canonical example of an alloyed-for-hardenability steel: 1 inch thick, low carbon, ~3% alloy (Ni, Cr, Mo) for through-thickness hardenability in submarine hull plate.

id: case:John Wolfe stainless steel sensitization patent (1940s)
cluster_id: John Wolfe stainless steel sensitization patent (1940s)
content: John Wolfe stainless steel sensitization patent (1940s) Wulff's 1940s patent: deliberately sensitize stainless steel, immerse in nitric acid overnight, dissolve chromium-depleted grain boundaries to produce stainless steel powder. Used pedagogically to show that the same intergranular attack mechanism that makes BWR welds fail is exploited industrially for powder production.

cluster_id: Saudi Arabia gas-reduction steel facility
content: Saudi Arabia gas-reduction steel facility Saudi natural gas as steel reductant — sidesteps coal-and-coke entirely. Imported iron ore + domestic natural gas + sovereign capital = integrated steelmaking. Part of the road-to-industrialization sequence (steel → ships → autos).

cluster_id: General Motors bankruptcy
content: General Motors bankruptcy "They earned it." Parallel to the steel-company bankruptcies of the 1980s. GM's $50 billion plant-and-equipment budget in the 1980s could have bought Toyota outright on the Tokyo exchange. GM bountied robots-for-people while Toyota developed the Toyota Production System.

cluster_id: Conductive polymers / polyacetylene hype
content: Conductive polymers / polyacetylene hype A young professor's claim that polyacetylene would replace copper because of higher *specific* electrical conductivity. Tom's shaving-mirror realization the next morning: aluminum already has higher specific conductivity than copper, but we don't use it in rotating machinery — because absolute conductivity is what matters, not specific.

id: case:WWII silver-wound magnets from Fort Knox
cluster_id: WWII silver-wound magnets from Fort Knox
content: WWII silver-wound magnets from Fort Knox Copper shortage during WWII forced Manhattan Project to borrow ~50 tons of silver from the U.S. Mint in Philadelphia for the Calutron magnetic separators at Oak Ridge; returned after the war undamaged.

cluster_id: MIT Building 20 asbestos liability
content: MIT Building 20 asbestos liability Tom's role in negotiating the demolition of Building 20 and the development of the Stata Center — proposing that engineering and science compete to raise funds. Engineering raised $115M in 18 months; final Stata Center cost $430M.

cluster_id: Sadoway/Allanore carbon-free metal reduction research
content: Sadoway/Allanore carbon-free metal reduction research Ellingham-diagram thermodynamic argument that any oxide can be reduced by carbon at sufficient temperature, but CO2 externalities are driving MIT research toward electron-based reduction routes.

id: case:Charles Martin Hall Niagara Falls Alcoa first reduction plant
cluster_id: Charles Martin Hall Niagara Falls Alcoa first reduction plant
content: Charles Martin Hall Niagara Falls Alcoa first reduction plant Aluminum smelting is sited at electricity sources — Norway, James Bay, and originally Niagara Falls for Alcoa's first plant.

cluster_id: India cultural gold reserve
content: India cultural gold reserve Cultural externality. Half the world's mined gold sits on the necks and wrists of Indian people; cultural color-match drives material demand.

cluster_id: Platinum jewelry in Asia
content: Platinum jewelry in Asia Platinum jewelry popular in Asia for color-match with skin tone.

id: case:AT&T regulated monopoly and the transistor
cluster_id: AT&T regulated monopoly and the transistor
content: AT&T regulated monopoly and the transistor Tom's debunking of the basic-research transistor myth. Bell Labs' 1925 statistical projection showed mechanical switch failure rates would collapse the phone system by the 1950s; transistor development was applied research justified within the 6% regulated-profit framework.

id: case:Utility LED light bulb rate-base subsidy
cluster_id: Utility LED light bulb rate-base subsidy
content: Utility LED light bulb rate-base subsidy Economic logic of utilities subsidizing efficient bulbs — $2000/kW installed cost of new plants justifies any kWh savings cheaper than that. Massachusetts DPU example.

cluster_id: Cape Wind / Nantucket windmill opposition
content: Cape Wind / Nantucket windmill opposition NIMBY externality. Residents would oppose tripled electric bills if framed honestly, but frame the objection as aesthetic.

cluster_id: Rhodesian chromite embargo
content: Rhodesian chromite embargo Embargo workaround case. Rhodesian chrome ore was uniquely high-grade — crushable directly into a steel furnace for stainless. Embargo was nominally enforced; black-market laundering through third countries was tacitly tolerated by customs.

cluster_id: US copper tubing manufacturing
content: US copper tubing manufacturing Transportation externality. Six US copper tubing plants survived 1980s–90s offshoring because the air-in-the-hole shipping cost was prohibitive. Reading Tube as the LGO thesis site.

id: case:Bombardier aircraft lightning testing - Canadian border incident
cluster_id: Bombardier aircraft lightning testing - Canadian border incident
content: Bombardier aircraft lightning testing - Canadian border incident Local-employment externality. Pittsfield MA lightning lab's technicians were barred at the Canadian border; engineers had to perform technician work in-country.

cluster_id: Norm Augustine socio-engineering 1993 Colorado talk
content: Norm Augustine socio-engineering 1993 Colorado talk Augustine's 1993 University of Colorado engineering centennial talk anticipated the externality-dominated era of materials selection. Posted as course reading.

cluster_id: Mike Ashby materials-over-the-ages plot critique
content: Mike Ashby materials-over-the-ages plot critique Tom's critique of Ashby's predicted decline of metals and rise of ceramics/composites — argues Ashby bought into 1980s ceramics fever.

cluster_id: Ceramics fever / NIST kitchen-sink talk
content: Ceramics fever / NIST kitchen-sink talk Tom's 1986 NIST talk after returning from Japan. Punchline: the only high-volume structural ceramics are portland cement and toilet bowls — "and I throw in the kitchen sink, but you have to line it with gray cast iron." Griffith fracture-mechanics argument: critical flaw size too small to inspect.

id: case:Eagar 1991 Welding Journal Future of Metals article
cluster_id: Eagar 1991 Welding Journal Future of Metals article
content: Eagar 1991 Welding Journal Future of Metals article Tom's June 1991 *Welding Journal* article. 95% of world metal is steel; in 1990, steel was a $500B industry at 2% growth — its absolute growth exceeded ceramics ($5B/20%), composites ($15B/10%), and semiconductors ($100B/5%) combined.

cluster_id: Torpedo tube welding distortion control
content: Torpedo tube welding distortion control Student-of-Tom anecdote. Balanced-weld procedure (alternating clock positions around the circumference) developed for ~40-foot-long torpedo tubes to control distortion.

cluster_id: Farm equipment engine fire (loose bolt)
content: Farm equipment engine fire (loose bolt) Current consulting case (referenced as "last week"). Bolt-came-loose engine fire on $700k farm equipment, 100 hours old. Defense attorney's theory converts an assembly defect into a design defect via the flatbed-transport argument.

cluster_id: Cement truck pressure vessel explosion (Pennsylvania)
content: Cement truck pressure vessel explosion (Pennsylvania) Extended teaching case. Aluminum water tank, no doubler plates, regulatory gap (DOT defers to ASME, ASME excludes water tanks, Pennsylvania attorney reads regs and concludes no code applies). Iraq-veteran welder killed during 100 psi over-pressure test repair. Earlier near-miss (leg amputation) had been attributed to a fluke; company responded by building a test cage. Tom got involved through Roger, ex-ASME committee. Hundred thousand similar vehicles on the road; National Board of Pressure Vessel Inspectors says they can't be inspected at that scale.

cluster_id: High-strength truck frame welding violations
content: High-strength truck frame welding violations General principle illustration. NHTSA-prohibited welding on HSLA tractor-trailer ladder frames; aftermarket welds cause failure at ~100k miles.

cluster_id: Nautilus submarine hull material (HY-80)
content: Nautilus submarine hull material (HY-80) HY-80 origin story — developed 1940s-50s by U.S. Steel, used in Nautilus, served until "recently being twenty years" on other subs.

cluster_id: Alaska Pipeline construction
content: Alaska Pipeline construction Bethlehem Steel in the mid-70s wanted to use a 1% nickel HSLA precursor steel for the Alaskan Pipeline. Would have consumed a substantial fraction of world nickel supply.

cluster_id: US Navy HSLA Steel Mill Investment
content: US Navy HSLA Steel Mill Investment Navy developed HSLA-60/80/100 in 1980s-90s for surface ships (more weldable than HY series). Subsequent NAVSEA/Newport News study of HSLA-60 for next-class carrier showed $1/lb material → $10/lb fabricated, killing the weight-saving case.

Story itself not delivered in this section. The exception to the "hydrogen diffuses out within a few days" rule — a weld frozen all winter in the High Sierras retained its hydrogen and cracked the next spring.

cluster_id: China rare earth embargo on Japan (2010)
content: China rare earth embargo on Japan (2010) Geopolitical externality. Tom uses the embargo to introduce how monopolies are built by undercutting price, then weaponized politically. Sets up the magnet discussion that follows.

cluster_id: Mountain Pass rare earth mine closure
content: Mountain Pass rare earth mine closure U.S. domestic capacity that closed when Chinese prices dropped; reopenable with five-to-ten-year lead time and ~$1B capex.

cluster_id: U.S. Steel 1962 price rollback (Kennedy standoff)
content: U.S. Steel 1962 price rollback (Kennedy standoff) Political externality. Kennedy forced U.S. Steel to roll back prices because steel was the global commodity benchmark and the price rise would have triggered worldwide inflation. Some old-timers blamed this for the industry's decline; Tom blames the 1945 hiring cohort instead.

Bethlehem's exploration of nuclear steel-making.

cluster_id: Quincy Shipyard barge cracking failure
content: Quincy Shipyard barge cracking failure Aluminum-cleaning rinse tank maintenance failure. Rinse water pH had drifted to 2.3 (Coca-Cola acidity). Used as cautionary example that chemical-bath cleaning requires maintenance discipline. Barges were destined to carry number six bunker oil. Brass heating pipes (3" dia, Dowtherm-heated) inside heavy-crude barges; stress corrosion cracking traced to rinse-water pH of 2.3. Recommendation: change rinse water weekly or daily, with pH monitoring.

id: case:Aviation aluminum crankcase weld repair dispute
cluster_id: Aviation aluminum crankcase weld repair dispute
content: Aviation aluminum crankcase weld repair dispute Recent (January 2014) consulting email from a family-owned engine-repair business in Oklahoma, one of the few FAA-approved shops for weld repair of Lycoming and TCM aircraft engine crankcases. The dispute: Canadian failure investigators criticized their use of 4043 filler (undermatching) on Aluminum Association 355 castings. Tom walks through the matching/undermatching/overmatching trade-off and the four classes of filler (4145 overmatching, 4009 matching, 4043 undermatching). Frames the case as a demonstration of how to give a client options without making the design decision yourself ("if an aircraft goes down...I don't want them coming back to me").

cluster_id: Ford Explorer chromic acid plating facility (1990s environmental retrofit)
content: Ford Explorer chromic acid plating facility (1990s environmental retrofit) Mid-1990s, Ford built an environmentally controlled chromic acid plating shop for Ford Explorers at a couple hundred million dollars. Used to mark the end of the chrome-plating gap that began in 1982.

content: Historical water conveyance material evolution Survey of water pipe material substitutions from 4000 BC clay pipes through Roman aqueducts, wood, cast iron / ductile iron, and into polymer transitions. Used to set up the embrittlement issue with century-old cast iron mains.

id: case:HDPE pipe fracture on Hudson River barge
cluster_id: HDPE pipe fracture on Hudson River barge
content: HDPE pipe fracture on Hudson River barge Holman's own consulting case. Thousands of feet of HDPE pipe fusion-welded on a barge and pulled under the Hudson; one fracture investigated. Used to introduce fusion-welded polymer pipe and the open question of century-scale durability.

id: case:Samsung Galaxy Note 7 thermal runaway recalls
cluster_id: Samsung Galaxy Note 7 thermal runaway recalls
content: Samsung Galaxy Note 7 thermal runaway recalls Student raises the iPhone 7 / Note 7 fires; Holman uses it to introduce battery thermal runaway and Samsung's 60% charge-cap response.

content: Vape pen battery spontaneous ignition Holman cites his own consulting work on vape pen fires as a class of cases parallel to phone-battery fires.

id: case:Skyscraper glass curtain wall panel breakage
cluster_id: Skyscraper glass curtain wall panel breakage
content: Skyscraper glass curtain wall panel breakage Holman's consulting work on structural glass failures in curtain walls. IGU optimization shrunk the gap layer, raised internal temperatures under morning sun, produced thermal stress breakage. Notes the LEED-credit trade-off.

cluster_id: Crane rail forging burst failure
content: Crane rail forging burst failure Holman's consulting case. Crane rail on a dredging barge turntable fractured; sectioning revealed an internal forging burst from refractory inclusion during manufacture. Should have been caught by pre-service ultrasonic inspection. Holman passes the sectioned sample around the class.

cluster_id: Container ship wire rope fracture
content: Container ship wire rope fracture Holman's consulting case on a fractured cargo-container lifting rope. Full-scale tensile test in a three-story vertical machine; broke above 300,000 lb (Holman conflates with ksi in delivery — see editorial register flag).

id: case:Lehigh University five-million-pound structural test machine
cluster_id: Lehigh University five-million-pound structural test machine
content: Lehigh University five-million-pound structural test machine Cited as the largest tensile/structural test facility Holman has seen; full-scale bridge section testing to failure. Used to make the cost argument for computer simulation.

id: case:Navy topside weight reduction composite structures study
cluster_id: Navy topside weight reduction composite structures study
content: Navy topside weight reduction composite structures study Holman's master's thesis work. Open- and closed-cell aluminum foam sandwich structures, dip-brazed in molten sodium fluoride, evaluated as topside-weight alternatives to monolithic aluminum. Holman shows samples. Discusses maintainability barrier to field deployment.

id: case:Miami Art Museum hanging garden failure
cluster_id: Miami Art Museum hanging garden failure
content: Miami Art Museum hanging garden failure Forensic consulting case (Tom retained by general contractor). 20-ton reinforced concrete cantilevered beams in a Miami building, hung by two three-quarter-inch threaded rods in tension, originally specified in 410 martensitic stainless. Tack welds caused delayed hydrogen cracking; beams fell in August and November 2012. Material substitution to 316 austenitic stainless raised chloride stress corrosion cracking concerns at the marine site; Tom refused to sign off as PE, sent a written notice to general contractor, who forwarded it to the owner. Final resolution: duplex stainless steel. Litigation pending as of recording (Summer 2014). Six-story hanging garden 100 yards from Biscayne Bay. 410 martensitic stainless steel tension bolts failed during construction (low fracture toughness + tack welds). 316 proposed; Tom warned of SCC. Settled on 2205 duplex (Sandvik recommendation), no weld details. Cost increase 7–8M on a 60M building. Tom refused to sign off as engineer of record. Used to teach martensitic vs duplex stainless steels, stress corrosion cracking, and consulting liability.

id: case:Tom Eagar's residential high-efficiency boiler chimney
cluster_id: Tom Eagar's residential high-efficiency boiler chimney
content: Tom Eagar's residential high-efficiency boiler chimney Personal anecdote, late 1970s. Tom declined to pay $2,000–$3,000 to line his chimney stack with superferritic stainless steel to route boiler exhaust up the stack rather than out the side wall; still vents through the side decades later. Used to illustrate the superferritic / chloride-cracking-resistance application and the role of mortgage-scale economics in materials selection at the consumer level.

cluster_id: Oil refinery pipe lot rejection
content: Oil refinery pipe lot rejection Brief reference. One leaky pipe out of 600 led purchaser to condemn entire lot and demand refund. Tom characterizes this as "not the appropriate way to handle that problem." Used to contrast statistical reality of NDT with overreaction to single failures.

id: case:Allegheny River interstate highway bridge crack
cluster_id: Allegheny River interstate highway bridge crack
content: Allegheny River interstate highway bridge crack Tugboat captain noticed a crack in an interstate highway bridge over the Allegheny in Pittsburgh growing between trips. By the time inspectors reached it, the crack was nine feet long and visible from 20-30 feet. Used to illustrate: (1) why pressure vessel safety factors exceed bridge/building safety factors (consequences of failure), (2) redundancy in bridge structures.

id: case:X-33 hydrogen tank adhesive joint failures
cluster_id: X-33 hydrogen tank adhesive joint failures
content: X-33 hydrogen tank adhesive joint failures Composite hydrogen tank originally designed for 2.0 safety factor. Manufacturing defects (potentially 3-4 inches in size) led program to recalculate as 1.05 safety factor to justify proceeding to test rather than scrapping $225M-$250M vessels. Failed in test at Huntsville. Used as exemplar of "political games" with safety factors. A piece of the X-33 hydrogen tank is shown as an example of a $12,000/lb fabricated structural material. Used as the high-end anchor of the price-per-pound argument that becomes §8. No failure discussion here. Half-size shuttle-replacement prototype. Adhesively bonded hydrogen tanks at $250M each, factor-of-safety reduced from 2.0 to 1.05 to meet schedule. Held during cryogenic test, failed on warm-up. $1.3B program cancellation. Two adhesively-bonded Nomex/carbon-fiber composite liquid hydrogen tanks built at $50 million apiece, ~4,000 pounds each, ~$12,000/lb fabrication cost. "Except it didn't [work]. But that's another story." Physical sample passed around class.

cluster_id: 1988 Northeast snowstorm building collapses
content: 1988 Northeast snowstorm building collapses Storm of the century, through Princeton NJ and eastern Pennsylvania. Prefabricated buildings with computer-optimized roof joists (designed to 1.67 minimum rather than the historical 2.0+ rule-of-thumb) collapsed under snow loads. Cause: optimization had eaten the implicit safety margin that had previously made 1.67 effectively higher.

cluster_id: 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire
content: 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire Tom misdates as "1912 or whatever." Triggered modern building codes for earthquake protection in the U.S.

cluster_id: Oakland Bay Bridge 1989 Loma Prieta partial collapse
content: Oakland Bay Bridge 1989 Loma Prieta partial collapse Tom mentions a section collapsed but doesn't recall fatalities. Brief reference; not developed.

id: case:Nova Scotia sailboat trailer weld failure
cluster_id: Nova Scotia sailboat trailer weld failure
content: Nova Scotia sailboat trailer weld failure Tom's forensic case. A farmer-built sailboat trailer with a slugged weld (bolt buried in the joint, then welded over) fractured on Route 24 south of Boston on the return trip from a Newport race, destroying the 40-foot sailboat. Used to illustrate why standards prohibit welding on tractor-trailer frames and what "slugging a weld" means.

id: case:Jet engine removal bolt design failure
cluster_id: Jet engine removal bolt design failure
content: Jet engine removal bolt design failure Stage-business case. Tom passes around a hardened steel bolt assembly used to dismount jet engines from aircraft wings. The bolt had two diameters with flats on the center shoulder for restraint; mechanics torqued only the outer nut, ignoring the shoulder, which over-torqued the assembly and initiated a crack. A 5-million-dollar engine dropped on the tarmac. Used to introduce load-path reasoning.

cluster_id: Stata Center (Frank Gehry conceptual design)
content: Stata Center (Frank Gehry conceptual design) Stage-business case. Tom crumples four sheets of paper to demonstrate how Frank Gehry presented the conceptual design of the Stata Center to MIT physical-plant head Vicki Sirianni. Budget went from $115M to $430M; MIT froze salaries for two years. Used to illustrate how informal conceptual designs become consequential.

id: case:Chevrolet Vega engine removal for spark plug service
cluster_id: Chevrolet Vega engine removal for spark plug service
content: Chevrolet Vega engine removal for spark plug service Brief design-foible aside in the Hyatt section. The 1978 Chevy Vega had to have its engine removed to change spark plugs because surrounding components blocked wrench access. Used as a low-stakes illustration of the same as-designed / as-serviceable gap.

id: case:General Motors sliding door van lemon-law case
cluster_id: General Motors sliding door van lemon-law case
content: General Motors sliding door van lemon-law case Personal forensic case, 1985. The sliding side door of Tom's GM van fell off five times. After a nasty letter from the dealership owner, Tom filed lemon-law demand; GM offered an executive vehicle, then offered cash instead when the executive's loaner wasn't ready. Used as a narrative bridge into the Taurus case and to illustrate manufacturer response patterns.

id: case:Bethlehem Steel looper program and Lackawanna depreciation case
cluster_id: Bethlehem Steel looper program and Lackawanna depreciation case
content: Bethlehem Steel looper program and Lackawanna depreciation case Tom's 20-month tenure at Bethlehem Steel, 1975. The looper rotation program (Martin Tower vice-presidential lectures). The Lackawanna 1910/1911 coke ovens "fully depreciated, costs us nothing" misconception. The MIT-PhD boss / Lehigh-PhD manager who vetoed a no-cost quality improvement. The Homer Research Labs executive dining room with tennis-ball-sized strawberries. Six of the top ten paid US executives at Bethlehem in the 1930s while the company was losing money. Eugene Grace's tonnage-based compensation. Gulfstream jets to Florida.

cluster_id: Boeing door product center manufacturing
content: Boeing door product center manufacturing mid-1990s plant tour. Deterministic manufacturing (orders three years out, doors one year out). Seven drillings per rivet hole. 750 doors, 250 employees → $50,000/door by the $100k-per-employee rule. Today probably a $100k door.

id: case:Andrew Carnegie and Eagar grandfather University of Chattanooga donation
cluster_id: Andrew Carnegie and Eagar grandfather University of Chattanooga donation
content: Andrew Carnegie and Eagar grandfather University of Chattanooga donation Tom's grandfather (former mayor of Chattanooga) sought $25,000 from Carnegie to complete a $500K matching grant (Rockefeller's $250K) for the University of Chattanooga. Carnegie asked his education level; grandfather said 13 months; Carnegie revealed he too had 13 months and granted the funds. The anecdote serves as a Carnegie character study and a generational bridge to the steel-industry narrative.

cluster_id: Dick Simmons private plane story
content: Dick Simmons private plane story Tom drove Simmons to "the airport"; only at general aviation did Simmons sheepishly admit he owned his own plane. Used to characterize Simmons's personal modesty against his financial scale.

id: case:America's Cup hydraulic cylinder stress corrosion cracking (Navtech consulting case)
cluster_id: America's Cup hydraulic cylinder stress corrosion cracking (Navtech consulting case)
content: America's Cup hydraulic cylinder stress corrosion cracking (Navtech consulting case) Worked fracture-mechanics example. 7075-T6 piston cylinder in a yacht winch hydraulic system, operating at 7,500 psi, failed by stress corrosion cracking from saltwater exposure. Critical flaw size calculation showed ~1 mm — confirmed by examination of the fracture surface. Solution: switch to 7075-T73 (over-aged, lower yield, higher toughness and corrosion resistance) with slightly thicker wall, achieving leak-before-break.

id: case:Wright brothers' aircraft engine precipitate coarsening (Smithsonian study)
cluster_id: Wright brothers' aircraft engine precipitate coarsening (Smithsonian study)
content: Wright brothers' aircraft engine precipitate coarsening (Smithsonian study) Brief teaching aside on natural aging. SEM study of the engine block in the Smithsonian showed aluminum-copper precipitates still coarsening after a hundred years at room temperature; data fell on a straight line on a log-time scale.

id: case:Aluminum-lithium development for Space Shuttle and Boeing 787
cluster_id: Aluminum-lithium development for Space Shuttle and Boeing 787
content: Aluminum-lithium development for Space Shuttle and Boeing 787 Thirty-year development arc. Soviets discovered aluminum-lithium alloys in the 1970s. Alcoa worked on it for thirty years through hot cracking and weldability problems. Used at the end of the Space Shuttle main tank lifetime and in Boeing 787 components. Lithium reduces density 10%, raises Young's modulus 10%, giving 20% improvement in E/ρ. Still difficult to weld, and lithium worsens corrosion.

cluster_id: Washington Monument aluminum apex
content: Washington Monument aluminum apex Brief historical anecdote — aluminum pyramid at the top of the Washington Monument as a lightning rod, made of aluminum because at the time (1880s) it was more valuable than gold.

cluster_id: Hall-Héroult aluminum refining discovery (1888)
content: Hall-Héroult aluminum refining discovery (1888) Simultaneous independent invention by Charles Martin Hall (founder of Alcoa) and Paul Héroult of France, within two months of each other and with no communication. This is the foundational moment for cheap aluminum.

cluster_id: Novelis Skooter co-cast Alclad process
content: Novelis Skooter co-cast Alclad process Modern Alclad manufacture. Traditional roll-bonding of pure-aluminum cladding onto a high-strength aluminum-alloy core had ~15% yield. Novelis (Alcan/Péchiney merger entity) developed co-casting that gives ~100% yield. Outside skin of Airbus aircraft is Alclad of this type.

cluster_id: Iridium engagement ring (Tom's wife)
content: Iridium engagement ring (Tom's wife) Tom electron-beam melted an iridium alloy for the ring because of its corrosion immunity. Sets up the Cannon-connector electrocution story.

id: case:Cannon connector arc tracking fault in electron beam melter
cluster_id: Cannon connector arc tracking fault in electron beam melter
content: Cannon connector arc tracking fault in electron beam melter While melting platinum-iridium in 1973, Tom heard repeated arcing inside a vacuum chamber for three weeks. Eventually traced to arc tracking inside an Army-surplus Cannon connector. Paired with the 1962 fatality on the same equipment.

id: case:Johnson & Johnson electrocauterization device corrosion failure
cluster_id: Johnson & Johnson electrocauterization device corrosion failure
content: Johnson & Johnson electrocauterization device corrosion failure Cardiac surgery cautery probes corroded under 100V across all metal candidates (stainless, nickel alloys, even platinum and gold). Tom's recommendation: make the tip disposable. Closing case for the voltage-and-bond-energy section. 100 V DC pitting on stainless steel tips at the anode; platinum tops out around 2 V, titanium around 5 V; bond-strength limit is the materials-science answer to a customer demanding a 100 V-corrosion-resistant tip.

cluster_id: 1948 seaplane exfoliation failure
content: 1948 seaplane exfoliation failure One of only two exfoliation corrosion cases Tom has personally seen. Crashed near Tom's Miami apartment.

id: case:Homemade aluminum water-jet fishing boat exfoliation failure
cluster_id: Homemade aluminum water-jet fishing boat exfoliation failure
content: Homemade aluminum water-jet fishing boat exfoliation failure Maine builder constructed a water-jet-propelled aluminum fishing boat; seawater velocity-driven exfoliation destroyed the hull within six months. The second of Tom's two personal exfoliation cases.

id: case:Dedham, Massachusetts 30-year-old brass plumbing valve failure
cluster_id: Dedham, Massachusetts 30-year-old brass plumbing valve failure
content: Dedham, Massachusetts 30-year-old brass plumbing valve failure Dealloying (dezincification) of a brass valve over 30 years caused a flood with half a million dollars damage.

id: case:Mass General subway station rust removal consult
cluster_id: Mass General subway station rust removal consult
content: Mass General subway station rust removal consult 1910-vintage subway station; engineering firm chipped half-inch-thick rust off structural beams down to white metal. Tom's recommendation: plug it back up — the rust was structural and stopping further corrosion.

id: case:High-strength bridge bolts hydrogen embrittlement in Northeast
cluster_id: High-strength bridge bolts hydrogen embrittlement in Northeast
content: High-strength bridge bolts hydrogen embrittlement in Northeast 140 ksi bolts on a pier in New Jersey or Connecticut; no cathodic protection or inadequate zinc coating; hydrogen embrittlement failures within one to two years.

id: case:Warehouse fire sprinkler pipe corrosion (leak-driven oxygen makeup)
cluster_id: Warehouse fire sprinkler pipe corrosion (leak-driven oxygen makeup)
content: Warehouse fire sprinkler pipe corrosion (leak-driven oxygen makeup) Large warehouse's entire fire sprinkler system was fully occluded with rust. Root cause: a tolerated leak introduced makeup water (and fresh oxygen) to what should have been a closed system. All piping required replacement.

id: case:Mexican airline jet turbine blade hot corrosion
cluster_id: Mexican airline jet turbine blade hot corrosion
content: Mexican airline jet turbine blade hot corrosion Hot corrosion by sulfur/oxygen occurs in a narrow 100°C window where the kinetics peak and the sulfide condenses. Mexican airline practiced no-warmup full-power takeoffs to save fuel, dwelling in the corrosion-sensitive temperature band for the critical minutes that they should have spent above it.

cluster_id: Ford plastic bumper painting failure
content: Ford plastic bumper painting failure Low-surface-energy plastic (PEO) wouldn't accept paint; Ford had to introduce sandblasting to convert to type-two mechanical interlocking. Used to set up the type-one vs. type-two adhesive bonding distinction.

id: case:Millennium cookware hydrogen cracking and Teflon coating
cluster_id: Millennium cookware hydrogen cracking and Teflon coating
content: Millennium cookware hydrogen cracking and Teflon coating Two-part teaching unit using the pot as prop. (1) The aluminum/stainless cold-bonded base illustrates that a deliberately weak bond (10% bonded area) is correct design for dissimilar-CTE joints — porosity accommodates thermal strain. (2) The plasma-sprayed inner surface for Teflon adhesion introduced hydrogen (95% argon / 5% hydrogen gas), which caused delayed cracking after shipping from Brooklyn to Japan. Martensite transformation in deformed 304 stainless was the susceptible microstructure.

id: case:Galvanized steel spot welding in automotive assembly
cluster_id: Galvanized steel spot welding in automotive assembly
content: Galvanized steel spot welding in automotive assembly Brief reference. Industry adopted galvanized steel to address rust but didn't know how to weld it; Tom had welding research projects throughout the 1980s on this.

cluster_id: Adhesive-bonded automotive door panels failure (1980s–1990s)
content: Adhesive-bonded automotive door panels failure (1980s–1990s) Water-soluble adhesives on inner/outer door panels failed in ~5 years from moisture/road salt attack. Door panels rattled. Affected Ford, GM, and especially the early Chrysler Dodge minivans.

id: case:Chrysler Dodge minivan adhesive bonding problems (early-to-mid 1980s)
cluster_id: Chrysler Dodge minivan adhesive bonding problems (early-to-mid 1980s)
content: Chrysler Dodge minivan adhesive bonding problems (early-to-mid 1980s) Early Dodge minivans (Iacocca era) were "a piece of junk" by 1985 from failed adhesive bonding. Used as the concrete example of the door-panel adhesive failure case.

cluster_id: Lord Corporation rubber-to-steel bonding patent (circa 1900)
content: Lord Corporation rubber-to-steel bonding patent (circa 1900) Origin of Lord Corporation in Erie, PA, on an MIT patent ca. 1900 for bonding rubber to steel (railroad shock-absorber applications). Thomas Lord left 50% of company to four universities and Cleveland Clinic on his death; the Lord Foundation of Massachusetts is 10% of company profits flowing to MIT.

id: case:Boeing aircraft skin and wing adhesive bonding
cluster_id: Boeing aircraft skin and wing adhesive bonding
content: Boeing aircraft skin and wing adhesive bonding Boeing was proud of using adhesive bonding to join skins and wings to last 30 years — but they put rivets in anyway, because over 30 years interface corrosion will weaken the bond. Used to illustrate that adhesive joints are never quite trusted for life-safety long-term use.

cluster_id: Presidential limousine glass armor
content: Presidential limousine glass armor Tom's standing prop (referenced, not produced today). Four layers of glass plus one layer of polycarbonate, adhesively bonded by hand layup with rollers, then pressed in a vacuum system to eliminate bubbles. Used to illustrate maximum-care surface preparation for life-safety adhesive joints.

cluster_id: Aviation carburetor icing failures
content: Aviation carburetor icing failures Tom's consulting work in aviation failures from carburetor icing. Drove the question of whether Teflon coating would prevent ice — answer depends on icing mechanism: water droplets in rain (non-wetting, Teflon helps) vs. vapor deposition from humid air (vapor-deposited frost adheres to Teflon and cannot be removed). Real solution is the cockpit deicing switch.

id: case:Canadian Aviation Authority Teflon carburetor coating test
cluster_id: Canadian Aviation Authority Teflon carburetor coating test
content: Canadian Aviation Authority Teflon carburetor coating test Tom obtained a copy of the Canadian aviation authority's report on Teflon-lined carburetor icing tests; informed his thinking on the vapor-deposition mechanism.

id: case:Boston Logan Airport deicing fluid transition
cluster_id: Boston Logan Airport deicing fluid transition
content: Boston Logan Airport deicing fluid transition Historical transition from polyethylene glycol (toxic — metabolizes to methanol, causes blindness, EPA-controlled with collection dams) to polypropylene glycol (food-additive grade, metabolizes to ethanol, used at the gate now). Used as biochemistry digression off the carburetor-icing teaching beat.

id: case:Tom Eagar's Teflon frying pan frost adhesion test
cluster_id: Tom Eagar's Teflon frying pan frost adhesion test
content: Tom Eagar's Teflon frying pan frost adhesion test Tom's own bench test. Cut out a Teflon pan bottom, soldered a cooling pad underneath, deposited water droplets and steam frost. Drops pop off easily; vapor-deposited frost cannot be removed without scraping off the Teflon. Empirically confirms the vapor-deposition-fills-asperities argument.

id: case:F-21 jet fighter engine diffusion bonding development
cluster_id: F-21 jet fighter engine diffusion bonding development
content: F-21 jet fighter engine diffusion bonding development Brief reference. Pratt & Whitney development of titanium diffusion bonding for the engine. Tom shows part as visual aid (mentioned: "I think I've shown it to you before"). Tom mis-stated as "F20"; bracketed [F-21] per convention. Diffusion-bonded titanium part from Pratt & Whitney research labs, recovered by a former student who had worked on engine joining technology for the F-22 program (Tom said "F-21"; corrected to F-22).

cluster_id: 1854 Broad Street cholera epidemic
content: 1854 Broad Street cholera epidemic Tufte's "successful" example of visual statistical thinking. John Snow plots cholera deaths on a London map, identifies the Broad Street pump as the cause, has the handle removed. Tom uses it to teach hypothesis-falsification, consideration of alternative explanations (people fleeing the neighborhood), and the role of outliers (the elderly woman who had pump water shipped to her).

cluster_id: Space Shuttle Columbia
content: Space Shuttle Columbia Tom's Cambridge courthouse anecdote. While testifying about an aircraft engine failure, he predicts NASA will lose another shuttle within 15–20 years; Columbia disintegrates the next morning. The opposing side settles the case. Tom uses it as a story about the strange theater of expert witness testimony.

cluster_id: Aircraft engine failure litigation (Cambridge courthouse)
content: Aircraft engine failure litigation (Cambridge courthouse) The unnamed aircraft engine case Tom was testifying on when Columbia disintegrated. Used here as the setting for the Columbia coincidence, not for its engineering content.

id: case:Lawrence Livermore National Ignition Facility dual-use
cluster_id: Lawrence Livermore National Ignition Facility dual-use
content: Lawrence Livermore National Ignition Facility dual-use Tom's neighbor's visit to Lawrence Livermore. Tom explains to her that NIF's stated mission (fusion energy) is cover for the real mission (simulating nuclear weapons effects after the test ban). Used as a parallel to the space-laser-on-the-shuttle case to teach how military programs are described to the public versus to Congress.

cluster_id: Space-based chemical laser weapon (Rockwell, 1978)
content: Space-based chemical laser weapon (Rockwell, 1978) Tom triangulates the classified laser-weapon design from three unclassified sources — Air Force 50 MW superconducting generator program, chemical laser efficiency at 10%, and Professor Bowen's one-meter potassium-chloride window forging at Lincoln Lab. Friend at Rockwell confirms the figure and the cargo-bay fit. Used to argue the shuttle's real purpose was military.

cluster_id: Lester Thurow lecture-circuit economics
content: Lester Thurow lecture-circuit economics $30,000-per-lecture in 1988 as benchmark for what top lecturers earn — and an argument that they don't use PowerPoint.

cluster_id: Edward Tufte information-display pedagogy
content: Edward Tufte information-display pedagogy The seminar ($500/day × 200 attendees = $100K/day), the four books on acid-free vellum, the handout pricing negotiation. Used as the source for the Napoleon's-march graph and the PowerPoint-Gettysburg satire.

content: Shuttle launch reliability
