id: case:Gas-fired power plant water filter corrosion investigation
cluster_id: Gas-fired power plant water filter corrosion investigation
content: Gas-fired power plant water filter corrosion investigation Tom's consulting case in Georgia — stainless steel filter baskets in 14-megohm water. Client suspected chloride corrosion; Tom diagnosed it as a thermal/design problem. Used as a foil to set up the GE BWR case that follows.

cluster_id: MIT inconel department griddles fabrication
content: MIT inconel department griddles fabrication Tom's "thirty-thousand-dollar griddles" — four Inconel sheet griddles made from surplus material in the early 1990s, used at department steak fries during his tenure as department head. Used to illustrate Inconel as a $30/lb fabricated material and the price scale of nickel-base alloys.

id: case:Dayton Walther aluminum truck wheel fatigue case
cluster_id: Dayton Walther aluminum truck wheel fatigue case
content: Dayton Walther aluminum truck wheel fatigue case Tom's late-1970s consulting case as a young assistant professor — Dayton Walther was the world's largest tire-rim manufacturer at the time, all in steel, trying to qualify aluminum rims to half-million- or million-mile fatigue limits. Welding-based approach failed; forging at Alcoa Cleveland ultimately succeeded.

cluster_id: Baseball bat performance study
content: Baseball bat performance study Tom's consulting case (one-week turnaround over a holiday weekend) on a Little League cardiac-arrest case in New Jersey. Tom recovered Feynman freshman-physics momentum/energy conservation; argued bat-and-ball stiffness matching at ~28-mil wall is engineered for maximum performance transfer. Used Naval Surface Weapons Lab high-speed video and compression-testing of balls. Eventually saw 10,000-50,000 pages of discovery.

id: case:Little League baseball bat cardiac arrest case
cluster_id: Little League baseball bat cardiac arrest case
content: Little League baseball bat cardiac arrest case New Jersey Little League pitcher hit in the chest by a ball off a minus-12 aluminum bat; cardiac arrest, permanent ventilator dependence. The triggering case for Tom's consulting engagement.

cluster_id: USS Sheffield fire (Falkland Islands War)
content: USS Sheffield fire (Falkland Islands War) Exocet missile strike ignites aluminum superstructure; cited to justify Navy's move away from aluminum superstructures in the 1980s.

id: case:Navy aluminum ship cracking / waffle-membrane steel superstructure program
cluster_id: Navy aluminum ship cracking / waffle-membrane steel superstructure program
content: Navy aluminum ship cracking / waffle-membrane steel superstructure program Early-1980s David Taylor effort to replace aluminum superstructures with lightweight corrugated high-strength steel, in response to the Falklands and Belknap fires.

id: case:LCS (Littoral Combat Ship) aluminum alloy redesign
cluster_id: LCS (Littoral Combat Ship) aluminum alloy redesign
content: LCS (Littoral Combat Ship) aluminum alloy redesign Post-Cold-War shift from Sea Wolf submarines to high-speed aluminum littoral combat craft; Navy's pendulum swing back to aluminum after the 1980s steel program. Navy's pivot to high-speed aluminum ships for the littoral battlefield. Tom notes that fatigue cracking and welded-construction design differences from steel create a learning curve for larger aluminum hulls.

id: case:David Taylor Model Basin aluminum replacement program
cluster_id: David Taylor Model Basin aluminum replacement program
content: David Taylor Model Basin aluminum replacement program Tom's summers working there; Severn River corrosion test as source of Navy corrosion data; classified sonar research building. Setting for the aluminum-replacement program.

id: case:Australian aluminum bridge doubler plate failure
cluster_id: Australian aluminum bridge doubler plate failure
content: Australian aluminum bridge doubler plate failure Brief mention as a famous fatigue failure from wrap-around doubler-plate weld details, ~50–60 years before lecture.

cluster_id: Wooden gas distribution pipes (Boston, 1880s)
content: Wooden gas distribution pipes (Boston, 1880s) Gun-drilled wooden logs caulked with oakum, used for the 1880s street-light gas system before cast iron and steel.

id: case:U.S. Army Underground Storage Tank Corrosion Study
cluster_id: U.S. Army Underground Storage Tank Corrosion Study
content: U.S. Army Underground Storage Tank Corrosion Study 25,000-tank study, 5–25 years to perforation depending on soil conditions. Used to quantify why the 1930s buried steel gas pipes leak. 1991 study at Construction Engineering Research Labs (Urbana-Champaign) of 108 leaking tanks; soil aggressiveness index and leak times from 6 to 40 years.

id: case:Corrugated stainless steel tubing (CSST) — central case
cluster_id: Corrugated stainless steel tubing (CSST) — central case
content: Corrugated stainless steel tubing (CSST) — central case The lecture's summative case. Japanese earthquake-driven product, brought to U.S. market via ANSI LC1 (written by Foster Wheeler consultant, approved in Canada first to bypass U.S. bureaucracy), introduced 1997. By 1998, NFPA data shows spike in lightning-induced gas fires. Industry knew by 2001, blamed plumbers' grounding through 2007, eventually developed conductive-jacket version (Gastite) and an inferior six-coulomb competitor. The 2003 Arkansas class action settled; one Texas county banned the product. Tom advised the Massachusetts State Plumbing Board in 2003, leading to the most restrictive state installation requirements in the country.

id: case:2003 Arkansas flexible gas piping class action
cluster_id: 2003 Arkansas flexible gas piping class action
content: 2003 Arkansas flexible gas piping class action Settled, terms unknown to speaker. The first major class-action response to the lightning-fire problem.

id: case:Texas county ban on flexible gas piping
cluster_id: Texas county ban on flexible gas piping
content: Texas county ban on flexible gas piping Unique among U.S. jurisdictions for outlawing CSST entirely.

id: case:Massachusetts flexible gas piping regulatory approval threat
cluster_id: Massachusetts flexible gas piping regulatory approval threat
content: Massachusetts flexible gas piping regulatory approval threat 2003 attempt by CSST manufacturer's attorneys to threaten the State Plumbing Board with a restraint-of-trade suit; Board, holding Tom's letter, countered with threat of public release. Resulted in Massachusetts's restrictive installation rules.

id: case:NFPA flexible gas piping product approval renewal deadline
cluster_id: NFPA flexible gas piping product approval renewal deadline
content: NFPA flexible gas piping product approval renewal deadline 2007/2008 NFPA letter to CSST manufacturers giving a 2014 deadline to prove product safety as a condition of approval renewal.

id: case:GE lightning research on stainless steel containers for nuclear waste isolation
cluster_id: GE lightning research on stainless steel containers for nuclear waste isolation
content: GE lightning research on stainless steel containers for nuclear waste isolation University of Florida triggered-lightning experiment on three-inch stainless steel cask for the Nevada nuclear waste repository; cited as a $10M study to prove what a one-line heat-flow calculation would have predicted.

id: case:GE Pittsfield Lightning Research Center (distribution transformer testing)
cluster_id: GE Pittsfield Lightning Research Center (distribution transformer testing)
content:
GE Pittsfield Lightning Research Center (distribution transformer testing) Historic site of distribution transformer lightning testing; where CSST manufacturers did their belated lightning research starting around 2001.

## Figures referenced in this lecture

id: case:GE/General Electric aerospace rhenium supply constraint
cluster_id: GE/General Electric aerospace rhenium supply constraint
content: GE/General Electric aerospace rhenium supply constraint Raised by a student as an extension of the rare-earths-as-political-leverage point. Tom acknowledges the case without prior familiarity, then connects it to his own turbine-blade work (six-percent-rhenium superalloys at roughly forty dollars per ounce).

cluster_id: Pennzoil Oil City refinery explosion
content: Pennzoil Oil City refinery explosion The lecture's central developed case. A welder was killed when a tank in the tank yard exploded. The forensic visit revealed that the ground was saturated with oil to a depth of two feet from ninety years of routine spills. Tom's insight, arrived at over breakfast the morning after, was that Pennzoil's continued operation of the dilapidated refinery was rational under externality pressure: closing it would convert it to a Superfund site and trigger taxpayer-then-stockholder cleanup liability. The refinery was eventually closed.

cluster_id: Roman lead plumbing
content: Roman lead plumbing Environmental externality. Roman lead production exceeded 10,000 tons per year for plumbing applications that would be impermissible today.

cluster_id: Lead paint poisoning case (Cambridge apartment)
content: Lead paint poisoning case (Cambridge apartment) Why children eat lead paint — lead oxide is sweet to the taste. Tom uses this as an aside on environmental externalities of historical materials choices.

id: case:Wind turbine ring vortex aircraft encounters
cluster_id: Wind turbine ring vortex aircraft encounters
content: Wind turbine ring vortex aircraft encounters Mentioned by Tom as an unexpected externality of wind-power siting: ring vortices from large-blade turbines have entrained small aircraft. Used jokingly in the context of Martha's Vineyard wind-farm opposition.

id: case:Electric Boat Quonset Point pressure-hull welding facility
cluster_id: Electric Boat Quonset Point pressure-hull welding facility
content:
Electric Boat Quonset Point pressure-hull welding facility Brief reference. Electric Boat's $200M indoor building at Quonset Point exists to maintain the circularity needed for steel pressure hulls. Used to set the scale of the manufacturing problem, but the Soviets and Tom were doing it with electroslag rather than the gas metal arc Electric Boat used. Not a developed case in this excerpt; flagged as a proposal because it doesn't match an existing cluster.

## Figures referenced

id: case:Dow Chemical magnesium price cartel (1946–1975) / Alcoa monopoly and price fixing with Dow Chemical
cluster_id: Dow Chemical magnesium price cartel (1946–1975) / Alcoa monopoly and price fixing with Dow Chemical
content: Dow Chemical magnesium price cartel (1946–1975) / Alcoa monopoly and price fixing with Dow Chemical Why Alcoa, with the technology to enter magnesium production, never did. Joel Clark's first doctoral student (George Kenney, ~1976) used sales-and-price data to prove the cartel.

cluster_id: Magnesium under-dashboard automotive components
content: Magnesium under-dashboard automotive components Where DOE-funded magnesium use actually landed in production cars: hidden, non-cosmetic, vehicle-life-only structural support.

cluster_id: Magnesium automotive paint flaking failure
content: Magnesium automotive paint flaking failure Why deck lids and hood lids are aluminum, not magnesium — atmospheric corrosion under paint.

id: case:Naval diver thermal protection using magnesium alloy / Navy diver salvage gas generation system (magnesium composite) / Fort Fundy magnesium-graphite composite diving application
cluster_id: Naval diver thermal protection using magnesium alloy / Navy diver salvage gas generation system (magnesium composite) / Fort Fundy magnesium-graphite composite diving application
content: Naval diver thermal protection using magnesium alloy / Navy diver salvage gas generation system (magnesium composite) / Fort Fundy magnesium-graphite composite diving application Ron Latanision's anecdote: water-based metallographic polishing solution corroded the composite faster than it could be polished. Used to demonstrate that magnesium's corrosion problem extends even to characterization in the lab.

cluster_id: Aluminum chloride kitchen reaction (personal anecdote)
content: Aluminum chloride kitchen reaction (personal anecdote) Used to illustrate aluminum chloride's instability relative to magnesium chloride; pure aluminum's protective oxide skin is the corollary.

cluster_id: Alcoa Wear-Ever pure-aluminum cookware
content: Alcoa Wear-Ever pure-aluminum cookware Example of pure aluminum's water-corrosion resistance. The 5000-series aluminum-magnesium alloys for seawater service contrast with copper-bearing aluminum's poor saltwater performance.

id: case:Terne plate (lead-coated steel) gas tanks and roofing
cluster_id: Terne plate (lead-coated steel) gas tanks and roofing
content: Terne plate (lead-coated steel) gas tanks and roofing Lead carbonate as a protective surface oxide; almost impossible to find today; recurs in §11.p2 in the context of Tom's eighty-five-year-old house's window flats.

id: case:Residential window flashing corrosion and replacement
cluster_id: Residential window flashing corrosion and replacement
content: Residential window flashing corrosion and replacement Tom's house replaced terne plate flats with copper (not plastic, despite the price difference: $5,000 plastic vs $9,000 copper). Used to teach copper's atmospheric corrosion resistance and the role of UV degradation in plastics.

id: case:Church building galvanized handrails and light posts paint failure / 1986 church building galvanized steel handrail paint failure
cluster_id: Church building galvanized handrails and light posts paint failure / 1986 church building galvanized steel handrail paint failure
content: Church building galvanized handrails and light posts paint failure / 1986 church building galvanized steel handrail paint failure Forensic case as personal narrative. Galvanized steel painted before zinc hydroxide formation specification observed → paint failed within a year. Acetic acid pre-treatment (hypothesized zinc acetate formation) → repaint lasted thirty years. Used to teach surface-chemistry preparation for paint adhesion on galvanized substrates.

cluster_id: Sandpaper manufacturing high-speed curing
content: Sandpaper manufacturing high-speed curing Used to motivate electron-beam cross-linking as a general manufacturing technology, before applying it to PEX-A.

id: case:Don Sadoway liquid metal battery / Ambri
cluster_id: Don Sadoway liquid metal battery / Ambri
content:
Don Sadoway liquid metal battery / Ambri Two distinct uses: (§2.p9) Bill Gates funding Don Sadoway's startup as a teaching/externality story; (§8.p8) the technical constraint that very few elements give the >1 V cell voltage Ambri's design requires, because IR losses in copper interconnects eat shallow cell potentials.

## Figures referenced (recurring numeric anchors, not cases)

- Steel labor content: 50% in Tom's early career → 5% today (§1.p7).
- 1980s steel industry productivity growth: 4% per year; manufacturing 2%; services 0% (§1.p8).
- 1980s mining productivity growth: 7% per year; compounded over 20 years = 20× improvement (§1.p9).
- Material cost as fraction of total product cost: ~10% (§9.p1) — restated from prior lecture.
- DOE magnesium-in-automobiles research spend: ~$100 million per year for forty or fifty years (§5.p1).
- Commercial jetliner lifetime: ~100,000 flight hours (§7.p2).
- H₂O electrochemical breakdown: ~1.1 V (§8.p3).
- Al₂O₃ / MgO decomposition: <2 V, probably <1.5 V (§8.p4).
- Primary bond energy: 1–3 eV (§8.p5, §11.p9).
- Energy/wavelength relation: E (eV) = 12,400 / λ (Å) = 1.24 / λ (μm) (§11.p10).
- UV cutoff: <0.310 μm → ~4 eV (§11.p11).
- Atmospheric CO₂: ~300 ppm; zinc carbonate formation timescale: ~1 year (§9.p9).
- Magnesium anode purity spec: <7 ppm nickel (§4.p9).

## Open questions for case index methodology

- The PEX cluster in the canon is named for the brass-fitting failure mode, but Tom's treatment here is purely the manufacturing-technology / cross-linking-science angle. Whether to split into two clusters or keep one cluster with multiple framing facets is a methodology decision.
- The magnesium-anode case is large enough (ten paragraphs in this lecture, the spine of the corrosion thread) that it should probably be a canonical cluster rather than the proposed status here. Recommend promotion at reconciliation.

cluster_id: Hawaiian helicopter tour operations
content: Hawaiian helicopter tour operations Brief aside off the Concorde-maintenance point — operators don't fly their own tour helicopters because they know the maintenance gap. Used as a "things you need to learn" coda.

cluster_id: Blowout preventer investigations (4-5 cases)
content: Blowout preventer investigations (4-5 cases) Tom's Louisiana BOP case (three failures in sequence, $100M loss, settled at 50 cents on the dollar) introduced as the under-the-radar precursor to the Deepwater Horizon BOP failure. Used to illustrate the "good old boys" culture of the oil industry and the role of contract-law enforcement when no fatalities occur.

id: case:Army brake shoes fraud and specification conflict
cluster_id: Army brake shoes fraud and specification conflict
content: Army brake shoes fraud and specification conflict Ohio supplier sorted brake shoes good-on-top, bad-on-bottom to defeat sampling inspection. Criminal case failed because the drawing and procurement contract disagreed. Used to illustrate (a) the difference between meeting specs and exceeding them, and (b) what happens when specifications conflict in litigation. One-line allusion — Tom invokes it as another example of Justice Department intervention resolving a procurement fraud. Captioner rendered as "RV brake shoes."

id: case:Initial cement truck tank explosion and worker leg amputation
cluster_id: Initial cement truck tank explosion and worker leg amputation
content: Initial cement truck tank explosion and worker leg amputation First in-plant failure of the cement truck tank line. Worker lost a leg during pressurization testing with 100 PSI air instead of water. Company paid insurance and continued production without investigation. The setup case for the fatal Pennsylvania failure.

cluster_id: Robert Merton Sloan-to-Harvard departure
content: Robert Merton Sloan-to-Harvard departure Lester Thurow's "extinct volcanoes" line, used as the punchline of Tom's "it's not what you say, it's how you say it" lesson. Not a materials case; a teaching-craft anecdote that touches on the 2008-era derivatives world tangentially.

cluster_id: Eagar three-thousand-spot-welds rhetorical figure
content: Eagar three-thousand-spot-welds rhetorical figure Tom's own 1989 Gatlinburg keynote where he coined "they put three thousand spot welds in the average automobile because you need two thousand good ones." Recurring rhetorical anchor in his teaching.

id: case:Hydrothermal quartz reactor explosion near Chicago
cluster_id: Hydrothermal quartz reactor explosion near Chicago
content: Hydrothermal quartz reactor explosion near Chicago Bob Laudise's hydrothermal quartz process at Bell Labs; the reactor walls run ~10 inches thick at ~10,000 psi, and one ruptured at a McDonald's near Chicago airport, killing a customer. Used to ground the "quartz watches became cheap because someone figured out how to grow quartz fast" story.

id: case:Swiss watch industry survival via quartz and luxury bifurcation
cluster_id: Swiss watch industry survival via quartz and luxury bifurcation
content: Swiss watch industry survival via quartz and luxury bifurcation Used as Tom's framing case for "what makes something expensive" — at the low end, Swatches sold as fashion; at the high end, titanium-cased, ceramic-bezeled fifty-thousand-dollar luxury watches. The titanium watch becomes the segue to the broader discussion of why titanium is even available as a metal.

id: case:Hot isostatic press / hydrothermal vessel explosion lineage
cluster_id: Hot isostatic press / hydrothermal vessel explosion lineage
content: Hot isostatic press / hydrothermal vessel explosion lineage

id: case:H.C. Starck Newton facility — MIT vacuum metallurgy spin-off
cluster_id: H.C. Starck Newton facility — MIT vacuum metallurgy spin-off
content: H.C. Starck Newton facility — MIT vacuum metallurgy spin-off Cited as an example of how WWII-era vacuum metallurgy at MIT spun off into commercial reactive-metals firms. Now a Bayer Chemical subsidiary.

cluster_id: Tesla Nevada gigafactory water siting
content: Tesla Nevada gigafactory water siting Tom argues the Nevada siting is a mistake because manufacturing requires enormous water input; recalls a similar GM Sloan-program team that proposed Nogales, Arizona for the same maquiladora-labor reason and was challenged on water access.

id: case:Aircraft landing gear high-strength steel and inspection
cluster_id: Aircraft landing gear high-strength steel and inspection
content: Aircraft landing gear high-strength steel and inspection Landing gear are designed first because they take the highest stresses, and they are steel at 250–280 ksi because no composite can match the critical-flaw-size / strength combination. Triple vacuum arc melted, magnetic particle inspected.

cluster_id: Ritchie 2014 cryogenic high-entropy alloy (CrMnFeCoNi)
content: Ritchie 2014 cryogenic high-entropy alloy (CrMnFeCoNi) Rob Ritchie (formerly MIT, now Berkeley) and collaborators published an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi alloy with excellent cryogenic fracture toughness in *Science*. Tom: "all they did was add iron to MP35N" and the strengthening mechanism (twinning) is the same. The Ashby plot reproduced in the paper is, in Tom's reading, a rediscovery.

id: case:MP35N cobalt-nickel-chrome-molybdenum alloy (Gaylord Smith / International Nickel)
cluster_id: MP35N cobalt-nickel-chrome-molybdenum alloy (Gaylord Smith / International Nickel)
content: MP35N cobalt-nickel-chrome-molybdenum alloy (Gaylord Smith / International Nickel) Tom's "favorite alloy." 35Co-35Ni-20Cr-10Mo, developed by Gaylord Smith at International Nickel in the 1960s. Non-magnetic, strengthens by twinning under cold work, reaches 280 ksi yield as bolt stock. Four MP35N bolts hold the 747 wing onto the fuselage. ASTM-specced for surgical implants since 1978.

cluster_id: Boeing 747 wing-to-fuselage MP35N bolt selection
content: Boeing 747 wing-to-fuselage MP35N bolt selection Four MP35N bolts, ~300 ksi, hold each 747 wing on. Sourced from Standard Pressed Steel (Philadelphia).

cluster_id: Brain aneurysm clip ferromagnetism controversy
content: Brain aneurysm clip ferromagnetism controversy Dr. McFadden (Johnson & Johnson consultant) and a rival neurosurgeon fought over what alloys could safely be implanted near the brain given 5-tesla MRI fields. The 304 stainless martensitic-transformation argument made some MDs argue any iron-containing alloy was unsafe; Tom recommended MP35N (zero iron) and resolved the ASTM-spec dispute in McFadden's favor.

content: Faberware 304 stainless pot magnetism demonstration

id: case:Army microcrystalline titanium kinetic-energy penetrator program (Schuh)
cluster_id: Army microcrystalline titanium kinetic-energy penetrator program (Schuh)
content: Army microcrystalline titanium kinetic-energy penetrator program (Schuh) Christopher Schuh (MIT DMSE) is funded by the Army to develop microcrystalline titanium as a non-radioactive high-density alternative to depleted uranium.

id: case:Hadlock platinum eyelid weights for facial reconstruction
cluster_id: Hadlock platinum eyelid weights for facial reconstruction
content: Hadlock platinum eyelid weights for facial reconstruction Dr. Tessa Hadlock (Mass Eye and Ear, HST graduate, Tom's ENT) embedded platinum weights in the eyelid of a young woman whose facial muscles had been severed, so she could close her eye. Platinum chosen for density (small weight, no bulge), corrosion resistance, and bio-inertness.

cluster_id: Tom Eagar's copper roof (personal)
content: Tom Eagar's copper roof (personal) $9,000 for ~50 sq ft of copper roofing on Tom's house, justified as a 100–300 year lifetime. Lateral example of when copper's price is worth paying.

cluster_id: Concorde maintenance and operational failures
content: Concorde maintenance and operational failures Tom's claim that the 2000 Paris crash (runway debris from a preceding aircraft) was used as cover for retiring a fleet that was already past its useful life. Personal note: Tom mentions consulting for the company that dropped the debris.

id: case:Qatar LNG tank explosion and Shell litigation
cluster_id: Qatar LNG tank explosion and Shell litigation
content: Qatar LNG tank explosion and Shell litigation Tom recalls (via Professor Pelloux) that roughly thirty years before this lecture, a Shell-designed LNG storage tank in the Persian Gulf at Qatar suffered brittle fracture and destroyed the harbor. The tank had been built to a 1940s API/British specification in the 1970s–'80s despite mature knowledge of brittle fracture, with poor steel and significant welding defects. Qatar took Shell to the World Court; Shell prevailed by arguing the failure was an RPG strike by the Emir's enemies rather than material/weld failure. Shell was barred from doing business in Qatar for several decades.

cluster_id: Cleveland LNG explosion
content: Cleveland LNG explosion Cited as the prototypical historical LNG disaster — a tank failure in the late 1940s destroyed a substantial portion of Cleveland, Ohio, and remains findable in public sources (in contrast to the Qatar event).

id: case:Big steel companies decline through market abandonment
cluster_id: Big steel companies decline through market abandonment
content: Big steel companies decline through market abandonment An early-1990s study found that essentially zero of the major steel-industry process innovations over the prior 75 years originated within steel companies. AOD came from gas-supply companies, continuous casting from machinery vendors, BOP from oxygen suppliers. Tom attributes this to complacent post-WWII US steel management — including the Bethlehem Steel executives whose Learjets at Allentown airport existed to ferry them to Florida golf weekends.

id: case:Generator rotor shaft welding feasibility study (US Steel)
cluster_id: Generator rotor shaft welding feasibility study (US Steel)
content: Generator rotor shaft welding feasibility study (US Steel) As a young engineer at Bethlehem Steel (~1975), Tom was asked whether two ~40-inch-diameter forgings could be welded together to make the 750,000-pound (375-ton) generator rotor shafts required for 1,000 MW power plants. Only Bethlehem Steel, US Steel, Creusot-Loire in France, and one Japanese forging house (Tom guesses "Tokyo Steel" but is uncertain — historically Japan Steel Works) had the ingot/forging/heat-treatment capacity, originally installed ~1910–1915 for battleship gun barrels. Forging takes more than a year per shaft. Electroslag or narrow-gap welding could in principle have done it; no one funded the trial.

id: case:MIT Plasma Fusion Center welding project
cluster_id: MIT Plasma Fusion Center welding project
content: MIT Plasma Fusion Center welding project Roughly 1990, MIT plasma-fusion researchers approached Tom about welding 20-inch-thick by ~4-foot stainless steel sections for the top dome of the ITER reactor (now being built in France) because no available forging shop could produce the part in one piece.

cluster_id: Bethlehem Steel BOF retiree suicide
content: Bethlehem Steel BOF retiree suicide During Tom's tenure at Bethlehem Steel, a recently retired employee returned to the plant and dove into the BOF molten steel bath; operators saw the body spread-eagled on the surface via TV monitor. The standard practice was to "bury" one ingot from that heat.

id: case:Steel mill worker injuries (1930s-1940s bar rolling)
cluster_id: Steel mill worker injuries (1930s-1940s bar rolling)
content: Steel mill worker injuries (1930s-1940s bar rolling) In 1930s–40s bar mills, mile-long red-hot bars traveled at ~40 mph and were caught with tongs by workers between rolling stands. A "cobble" — the bar curving as it exited — could amputate an arm while simultaneously cauterizing the wound. Tom's second child was born in Bethlehem, PA, in a hospital located steps from the steel mill, sized accordingly.

cluster_id: Bethlehem Steel forge-shop slag-shoveling anecdote
content: Bethlehem Steel forge-shop slag-shoveling anecdote Two bare-chested workers shoveling ~1000°F slag in perfect alternating rhythm across a hot July forge-shop floor — thirty years of practice synchronized them so neither caught the other's throw in the face.

id: case:Henry Rowan Inductotherm acquisition and Rowan University endowment
cluster_id: Henry Rowan Inductotherm acquisition and Rowan University endowment
content: Henry Rowan Inductotherm acquisition and Rowan University endowment MIT alumnus Henry Rowan acquired Inductotherm and Lepel — the two or three dominant induction-melting furnace builders — and consolidated near-monopoly. Wanting a university named for him, he was rebuffed by MIT and NJIT (the latter declining at $100–200M) before endowing what became Rowan University in New Jersey.

cluster_id: Wind turbine shaft clink failure (Dallas)
content: Wind turbine shaft clink failure (Dallas) Tom's second-ever encounter with a clink defect: roughly 2000, a ~24-inch wind-turbine generator shaft in a Dallas metallurgical shop showed a brittle fracture surrounded by fatigue, which the shop had been unable to diagnose. Tom identified it immediately from the Libra precedent.

cluster_id: Bethlehem Steel Learjet corruption (Allentown airport)
content: Bethlehem Steel Learjet corruption (Allentown airport) Three or four Learjets parked at the Allentown airport whose primary winter function was ferrying Bethlehem Steel executives to Florida golf outings. Tom's parallel example: US Air Force Reserve C-5As flying cases of Coca-Cola to Tokyo so reservist pilots could log flight hours while shopping for cheap stereos.

id: case:Rolls-Royce M250 BLISK (bladed disk) for helicopters
cluster_id: Rolls-Royce M250 BLISK (bladed disk) for helicopters
content: Rolls-Royce M250 BLISK (bladed disk) for helicopters Cited as the only high-volume cast blisk engine in production (~50,000 units, 30+ years). Used to introduce the collateral-weight-savings argument.

id: case:Sprague's first law (framing principle, not a case)
cluster_id: Sprague's first law (framing principle, not a case)
content: Sprague's first law (framing principle, not a case) Bob Sprague (head of materials, GE aircraft engines, Cincinnati): first reported properties of a new material are the best it will ever have. Corollary (Jim Williams): first price is the lowest it will ever have.

id: case:Bringing New Materials to Market" (1995 Technology Review article)
cluster_id: Bringing New Materials to Market" (1995 Technology Review article)
content: Bringing New Materials to Market" (1995 Technology Review article) Tom's own publication. Twenty-year payback for new materials companies; at 8% IRR, $1 invested today must return $20 in twenty years. Used to explain why venture capital avoids materials.

id: case:Twenty-year oil reserves industry investment floor
cluster_id: Twenty-year oil reserves industry investment floor
content: Twenty-year oil reserves industry investment floor Industry maintains twenty years of proven reserves because longer-horizon returns are uneconomic at typical IRRs. Used as parallel example to the materials-investment problem.

id: case:National Academy of Sciences Air Force propulsion research committee
cluster_id: National Academy of Sciences Air Force propulsion research committee
content: National Academy of Sciences Air Force propulsion research committee Tom's NRC service ~12 years before this lecture (c. 2004). Forty-member committee advising Air Force on $300M/year for improved jet engines.

id: case:Baltimore Gas and Electric under-deposit corrosion
cluster_id: Baltimore Gas and Electric under-deposit corrosion
content: Baltimore Gas and Electric under-deposit corrosion Brief reference — Admiralty brass condenser tubes failed by under-deposit attack thirty or forty years ago at BG&E.

id: case:New England Aquarium sea water piping corrosion
cluster_id: New England Aquarium sea water piping corrosion
content: New England Aquarium sea water piping corrosion Stainless steel failed (pitting from dirt), Monel was intermediate, titanium would have been best but cost-prohibitive. Used to illustrate the trade-off ladder for seawater service.

id: case:Under-deposit corrosion in cast iron (Hurricane Sandy context)
cluster_id: Under-deposit corrosion in cast iron (Hurricane Sandy context)
content: Under-deposit corrosion in cast iron (Hurricane Sandy context) Student-presented case (Brian). Graphitic corrosion of cast iron component exposed to seawater after Hurricane Sandy; the silicon-derived glassy passive film was breached by chlorides under deposits. Tom appends the "cleanliness is next to godliness" corrosion rule.

id: case:Mormon Temple heat exchanger erosion-corrosion failure
cluster_id: Mormon Temple heat exchanger erosion-corrosion failure
content: Mormon Temple heat exchanger erosion-corrosion failure Belmont, MA. Copper heat exchanger failed by erosion-corrosion at tube-sheet inlet after one year. Tom recommended 70/30 cupro-nickel; only 90/10 was available within the two-week shutdown window; 90/10 has worked for fifteen years. Sub-plot on contractor markup (16k quoted vs 6k from manufacturer).

id: case:Phoenix warehouse accelerated corrosion during construction
cluster_id: Phoenix warehouse accelerated corrosion during construction
content: Phoenix warehouse accelerated corrosion during construction Million-square-foot warehouse roof. Insulation got wet during construction rainstorm; deck closure trapped moisture in an 8-inch greenhouse cavity under Arizona sun. Corrosion rate of 20 mils/year (5× typical) perforated 1/16" sheet metal within three years.

cluster_id: Helms Project penstock
content: Helms Project penstock Tom's most-developed case in the session. Eight-and-a-half-month delayed hydrogen crack on a 22-foot-diameter PG&E penstock at 6,000 ft elevation. Used to illustrate (a) that hydrogen crack delay can extend far beyond the standard "first couple of weeks" rule if the weld is frozen, (b) that boiler-and-pressure-vessel-code exceptions for inch-and-a-quarter material with fillet welds can be load-bearing in failure analysis, and (c) the litigation politics of expert witnesses ("the guy whose wife drove around in a Rolls-Royce"). Full forensic case study. PG&E pumped-storage project in the Sierra Nevada; American Bridge (division of U.S. Steel) field-fabricated a 22-foot diameter, inch-and-a-quarter wall penstock across a granite canyon. Welders skipped preheat in winter (welding inch-and-a-quarter steel with three feet of snow inside the pipe), skipped post weld heat treatment, and after frozen storage and spring pressurization the vessel failed by delayed hydrogen cracking 20 hours after reaching 188 psi service pressure. Released the upper lake, scoured 100 feet of granite, $100M loss on $800M project. Six-week trial in Fresno (early 1990s); jury found for American Bridge on a foundational-failure theory; Tom testified as the last witness.

id: case:Boston Navy Yard destroyer boiler pipe weld (stainless-to-chromemoly transition)
cluster_id: Boston Navy Yard destroyer boiler pipe weld (stainless-to-chromemoly transition)
content: Boston Navy Yard destroyer boiler pipe weld (stainless-to-chromemoly transition) Tom's first big consulting case as a young MIT faculty member, ~1978. Stainless-to-2.25Cr-1Mo transition weld with persistent root cracking; NAVSEA procedure specified Inconel filler, contractor wanted to substitute stainless steel. Tom's solution: change the joint geometry (J-prep with a long land) to reduce restraint, leaving filler-metal specification intact. Used to illustrate (a) the Venn-diagram methodology applied under constraint and (b) that solutions sometimes come from the only variable left when the obvious ones are fixed.

cluster_id: Seawolf submarine hull cracking
content: Seawolf submarine hull cracking Recap from an earlier session. Over-matching by 30–40% combined with insufficient preheat for the resulting higher hardenability. Used here as the lead-in to the Helms Project — "this still occurs on a fairly regular basis."

id: case:Nautilus submarine austenitic filler metal foundations
cluster_id: Nautilus submarine austenitic filler metal foundations
content: Nautilus submarine austenitic filler metal foundations Brief reference. Early Nautilus foundations welded with austenitic filler (half the strength of HY80) as a deliberate under-matching strategy to absorb hydrogen and limit residual stress, until higher-strength procedures were qualified.

id: case:Navy under-matching filler metal studies (multiple rounds)
cluster_id: Navy under-matching filler metal studies (multiple rounds)
content: Navy under-matching filler metal studies (multiple rounds) Tom's "about every twenty-five years" lament. The Navy spent millions in the 1960s on near-full-scale under-matched test panels with explosive loading; spent millions again about 25 years later; reached the same conclusion both times. Used to make the fracture-mechanics point: severe undermatching concentrates strain in the weld metal.

cluster_id: Newport News engineering oversight failure (foreshadowed)
content: Newport News engineering oversight failure (foreshadowed) Tom refers back to a student presentation from the previous day. Used to land the "real engineering expertise" point closing §5. Not developed here.

id: case:Lead-acid battery terminal corrosion from road salt
cluster_id: Lead-acid battery terminal corrosion from road salt
content: Lead-acid battery terminal corrosion from road salt Used as a real-world illustration of how trace chloride catalyzes a self-regenerating corrosion cycle on lead — Tom's mechanism for why halogen-activated flux residue destroys printed circuit boards.

cluster_id: Tom's aluminum soldering demonstration failure
content: Tom's aluminum soldering demonstration failure Personal anecdote — Tom's assistant-professor-era aluminum soldering demo using tin/zinc chloride flux fell apart in his hands a year later because retained flux on blind joints was hygroscopic. Illustrates why reaction fluxes for aluminum are limited in practice.

cluster_id: Amtrak derailment near Philadelphia
content: Amtrak derailment near Philadelphia Used as the worked example of the Five Whys root-cause technique. Tom walks through alternative causation hypotheses — texting, drugs, rock-dropping from overpasses — that were being explored in the press at the time.

cluster_id: Teenage rock-dropping from overpasses
content: Teenage rock-dropping from overpasses Hypothesized as an alternative cause for the Amtrak derailment. Tom uses it to motivate the protective-fencing practice on busy highways.

cluster_id: Lehigh University welding metallurgy program (1940s–1970s)
content: Lehigh University welding metallurgy program (1940s–1970s) Origin story for the metallurgical bias in American welding education — "if the only tool you have is a hammer." Tom names Bob Stout, *Stout & Doty Weldability of Steels* (1940s), and the migration of Lehigh graduates to US Steel for HY steel development. Returns at §6.p4 to discuss Karl Meyer's reheat-cracking thesis.

cluster_id: Rensselaer welding metallurgy program (Warren Savage)
content: Rensselaer welding metallurgy program (Warren Savage) Parallel to the Lehigh tradition. Doc Savage as the second great American welding metallurgy mentor, with John Lippold as one of his last students.

id: case:Bay Bridge California corrosion-induced hydrogen cracking
cluster_id: Bay Bridge California corrosion-induced hydrogen cracking
content: Bay Bridge California corrosion-induced hydrogen cracking Don Sadoway forwarded Tom a link to this case. Tom uses it to illustrate that hydrogen embrittlement of steel doesn't require a welding arc — corrosion in seawater plus stress is enough. The 46-inch-diameter steel tie rods cracked within weeks after corrosion-generated hydrogen diffused into the steel. Used to extend the hydrogen-cracking framework from welds to corrosion.

id: case:Pipeline Safety Administration buried pipe property verification (2010s)
cluster_id: Pipeline Safety Administration buried pipe property verification (2010s)
content: Pipeline Safety Administration buried pipe property verification (2010s) 45,000 miles of buried oil and gas distribution pipe, much of it installed in the 1940s–50s. DOT requirement that pipeline companies prove the in-ground properties. Motivates Belmar's instrumented scratch-test commercialization.

cluster_id: Belmar instrumented scratch test (MIT spinout)
content: Belmar instrumented scratch test (MIT spinout) Brendan Belmar's MIT doctoral thesis on metal-on-metal scratching scaled to a startup deriving the full stress-strain curve from groove geometry. Coupled with the DOT buried-pipe case as the customer.

id: case:Nazi ball bearing factory management failure
cluster_id: Nazi ball bearing factory management failure
content: Nazi ball bearing factory management failure Told as the United Technologies VP of manufacturing's parable about how management overhead inflates to fill available space. Origin story attributed to a colonel running an underground Hitler-era ball-bearing plant.

cluster_id: MIT metallurgy department founding (1888)
content: MIT metallurgy department founding (1888) Brief institutional history — MIT founded 1865 as geology and mining; metallurgy arrives 1888 in concert with Sorby and the petrography-to-steel turn.

id: case:Bethlehem Steel offshore platform lamellar tearing (mid-1970s)
cluster_id: Bethlehem Steel offshore platform lamellar tearing (mid-1970s)
content: Bethlehem Steel offshore platform lamellar tearing (mid-1970s) Tom's first-hand context for the lamellar tearing era. Big oil-platform plates 3–4 inches thick, 400 ppm sulfur in the steel, dirty 1911-era blast furnaces. Tom's office mate at Bethlehem worked on it.

cluster_id: Karl Meyer reheat cracking thesis (Lehigh)
content: Karl Meyer reheat cracking thesis (Lehigh) Meyer was Tom's supervisor at Bethlehem Steel. His thesis identified residual sulfur, arsenic, phosphorus, and antimony as the agents of reheat cracking during stress relief.

id: case:Bethlehem Steel Charpy bar machining workaround
cluster_id: Bethlehem Steel Charpy bar machining workaround
content: Bethlehem Steel Charpy bar machining workaround Lesson about supplier relationships: time your machining requests to the foreman's slack capacity to get cheaper bars. Tom presents this as a transferable management insight.

id: case:LNG vessel heat treatment coupon substitution and testing failure
cluster_id: LNG vessel heat treatment coupon substitution and testing failure
content: LNG vessel heat treatment coupon substitution and testing failure Same case as above, framed from the testing-circumvention angle. Tom presents this as a generalizable pattern of how shipyards game qualification testing.

cluster_id: Watertown Arsenal Charpy bar standards
content: Watertown Arsenal Charpy bar standards The historical source of calibrated standard Charpy bars, now superseded by NIST. Tom notes Watertown Arsenal is "a mall now." Origin story of Charpy bar calibration — Army arsenal at Watertown (now Watertown Mall) calibrated impact bars from ~1900 because Army was interested in steel impact properties. NIST took over after Mansfield Amendment (~1972).

id: case:Pre-stressed concrete core test report fraud (Boston-area lab)
cluster_id: Pre-stressed concrete core test report fraud (Boston-area lab)
content: Pre-stressed concrete core test report fraud (Boston-area lab) Aside in response to a student's incredulity. Tom names (in general terms) a Boston-south test lab that issues qualification reports without receiving the cores. Used to extend the LNG test-plate point.

cluster_id: Bethlehem-vs-US-Steel weathering steel bridge fingerprint
content: Bethlehem-vs-US-Steel weathering steel bridge fingerprint Tom's first job at Bethlehem Steel. A highway bridge plate with terrible toughness was blamed on Bethlehem; Tom showed by chromium content that it was actually US Steel weathering-steel chemistry. Companion case to the Gulf of Mexico pipeline at §9.p3–§9.p9.

id: case:Untempered 100 ksi bridge plate (mill processing failure)
cluster_id: Untempered 100 ksi bridge plate (mill processing failure)
content: Untempered 100 ksi bridge plate (mill processing failure) Bob Summers's scuttlebutt explanation for a plate with 160 ksi strength and 5 foot-pound Charpy toughness — it slipped through the mill without tempering.

id: case:Submarine and rocket fastener heat-treatment recall
cluster_id: Submarine and rocket fastener heat-treatment recall
content:
Submarine and rocket fastener heat-treatment recall Recounted by a student (likely a Navy officer in the class) as a paperwork-fraud case: fastener manufacturer's certs claimed compliance "if heat-treated," but the parts were never heat-treated. Tom uses this as the lecture's climactic illustration that paperwork ≠ properties.

## Cases / figures referenced as background

id: case:General Electric vacuum tube laser repair
cluster_id: General Electric vacuum tube laser repair
content: General Electric vacuum tube laser repair Earliest commercial laser welding application. GE used a soft electron-laser pulse to make contact between failed tungsten/molybdenum wires inside a sealed glass vacuum tube, then a power pulse to weld, saving the tube without breaking the vacuum.

cluster_id: Avco Everett laser welder demonstrations (early 1980s)
content: Avco Everett laser welder demonstrations (early 1980s) AVCO Everett Research Labs developed 25-kilowatt lasers under government contract for heavy-steel laser welding. Tom's student worked there; his main job was making sure the laser worked for customer demos, because 90% of the time it didn't.

id: case:US Navy particle beam weapons welding research
cluster_id: US Navy particle beam weapons welding research
content: US Navy particle beam weapons welding research Navy spent a quarter billion dollars on proton-beam anti-missile weapons through the mid-80s to early 90s. After the Cold War ended, the program looked for applications. Tom was invited to a workshop to assess welding nuclear submarines with the 5-megawatt beams; he pointed out you only need tens of kilowatts. He got a mid-90s research project to evaluate the technology for welding and heat treatment.

id: case:Soviet underwater welding program at Paton Institute
cluster_id: Soviet underwater welding program at Paton Institute
content: Soviet underwater welding program at Paton Institute B. E. Paton Sr. weld-repaired Soviet tanks during WWII; his son took over the institute named after him. As one of seven members of the Soviet Academy of Sciences and head of the Ukrainian branch, Paton directed disproportionate national research funding to his 10,000-person institute. Tom: "Corruption at its best." Used as background for Soviet titanium submarine welding capability.

id: case:Soviet Alpha-class titanium submarine creep-fatigue failure
cluster_id: Soviet Alpha-class titanium submarine creep-fatigue failure
content: Soviet Alpha-class titanium submarine creep-fatigue failure Soviets built titanium submarines using Paton Institute technology. Within 2–3 years, they parked them in harbor due to leaks. Tom in 1980 was asked at Navy workshops how the Soviets solved the creep-fatigue interaction problem in titanium under continuous compressive stress; answer: they didn't.

cluster_id: Bullet-resistant glass installation failure investigation
content: Bullet-resistant glass installation failure investigation Show-and-tell artifact: 3 layers of glass + polycarbonate, adhesively bonded, voids forbidden. Military vehicles use ~5-inch laminate; presidential limousine also ~5 inches; rated against shaped-charge anti-tank rounds.

id: case:Residential gas pipeline explosions from plastic pipe use
cluster_id: Residential gas pipeline explosions from plastic pipe use
content: Residential gas pipeline explosions from plastic pipe use Steel gas mains corrode after 30–40 years, leak into soil, blow up homes. Plastic replaces steel; corrosion-resistant but can fail at welded joints.

cluster_id: Fighter jet canopy ejection system
content: Fighter jet canopy ejection system Laser-welded aluminum tube filled with explosive; provides non-electrical percussive ejection of canopy when pilot loses electrical power. Made at a California factory; shown as physical sample.

cluster_id: Asbestos fibers strength measurement
content: Asbestos fibers strength measurement Asbestos fibers measured at ~700,000 PSI. Used to compare claimed (untested) carbon-nanotube strengths against historically validated single-crystal fiber strengths.

id: case:ALVIN deep research submarine hull transition
cluster_id: ALVIN deep research submarine hull transition
content: ALVIN deep research submarine hull transition Only US titanium submarine ever built; built as Navy prototype program "to learn to weld titanium for bigger ships."

id: case:Comfort Adams and the founding of the American Welding Society (1921)
cluster_id: Comfort Adams and the founding of the American Welding Society (1921)
content: Comfort Adams and the founding of the American Welding Society (1921) AWS founded in 1921 after Adams's WWI shipbuilding service; AWS motto "to foster the art and science of welding" — admits welding is an art.

cluster_id: Building demolition with shaped charges
content: Building demolition with shaped charges The milled-90-degree-slot copper bar with dynamite — how demolition crews actually slice I-beams. Used as the lead-in to the World Trade Center thermite debunking.

cluster_id: Electrically conductive polymers (polyacetylene) misconception
content: Electrically conductive polymers (polyacetylene) misconception Brief reference back to a previous discussion. Used as an example of overselling — single-property optimization (specific electrical conductivity) without the design figure of merit.

id: case:High-temperature superconductor for wind turbine generators
cluster_id: High-temperature superconductor for wind turbine generators
content: High-temperature superconductor for wind turbine generators The actual niche HTS found — lightweight generators for very large wind turbines, where 20-inch steel shafts need lighter conductors than copper.

id: case:Superconducting DC transmission line trial in Manhattan
cluster_id: Superconducting DC transmission line trial in Manhattan
content: Superconducting DC transmission line trial in Manhattan Half-mile trial in Manhattan because underground is crowded. Tom doesn't know if anything went beyond the trial.

id: case:NASA X-33 liquid hydrogen tank failure
cluster_id: NASA X-33 liquid hydrogen tank failure
content: NASA X-33 liquid hydrogen tank failure Extended teaching unit with physical artifact. $1.3 billion program, cancelled. Rapid prototyping forced substitution of 3M adhesive + Nomex honeycomb + graphite tape for the originally specified 3D-woven composites. Adhesive shelf life trap: data sheet said 10 days out of refrigeration; actual strength after 10 days was 10% of new. Delaminations dropped safety factor from 2 to 1.05. Liquid hydrogen got into the pores and exploded during the Huntsville test.

cluster_id: Military ultra-long-range aircraft requirement
content: Military ultra-long-range aircraft requirement Air Force wanted a 25,000-mile-unrefueled aircraft because they anticipated losing all overseas air bases (Philippines, Okinawa, Diego Garcia). Tom's response: the earth's circumference is 25,000 miles, so 12,000 miles is the maximum useful range; he had just flown Dallas-Sydney on an A380 (17 hours, ~12,000 miles) to make the point.

cluster_id: V-22 Osprey prototype Ship 2 crash
content: V-22 Osprey prototype Ship 2 crash Boeing Vertol Philadelphia. Ship 2 was hovering 10–12 feet up; oscillated and flipped on its back because two control wires had been miswired (right and left reversed). Test pilot walked away. "Sort of an embarrassment."

id: case:BMW i8 carbon fiber composite quality assessment
cluster_id: BMW i8 carbon fiber composite quality assessment
content:
BMW i8 carbon fiber composite quality assessment Tom's former student Chris (polymers thesis) bought a discounted BMW i8 (~$100K vs. $140K list) and judged the carbon fiber resin transfer molding would never pass aerospace QA. "Low quality, high cost material. But they've innovated."

## Figures referenced

id: case:Wang Laboratories 4K minicomputer (early-1970s MIT lab purchase)
cluster_id: Wang Laboratories 4K minicomputer (early-1970s MIT lab purchase)
content: Wang Laboratories 4K minicomputer (early-1970s MIT lab purchase) Opening anecdote about the cost of memory in the early 1970s — $4,000 for 4K of storage, used to set up the contrast with modern computing.

id: case:Belmar portable hardness tester startup (frictional-sliding yield-strength field instrument)
cluster_id: Belmar portable hardness tester startup (frictional-sliding yield-strength field instrument)
content: Belmar portable hardness tester startup (frictional-sliding yield-strength field instrument) Belmar's own NSF-supported startup, used as the live case material for his portion of the course. Revenue grew from $200K (2016) to $500K (2017) to projected $1-2M (2018).

id: case:SBIR small-business research mandate (10% federal R&D set-aside, ~1990–present)
cluster_id: SBIR small-business research mandate (10% federal R&D set-aside, ~1990–present)
content: SBIR small-business research mandate (10% federal R&D set-aside, ~1990–present) Tom frames SBIR as the institutional backdrop for Belmar's NSF-supported startup. Notes Congressional finding that new jobs come from small companies, hence the 10% set-aside.

id: case:Jesús del Alamo / Joel Moses "promised land" letter
cluster_id: Jesús del Alamo / Joel Moses "promised land" letter
content: Jesús del Alamo / Joel Moses "promised land" letter MIT-administration humor anecdote. Joel Moses, then head of EE, wrote the offer letter to Jesús del Alamo and signed it "Moses."

cluster_id: Engineering Council / daycare-center joke
content: Engineering Council / daycare-center joke Used to set up the "you're right too" rabbi parable in §3.p8. The only time Tom saw Joel Moses not laugh at a joke.

cluster_id: You're right too" rabbi parable
content: You're right too" rabbi parable Tom uses the parable to defuse the student's contradiction about whether this is a half-semester or full-semester course. ("You're right" / "You're right" / "You're right too.")

id: case:Eagar TQM origin story — Chipman Room undergraduate exchange
cluster_id: Eagar TQM origin story — Chipman Room undergraduate exchange
content: Eagar TQM origin story — Chipman Room undergraduate exchange Tom recounts asking undergraduates ~20-25 years prior what TQM was; one answered "it's BS." Tom's response — "you may be right, but why do top CEOs believe it's a revolution" — frames the entire course this semester.

id: case:École Polytechnique as first engineering school (18th century France)
cluster_id: École Polytechnique as first engineering school (18th century France)
content: École Polytechnique as first engineering school (18th century France) Origin of the word "engineer" as "maker of war machines" in French.

id: case:West Point (1797) — first US engineering school
cluster_id: West Point (1797) — first US engineering school
content: West Point (1797) — first US engineering school Until 1845, the commandant of West Point had to come from the Corps of Engineers.

id: case:Rensselaer Polytechnic (1823) — coining of civil engineering
cluster_id: Rensselaer Polytechnic (1823) — coining of civil engineering
content: Rensselaer Polytechnic (1823) — coining of civil engineering Origin of the term "civil engineering" and why Course One at MIT carries that designation.

id: case:MIT founding (1861/1863/1865) and Course One/Two/Three numbering origin
cluster_id: MIT founding (1861/1863/1865) and Course One/Two/Three numbering origin
content: MIT founding (1861/1863/1865) and Course One/Two/Three numbering origin Morrill Act, land-grant status, doors opening 1865. Course One = Civil (only non-military engineering known), Course Two = Mechanical (William Barton Rogers's "mechanical arts"), Course Three = geology and mining (Metallurgy added 1883).

id: case:Harvard attempts to acquire MIT (1873–1917) and Gordon McKay trust Supreme Court ruling
cluster_id: Harvard attempts to acquire MIT (1873–1917) and Gordon McKay trust Supreme Court ruling
content: Harvard attempts to acquire MIT (1873–1917) and Gordon McKay trust Supreme Court ruling Three Harvard attempts; 1914–1917 students received dual degrees; Massachusetts Supreme Court blocked the merger ruling McKay trust funds could not be used to purchase MIT.

content: Harvard Business School founding (1921, Allston) — Carnegie land gift, Frederick W. Taylor faculty Carnegie's $100K land purchase, 1921 opening, Taylor as industrial-management/industrial-engineering founder. Used to argue Harvard's engineering ambitions are old, not new.

id: case:Naval ship recuperator heat exchanger failure
cluster_id: Naval ship recuperator heat exchanger failure
content: Naval ship recuperator heat exchanger failure $100 million Navy program (early 1990s), Rolls-Royce-built room-sized brazed stainless steel heat exchanger for preheating destroyer/frigate combustion air. Designed for 100,000 hours; failed in two minutes. Cause: 2D finite element model assumed symmetric gas flow; asymmetric heating snapped six-inch hardened-steel tie bars. Tom served on the post-mortem team. Teaching point: "wishful thinking is not good engineering."

id: case:Aerospace company gold-nickel braze powder inventory control failure
cluster_id: Aerospace company gold-nickel braze powder inventory control failure
content: Aerospace company gold-nickel braze powder inventory control failure Mid-1970s New England aerospace company. Turbine shroud honeycomb seals brazed with 82Au-18Ni alloy applied from a literal salt shaker (50-oz jars, ~$16,000/jar at $400/oz gold). Brazing supervisor doubled his requisition during a production scale-up, kept the rate after scale-down, and stole one jar/week for 16 months — $1.6M to $2.5M total. Caught by tip, not by controls. Tom hired by the insurance bonding company (not the aerospace contractor, which was on cost-plus) to audit losses. Connecticut thief got one-year sentence; New York middleman six months suspended; NYC fence walked.

id: case:Molybdenum-copper cross-field amplifier radar waveguide braze joint
cluster_id: Molybdenum-copper cross-field amplifier radar waveguide braze joint
content: Molybdenum-copper cross-field amplifier radar waveguide braze joint Brief reference back to a prior lecture's case. 82Au-18Ni braze of Mo to Cu formed Ni3Mo intermetallic, snapping at five degrees of bend. Reformulated to a low-Ni transient-liquid-phase braze (3% Ni, mostly Cu) — eliminated intermetallics, allowed 180° hairpin bend.

id: case:San Diego vacuum brazing furnace zinc contamination disaster
cluster_id: San Diego vacuum brazing furnace zinc contamination disaster
content: San Diego vacuum brazing furnace zinc contamination disaster $2M brazing furnace contaminated when wrong (Zn-bearing) braze alloy was run. Attempted recovery by raising furnace temperature to vaporize Zn out; instead redistributed Zn from hot zones to cooler water-cooled walls. Recovery attempt destroyed the furnace.

cluster_id: Aluminum radiator field brazing development
content: Aluminum radiator field brazing development Pre-1980, automotive radiators were Cu, field-repairable by mechanics with propane torches. All-Al radiators (e.g., Corvette) required factory brazing only. Around 1980, Alcan Aluminum developed a fluoride-based field-brazable flux for Al. Result: industry-wide transition Cu → Al for radiators.

id: case:Louisiana polymer laboratory production scaling anecdote
cluster_id: Louisiana polymer laboratory production scaling anecdote
content: Louisiana polymer laboratory production scaling anecdote Standalone parable. Chemical company's order for 10g of a novel polymer triggers a graduate-student-orders-from-third-party-who-orders-from-graduate-student Ponzi loop. Illustrates that "commercially available" can be a recursive fiction for boutique materials.

content: GE 1950s vacuum tube laser repair Earliest commercial laser welding application. Used to illustrate that any new heat source gets tried for welding.

id: case:Naval Surface Warfare Center particle beam weapon program
cluster_id: Naval Surface Warfare Center particle beam weapon program
content: Naval Surface Warfare Center particle beam weapon program Post-Cold-War repurposing question — could relativistic electron beams weld submarines? Tom's answer: too much power, too much shielding, not practical. Used to illustrate the upper end of the heat-intensity scale and the limits of "just throw more energy at it."

id: case:*figure, not a case* — framing physics anchor for the lecture
cluster_id: *figure, not a case* — framing physics anchor for the lecture
content: *figure, not a case* — framing physics anchor for the lecture q = -k∇T. The mathematical backbone of the entire one-dimensional heat-intensity argument.

cluster_id: World Trade Center collapse article
content: World Trade Center collapse article Tom's 2001 article (written three weeks after 9/11) used as a handout to teach flame chemistry. The teaching point: steel did not melt — it can barely be melted with oxy-acetylene in air. Bessemer's 1856 process exists *because* melting steel is hard.

cluster_id: MAPP gas discontinuation
content: MAPP gas discontinuation Live torch demonstration comparing C₃H₈ (propane) vs C₃H₄ (MAPP) — MAPP heats faster, steel reaches red heat first. Used to illustrate enthalpy-of-reaction effect on flame temperature. Side teaching: MAPP no longer manufactured (EPA closure of Chicago plant ~2011); plumbers now use propylene C₃H₆ in yellow cylinders.

id: case:Elihu Thomson invention of resistance spot welding
cluster_id: Elihu Thomson invention of resistance spot welding
content: Elihu Thomson invention of resistance spot welding Historical origin of automotive spot welding. Thomson — MIT EE professor, one-year MIT president, GE co-founder with Edison in Lynn, MA. ~380 patents (#2 after Edison's ~400).

id: case:Automotive spot welding (GM and Ford volumes)
cluster_id: Automotive spot welding (GM and Ford volumes)
content: Automotive spot welding (GM and Ford volumes) 3,000 spot welds per automobile to get 2,000 good ones; nickel per weld → ~$150/car. GM ~50 billion spot welds per year. Aerospace combustor cans: ~$3/weld due to QC overhead.

cluster_id: Lawrence Livermore plutonium weld observation
content: Lawrence Livermore plutonium weld observation Tom shown a weld cross-section with no visible heat affected zone. Material concealed; Tom pinned them down after asking four or five times. Answer: plutonium, very low thermal conductivity. Used to illustrate that HAZ size scales with thermal conductivity.

id: case:Avco Everett 25 kW laser welder development
cluster_id: Avco Everett 25 kW laser welder development
content: Avco Everett 25 kW laser welder development Tom's student hired in early '80s to keep the laser working when customers came for demos — 90% of the time it wasn't running. Used to illustrate that high-power laser welding was a research curiosity, not a production tool, despite the capital investment. Avco facility location: Everett, across from BNY Mellon building.

id: case:Naval Research Laboratory 25 kW laser welder
cluster_id: Naval Research Laboratory 25 kW laser welder
content: Naval Research Laboratory 25 kW laser welder First non-classified 25 kW laser welder in the country, mid-1970s. Cited as a Navy investment that didn't pan out economically because shipyard work lacks both aerospace value-add and automotive volume.

id: case:Ford catalytic converter electron beam welding
cluster_id: Ford catalytic converter electron beam welding
content: Ford catalytic converter electron beam welding Six out-of-vacuum EB welders at Ford sealing stainless-steel clamshell converters around ceramic filters. Speed ~60 cm/s. Used as the canonical automotive high-volume EB case. Maintenance nightmare on out-of-vacuum head (deferred to later lecture). Ford used six Westinghouse out-of-vacuum EB machines to weld stainless steel clamshells on catalytic converters — would have needed ~200 gas tungsten arc stations for equivalent throughput. Maintenance was a nightmare (the German-trained engineer who pitched it; the Ford plant manager who would "pull out a knife" at the mention of the technology). Ford eventually abandoned.

id: case:GE titanium compressor case EB porosity (the acetone case)
cluster_id: GE titanium compressor case EB porosity (the acetone case)
content: GE titanium compressor case EB porosity (the acetone case) Extended teaching case (~9 minutes, the longest narrative unit of the lecture). Two $30K titanium rings welded circumferentially in a chamber half the size of the room. Persistent porosity. Tom diagnoses: industrial-grade acetone (oil-contaminated, demonstrated via Newton's rings on a glass slide) + dust falling on the joint surface in the welding room. Fix: reagent-grade acetone. Savings: $500K/year. Tom: no credit, no payment, no letter of commendation; engineer Lyle got a letter.

id: case:GE SWAC (Spot Welding Adaptive Control) failure
cluster_id: GE SWAC (Spot Welding Adaptive Control) failure
content: GE SWAC (Spot Welding Adaptive Control) failure GE Research Schenectady spent $7M over 5-6 years developing adaptive feedback control for spot welding combustor cans. Tom (with postdoc and grad student, while Tom was in Japan as ONR liaison) demonstrated the algorithm didn't start measuring until 0.2 sec into a process that completes in 0.1 sec — controlling after the fact. Tom was funded as a "whipping boy" to discipline GE Research; he received ~$40-50K against their >$1M/year.

id: case:Bimetallic bandsaw/hacksaw blade electron beam welding
cluster_id: Bimetallic bandsaw/hacksaw blade electron beam welding
content: Bimetallic bandsaw/hacksaw blade electron beam welding Springfield (western Mass) firm with vacuum air feed-through EB system welding strip of high-speed steel (Mo/W tooth alloy) to spring-steel backing strip. Goes back to late '40s/'50s, among the earliest EB applications. Teaching point: niche EB application where the production-volume and value-added economics work.

cluster_id: Alcoa Davenport quench-and-temper failure
content: Alcoa Davenport quench-and-temper failure A plugged water jet on the world's largest aluminum rolling mill at Davenport produced under-quenched streaks in plate that had already been machined onto flying Boeing aircraft. Government-Alcoa-airlines partnership developed an electrical-resistivity NDT probe to find affected wings in service.

cluster_id: Citicorp Tower
content: Citicorp Tower Used to illustrate Tom's thesis that very large failures get resolved cooperatively when senior leadership (John Reed) sets attorneys aside and authorizes at-cost repair work. Tom partially corroborated the story with Reed himself.

cluster_id: Bell Helicopter supplier liability case
content: Bell Helicopter supplier liability case Brief invocation of the Bell chief counsel's rule that you can't sue your suppliers because they'll stop supplying you. Used as a general principle, not developed.

cluster_id: Johnson & Johnson Tylenol recall
content: Johnson & Johnson Tylenol recall The credo-driven recall as a case where doing the right thing improved the business by more than the cost.

id: case:Amtrak catenary wire procurement fraud case
cluster_id: Amtrak catenary wire procurement fraud case
content: Amtrak catenary wire procurement fraud case A British contractor on the Amtrak Northeast Corridor electrification project tried to install a sub-spec copper wire (Rome, NY) to capture margin on a fixed-cost contract, told the federal government no other supplier existed, and was caught when the FBI walked passports off the executive team after a mediation Tom helped resolve. The Providence test track shows the inferior wire arcing on the train pass.

id: case:Destroyer rudder steel preheating logistics case
cluster_id: Destroyer rudder steel preheating logistics case
content: Destroyer rudder steel preheating logistics case Student in the class describes welding thick destroyer rudder steel where preheat made the work environment an oven.

cluster_id: USS Cole
content: USS Cole Cited as another case where the repair cost exceeded new-build cost, for strategic-signaling reasons — the US didn't want to concede the loss of a capital ship.

id: case:Naval Research Lab HY80 laser welding study
cluster_id: Naval Research Lab HY80 laser welding study
content: Naval Research Lab HY80 laser welding study Early-1980s NRL finding that laser welding HY-80 vaporized inclusions and gave better toughness — used to argue that ultra-clean steel resists hydrogen cracking, but isn't producible at tonnage scale.

id: case:America's Cup yacht keel beam — 4340 steel welding procedure
cluster_id: America's Cup yacht keel beam — 4340 steel welding procedure
content: America's Cup yacht keel beam — 4340 steel welding procedure Tom's consulting case with Prof. Jerry Ingram (MIT Course 13) on a David Koch–funded America's Cup yacht. Four-inch HY-80 centerboard was bending in sea trials; Tom developed a 4340 welding procedure with 600°F preheat. Used to teach the cost/weldability tradeoff in high-strength alloy steels.

id: case:USS Sea Wolf submarine high-side weld chemistry and HY-100 cracking
cluster_id: USS Sea Wolf submarine high-side weld chemistry and HY-100 cracking
content: USS Sea Wolf submarine high-side weld chemistry and HY-100 cracking Sea Wolf welding wire chemistry was on the high side of every alloying-element range, producing weld metal that behaved like HY-130 rather than HY-100. Cracking resulted. Repair required 400°F preheat with welders in cooled "blue jelly suits"; $500K hull required $2B repair.

id: case:Inland Steel HSLA development and Navy / Japan technology transfer
cluster_id: Inland Steel HSLA development and Navy / Japan technology transfer
content: Inland Steel HSLA development and Navy / Japan technology transfer Inland Steel pioneered water-spray cooling for HSLA sheet in the early 1960s but couldn't sell it to automakers. Japanese steel mills applied the technique to shipbuilding plate (sweetheart deal with shipyards). Tom's 1980s Navy-sponsored ONR trip to Japan led to $100M of Title III funding for Lukens Steel's HSLA plate line in the 1990s.

id: case:Quonset Point submarine sections and Soviet satellite reconnaissance
cluster_id: Quonset Point submarine sections and Soviet satellite reconnaissance
content: Quonset Point submarine sections and Soviet satellite reconnaissance Submarine hull sections fabricated indoors or under tarps at Quonset Point because Soviet satellites could measure wall thickness from space, revealing classified diving depth. Used as an aside about how hull thickness encodes operational capability.

id: case:1920s steel bridge repair consulting (MTA/MGH station)
cluster_id: 1920s steel bridge repair consulting (MTA/MGH station)
content: 1920s steel bridge repair consulting (MTA/MGH station) Consulting work for a Boston civil engineering company on a 1920s-vintage steel structure with no ASTM spec. Tom's procedure: get drillings analyzed for composition + thickness, match against Stout & Doty's table of 200 steels, retrieve welding procedure. Used to teach that being-an-expert is sometimes just knowing where to look.

id: case:Fire sprinkler system plastic pipe failures
cluster_id: Fire sprinkler system plastic pipe failures
content: Fire sprinkler system plastic pipe failures Plastic sprinkler pipes cracking due to biocide polymer leaching from steel pipes into stagnant water. Used to extend the previous lecture's theme on material substitution failures in fluid-conveyance systems.

id: case:Turbine blade cooling and thermal barrier coatings
cluster_id: Turbine blade cooling and thermal barrier coatings
content: Turbine blade cooling and thermal barrier coatings Internal air cooling above the melting point of the alloy; zirconium oxide TBCs as the only ceramic matching the CTE of nickel; $5,000-per-blade cost driven by EB vapor deposition.

id: case:Air Force engine research committee and Mach 17 / National Aerospace Plane
cluster_id: Air Force engine research committee and Mach 17 / National Aerospace Plane
content: Air Force engine research committee and Mach 17 / National Aerospace Plane Tom's service on an Air Force engine-research advisory committee (~2005) where the Mach 17 air-breathing strike requirement was justified by the bin Laden ordnance-reach problem. Used to teach the divergence of military and civilian engine technology, and the implausibility of the National Aerospace Plane copper-skin / liquid-hydrogen design.

cluster_id: Niobium silicide intermetallics (Air Force research)
content: Niobium silicide intermetallics (Air Force research) Higher melting point (~2000°C) but unsolved brittleness problem; Tom's dismissive close ("I'm not invested in that one right now").

cluster_id: Polyurethane insulation fires in homes
content: Polyurethane insulation fires in homes Exothermic polymerization of polyurethane sprayed too thickly (more than 2 inches) self-ignites. Demonstrated experimentally by Tom's group with cast blocks. Codes now restrict layer thickness.

id: case:Roman concrete longevity and volcanic ash chemistry
cluster_id: Roman concrete longevity and volcanic ash chemistry
content: Roman concrete longevity and volcanic ash chemistry 2,000-year durability of Roman concrete vs. 100–200-year modern concrete, attributed to volcanic ash chemistry. Source for student papers.

cluster_id: Adobe construction with manure binder (Mexico)
content: Adobe construction with manure binder (Mexico) Past student project on traditional adobe in Mexico — straw plus manure (the manure repels flies, but the house smells for a few years).

cluster_id: Bessemer converter invention (1856)
content: Bessemer converter invention (1856) Henry Bessemer in 1856 develops air-blown cast-iron conversion to steel, enabling the Carnegie steel era.

id: case:Andrew Carnegie steel empire and philanthropy
cluster_id: Andrew Carnegie steel empire and philanthropy
content: Andrew Carnegie steel empire and philanthropy Carnegie's rise via Bessemer steel, his quote ("Take away my people, leave my factories..."), his philanthropy (Carnegie libraries, Carnegie Mellon), juxtaposed with Rockefeller [misspoken as "Roosevelt"] handing out dimes. Tom's grandfather's role at the University of Chattanooga briefly invoked.

cluster_id: Linz BOF development (Austria)
content: Linz BOF development (Austria) 1950s Linz, Austria — replaced air-blown Bessemer with pure-oxygen blow using Linde liquefaction. 300 tons of steel in 20 minutes vs. 24–48 hours in open hearth. By the 1970s had taken over the global industry. U.S. Steel built the last open hearth in the early 70s — "they were stupid to build that one."

cluster_id: U.S. Steel's last open hearth
content: U.S. Steel's last open hearth Built in the early 1970s when the BOF had already won; Tom's verdict: "they were stupid to build that one."

id: case:LNG tanker tail shaft fatigue failure, Philippine Sea (1985)
cluster_id: LNG tanker tail shaft fatigue failure, Philippine Sea (1985)
content: LNG tanker tail shaft fatigue failure, Philippine Sea (1985) Illustration of an internal forging defect originating in the as-cast structure of a great-big forging blank: solidification weakness at the centerline gets carried through forging, then propagates as a fatigue crack. Ship stopped dead with a full cargo of LNG in the Philippine Sea.

id: case:Lou Gerstner IBM building access incident
cluster_id: Lou Gerstner IBM building access incident
content: Lou Gerstner IBM building access incident First day as CEO, Gerstner can't get into the building (no ID); when finally inside, turns off the PowerPoint projector mid-meeting and asks executives to "just talk about your business." Tom uses this as the centerpiece of his anti-PowerPoint argument, sourced from Tufte.

id: case:IBM Customer Driven Quality MIT faculty training week (1990s))
cluster_id: IBM Customer Driven Quality MIT faculty training week (1990s))
content: IBM Customer Driven Quality MIT faculty training week (1990s)) Mid-1990s, when Tom was department head. MIT paired with IBM as part of an industry-elite-universities TQM initiative. Seventy-five MIT faculty spent a week at IBM's executive training center on the Hudson. The episode includes the 410K→320K headcount story and Tom's question about whether eliminating 90,000 middle managers revealed more problems escalating (answer: no).

cluster_id: Vera Kistiakowsky quantum mechanics course
content: Vera Kistiakowsky quantum mechanics course The night-before-final pedagogical epiphany — Tom skimmed the textbook for high points, finished a three-hour final in 80 minutes, got an A. The origin story for Tom's "guess my lecture" method and his abandonment of note-taking.

id: case:Paul Gray on MIT pace and pressure (retirement reflection)
cluster_id: Paul Gray on MIT pace and pressure (retirement reflection)
content: Paul Gray on MIT pace and pressure (retirement reflection) Quoted as supporting the "flexibility and stress-free environment" theme: Gray's retirement-era admission that one of his big disappointments was not having reduced MIT's pace and pressure.

id: case:General Motors MIT distance education welding course (late 1980s)
cluster_id: General Motors MIT distance education welding course (late 1980s)
content: General Motors MIT distance education welding course (late 1980s) Tom's first videotaped course, ~30 years prior to 2018. Thirteen-to-fifteen GM employees enrolled as MIT special students. The Detroit-trip discovery that the students were rewinding-and-replaying the tapes, which is what made Tom realize the medium had pedagogical value. Linked forward to Stanford's "tutored video instruction" finding.

cluster_id: Stanford tutored video instruction (1980s)
content: Stanford tutored video instruction (1980s) Cited as parallel to Tom's GM experience — Stanford found that students taking courses via tutored video instruction outperformed live-class students, attributed to the replay capability.

Used as one of last spring's three live modules.
